explanation: Both keep two positions in one structure and move them under a rule, replacing a nested loop with one pass. That shape recurs far beyond linked lists.

prompt: Python's list and JavaScript's Array are dynamic arrays rather than linked lists. What does that tell you?
optionA: Language designers judged indexed access and cache behaviour to matter more in ordinary code
optionB: Linked lists cannot be implemented in those languages
optionC: Linked lists are only genuinely useful in languages with manual memory management
optionD: Dynamic arrays have better complexity for every operation
correctAnswerText: Language designers judged indexed access and cache behaviour to matter more in ordinary code
explanation: Insertion into the middle is genuinely worse on an array; the designers took that trade knowingly, because reading by position is what most code actually does.

prompt: What does sorting a collection produce?
optionA: A collection with duplicate items removed
optionB: The same items grouped by how often they appear
optionC: The same items arranged in a defined order
optionD: A collection reduced to its distinct values
correctAnswerText: The same items arranged in a defined order
explanation: Sorting rearranges; it never adds or removes anything. Removing duplicates and grouping are separate operations that are often performed alongside it.

prompt: What does bubble sort do on each pass?
optionA: Finds the smallest remaining item and moves it to the front
optionB: Inserts each item into its place among those already sorted
optionC: Compares neighbouring items and swaps any that are out of order
optionD: Splits the collection in half and sorts each half
correctAnswerText: Compares neighbouring items and swaps any that are out of order
explanation: Neighbour comparison and swapping is bubble sort. The other three describe selection sort, merge sort and insertion sort respectively.

prompt: What does selection sort do on each pass?
optionA: Divides the collection around a chosen pivot value
optionB: Merges two already-sorted halves into one
optionC: Swaps every neighbouring pair that is out of order
optionD: Finds the smallest remaining item and places it at the end of the sorted part
correctAnswerText: Finds the smallest remaining item and places it at the end of the sorted part
explanation: It selects the minimum from what is left, which is where the name comes from. It always performs the same number of comparisons, whatever the input order.

prompt: What is the typical cost of bubble, selection and insertion sort?
optionA: Linear — proportional to the number of items
optionB: Quadratic — proportional to the square of the number of items
optionC: Constant — independent of the number of items
optionD: Logarithmic — proportional to the logarithm of the number of items
correctAnswerText: Quadratic — proportional to the square of the number of items
explanation: All three compare roughly every item against every other. Doubling the input multiplies the work by about four, which is why none of them is used at scale.

prompt: What is the cost of merge sort and of a well-implemented quicksort on typical input?
optionA: Linear in the number of items
optionB: Logarithmic in the number of items
optionC: n squared
optionD: n log n
correctAnswerText: n log n
explanation: Both halve the problem repeatedly and do linear work at each level. No comparison-based sort can do better in general, which is a proven bound rather than a current limitation.

prompt: What does it mean for a sort to be stable?
optionA: It never crashes, whatever the input
optionB: Items comparing equal keep the order they had before sorting
optionC: It produces exactly the same result on every single run
optionD: It always takes the same amount of time
correctAnswerText: Items comparing equal keep the order they had before sorting
explanation: Stability is about ties keeping their relative order. It matters whenever a second sort is applied on top of a first one.

prompt: What does merge sort do?
optionA: Partitions the collection around a pivot and recurses on each side
optionB: Places each item into a bucket and sorts the buckets
optionC: Repeatedly swaps neighbouring items until none are out of order
optionD: Splits the collection in half, sorts each half, then merges the two
correctAnswerText: Splits the collection in half, sorts each half, then merges the two
explanation: Split, sort, merge — the classic divide and conquer. Partitioning around a pivot is quicksort, which is a different division of the same idea.

prompt: What does quicksort do?
optionA: Selects the minimum item on each pass and moves it forward
optionB: Counts how many times each value appears and then rebuilds the whole collection
optionC: Repeatedly merges pairs of sorted runs until one remains
optionD: Chooses a pivot, puts smaller items on one side and larger on the other, then recurses
correctAnswerText: Chooses a pivot, puts smaller items on one side and larger on the other, then recurses
explanation: Partitioning around a pivot puts that one item in its final place and leaves two smaller problems. The counting option describes counting sort.

prompt: What does it mean for a sort to work in place?
optionA: It needs only a small fixed amount of extra memory beyond the collection
optionB: It leaves the original collection unchanged
optionC: It can be stopped and resumed later without losing any progress
optionD: It sorts the items where they are stored on disk
correctAnswerText: It needs only a small fixed amount of extra memory beyond the collection
explanation: In place means no second copy of the data. Leaving the original unchanged is the opposite — that requires allocating a copy.

prompt: In production code, what should you normally use to sort a collection?
optionA: Bubble sort, because it is the simplest to verify
optionB: The language's built-in sort
optionC: Whichever algorithm the team knows best
optionD: A hand-written quicksort tuned to the data
correctAnswerText: The language's built-in sort
explanation: Built-in sorts are hybrid, heavily optimised and thoroughly tested. Writing your own is worth it only for a constraint the library genuinely cannot meet.

prompt: After one full pass of bubble sort over [5, 1, 4, 2], what is the arrangement?
explanation: Each pass carries the largest remaining value to the end, so 5 arrives at the back and the rest shift down one. One pass rarely finishes the job.

prompt: After one pass of selection sort over [5, 1, 4, 2], which item is certainly in its final place?
optionA: None — selection sort places nothing until the end
optionB: The largest, now at the end
optionC: The pivot, now in the middle
optionD: The smallest, now at the front
correctAnswerText: The smallest, now at the front
explanation: Selection sort finds the minimum and puts it first, so that position is settled. Bubble sort is the one that settles the largest at the back.

prompt: A quadratic sort takes one second on 10,000 items. Roughly how long on 20,000?
optionA: About four seconds
optionB: About sixteen seconds
optionC: About one second
optionD: About two seconds
correctAnswerText: About four seconds
explanation: Doubling the input quadruples quadratic work. An n log n sort would take a little over twice as long, which is the practical difference between the two classes.

prompt: Orders are sorted by date, then by customer with a stable sort. What is the result?
optionA: Grouped by customer, with the dates in an arbitrary order
optionB: Sorted by date only, because the second sort undoes the first
optionC: Grouped by customer, and within each customer still in date order
optionD: Sorted by customer and date combined into one key
correctAnswerText: Grouped by customer, and within each customer still in date order
explanation: A stable sort preserves the earlier ordering among ties, which is what makes sorting by successive keys work. An unstable sort would scramble the dates.

prompt: Insertion sort on an already-sorted collection costs:
optionA: The same as on random input, since the comparisons are fixed
optionB: Quadratic time, because the algorithm cannot detect the order
optionC: n log n, matching the efficient sorts
optionD: Linear time, because each item is compared once and not moved
correctAnswerText: Linear time, because each item is compared once and not moved
explanation: Each item is already in place, so one comparison settles it. This is why insertion sort is used inside hybrid library sorts for small or nearly ordered runs.

prompt: What is quicksort's worst-case cost?
optionA: Linear, when the input is already sorted
optionB: n log n, the same as its typical case
optionC: Logarithmic, because the problem halves itself at each step
optionD: Quadratic, when the pivot repeatedly splits off almost nothing
correctAnswerText: Quadratic, when the pivot repeatedly splits off almost nothing
explanation: A pivot that is always the smallest or largest leaves one partition nearly empty, so the depth becomes n rather than log n. Merge sort has no such case.

prompt: What does merge sort need that quicksort does not?
optionA: The items to be comparable with each other
optionB: Extra memory proportional to the size of the collection
optionC: A randomly chosen pivot at every level of recursion
optionD: The collection to be held in a linked list
correctAnswerText: Extra memory proportional to the size of the collection
explanation: Merging writes into a second buffer, so the space cost is linear. Quicksort partitions within the existing array and needs only the recursion stack.

prompt: What does a comparator function supplied to a sort do?
optionA: Removes items that compare equal to each other
optionB: Decides how many items to compare on each pass
optionC: Chooses which sorting algorithm will be used
optionD: Tells the sort which of two items should come first
correctAnswerText: Tells the sort which of two items should come first
explanation: The comparator defines the order; the algorithm is the library's choice. Every sort of objects by a field is a comparator being supplied.

prompt: Why can no comparison-based sort beat n log n in general?
optionA: Because every known algorithm has been tested and none is faster
optionB: Because computers can only compare two items at a time
optionC: Because memory access rather than comparison is the limiting factor on modern hardware
optionD: Each comparison yields one bit, and distinguishing every possible ordering needs about n log n of them
correctAnswerText: Each comparison yields one bit, and distinguishing every possible ordering needs about n log n of them
explanation: It is an information-theoretic proof about how many orderings must be told apart, not an observation about current algorithms. Sorts that beat it do not compare items.

prompt: Counting sort can run in linear time. What does it require?
optionA: The collection to be already nearly sorted
optionB: Keys from a small known range of integers
optionC: The collection to fit entirely in cache
optionD: A comparator that runs in constant time
correctAnswerText: Keys from a small known range of integers
explanation: It counts occurrences of each possible key, so the range must be small enough to index. It escapes the n log n bound precisely by not comparing items.

prompt: A collection is searched many times. When is sorting it first worthwhile?
optionA: Only when the items are numbers rather than text
optionB: Never — searching is always cheaper than sorting
optionC: When the sort cost is repaid by many later logarithmic searches
optionD: Whenever the collection holds more than a hundred items
correctAnswerText: When the sort cost is repaid by many later logarithmic searches
explanation: Sorting is paid once and each later search becomes logarithmic rather than linear. For a single search it is pure loss, and a hash map is often better than either.

prompt: Code sorts a list of a million values to find the largest. What is wrong with it?
optionA: One pass finds the largest in linear time; sorting does far more work than asked
optionB: Nothing at all, because sorting is the standard approach to a problem like this
optionC: The sort will exhaust memory on a list that size
optionD: Sorting cannot find a maximum reliably
correctAnswerText: One pass finds the largest in linear time; sorting does far more work than asked
explanation: Sorting answers a much bigger question than the one asked. This is among the commonest avoidable inefficiencies in real code.

prompt: The ten largest of a million values are needed. What is better than sorting everything?
optionA: Keeping a heap of the ten best seen so far, in one pass
optionB: Sorting twice and comparing the two results
optionC: Sorting in descending order instead of ascending
optionD: Sorting the first thousand and taking the top ten from those
correctAnswerText: Keeping a heap of the ten best seen so far, in one pass
explanation: A heap of fixed size makes the pass proportional to n log 10 rather than n log n. Sorting a sample gives an answer that is simply wrong.

prompt: In which situation does stability genuinely matter?
optionA: Sorting by a second key while wanting the first key's order preserved among ties
optionB: Sorting a collection that is already fully ordered
optionC: Sorting a collection of unique integers into ascending order
optionD: Sorting a collection where every item compares differently from every other one
correctAnswerText: Sorting by a second key while wanting the first key's order preserved among ties
explanation: With no ties there is nothing for stability to preserve, so it is irrelevant in the other three. It matters exactly where equal keys exist and their prior order carries meaning.

prompt: Memory is tight and the collection nearly fills it. Which sort suits?
optionA: An in-place sort such as heapsort or quicksort
optionB: Merge sort, because it is the most predictable
optionC: Any of them — sorting does not affect memory use
optionD: Counting sort, because it uses no comparisons
correctAnswerText: An in-place sort such as heapsort or quicksort
explanation: Merge sort needs a second buffer the size of the data, which is exactly what is unavailable. Counting sort needs space proportional to the key range instead.

prompt: Library sorts often switch to insertion sort for small sub-problems. Why?
optionA: It is the only sort that works correctly on very small inputs
optionB: It guarantees stability where the main algorithm cannot
optionC: Its low overhead beats the recursion cost once the piece is small
optionD: It uses less memory than the main algorithm needs
correctAnswerText: Its low overhead beats the recursion cost once the piece is small
explanation: Asymptotic advantage does not apply at ten items, where the constant factors dominate. The switch is measured rather than theoretical.

prompt: Records must be ordered by department, then by salary within each. What is the usual approach?
optionA: Sort by department, then sort each group separately by salary
optionB: Sort by salary, then by department, relying on instability
optionC: Concatenate the two fields into one string and sort that
optionD: One comparator that compares department first and salary only on a tie
correctAnswerText: One comparator that compares department first and salary only on a tie
explanation: A single comparator expresses the whole ordering in one pass. Concatenating fields breaks as soon as a numeric field is involved, since "100" sorts before "20" as text.

prompt: A file far larger than memory must be sorted. What is the standard approach?
optionA: Load the file one line at a time and use insertion sort on it
optionB: Compress the file until it fits in memory
optionC: Sort it in chunks that fit, write them out, then merge the sorted chunks
optionD: Sort it in place on disk with quicksort
correctAnswerText: Sort it in chunks that fit, write them out, then merge the sorted chunks
explanation: External merge sort works because merging needs only the front of each run in memory at once. It is why merge sort remains important despite its space cost.

prompt: Rows are fetched from a database and sorted in application code. When is that the wrong choice?
optionA: Only when more than a million rows are involved
optionB: Only when the application happens to be written in a slow language
optionC: Never — sorting in the application is more flexible
optionD: Almost always — the database can sort using an index and return fewer rows
correctAnswerText: Almost always — the database can sort using an index and return fewer rows
explanation: ORDER BY with a matching index may avoid sorting altogether, and paging then transfers far less data. Fetching everything to sort it is a common and costly habit.

prompt: A naive quicksort taking the first element as pivot is given already-sorted input. What happens?
optionA: It finishes almost immediately, having detected the order already present
optionB: It performs at its best, because comparisons always succeed
optionC: It produces an incorrectly ordered result
optionD: It degrades to quadratic time, because every partition splits off one item
correctAnswerText: It degrades to quadratic time, because every partition splits off one item
explanation: Sorted input is the worst case for that pivot choice, which is why real implementations choose a median of three or a random pivot.

prompt: A report sorted by date, then by region, shows dates jumbled inside each region. What is the cause?
optionA: The two sorts were applied in the wrong order
optionB: The second sort is not stable, so it did not preserve the date order among ties
optionC: The first sort failed silently and left the dates completely unordered
optionD: The region values compare equal to each other
correctAnswerText: The second sort is not stable, so it did not preserve the date order among ties
explanation: Successive sorting relies on stability. The alternative is a single comparator that handles both keys, which does not depend on the algorithm's properties.

prompt: Sorting the values 2, 10 and 100 gives the order 10, 100, 2. What has happened?
optionA: The sort is unstable and has scrambled the values
optionB: The comparator is reversing the order of the items
optionC: They are being compared as text, where "1" precedes "2"
optionD: The values overflowed during comparison
correctAnswerText: They are being compared as text, where "1" precedes "2"
explanation: Text comparison proceeds character by character. In JavaScript this is the default for Array.sort, which catches people constantly.

prompt: After sorting a list for display, another part of the program shows items in the wrong order too. Why?
optionA: The sort returned a copy that the display is not using
optionB: The two parts are reading different collections entirely
optionC: The sort worked in place and reordered the shared list itself
optionD: The sort left the original list partially ordered
correctAnswerText: The sort worked in place and reordered the shared list itself
explanation: An in-place sort mutates what it is given, and anything else holding that list sees the change. Sorting a copy is the fix, and it is why many languages offer both.

prompt: A custom comparator sometimes reports that a is before b and also that b is before a. What follows?
optionA: The result is undefined, and some implementations raise or loop
optionB: Only the items involved end up out of order
optionC: The sort takes longer but still produces the right order
optionD: The sort silently falls back to the default ordering
correctAnswerText: The result is undefined, and some implementations raise or loop
explanation: Sorts assume a consistent total order. A contradictory comparator breaks the assumption the algorithm is built on, and the failure is not confined to those items.

prompt: Code sorts a collection inside a loop that runs once per item. What is the cost?
optionA: The same as sorting once, since the result does not change
optionB: n log n, because sorting an ordered collection is free
optionC: n squared log n, because a full sort happens on every iteration
optionD: Linear, because the collection is already sorted after the first pass
correctAnswerText: n squared log n, because a full sort happens on every iteration
explanation: The sort does not become free because the data is ordered — most algorithms still traverse it. Hoisting the sort out of the loop is the fix.

prompt: A recursive quicksort overflows the stack on a large sorted input but not on random input. Why?
optionA: Sorted input needs a great deal more memory to hold the partitions
optionB: The base case is never reached on ordered data
optionC: Bad pivots make the recursion depth proportional to n rather than log n
optionD: Sorted input makes each comparison more expensive
correctAnswerText: Bad pivots make the recursion depth proportional to n rather than log n
explanation: The same degradation that makes it quadratic also makes it deep. Recursing into the smaller partition first bounds the depth even with poor pivots.

prompt: A numeric sort produces an order that looks partly random, and the data contains some missing values. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The missing values are being treated as zero
optionB: The missing values compare as neither less than nor greater than anything
optionC: The comparator is returning a boolean value rather than a number
optionD: The sort is unstable and the missing values are ties
correctAnswerText: The missing values compare as neither less than nor greater than anything
explanation: A value that breaks the ordering relation corrupts the whole result, not just its own position. Missing values should be filtered or given an explicit rank first.

prompt: Code sorts a million rows and then keeps only the fifty that match a filter. What should change?
optionA: Nothing — the sort must happen before the filter is applied
optionB: Sort in descending order to reach the matches sooner
optionC: Sort twice, once before and once after filtering
optionD: Filter first, so only the matching rows are sorted
correctAnswerText: Filter first, so only the matching rows are sorted
explanation: Filtering first reduces the sort from a million rows to fifty. The order of cheap and expensive operations is one of the easiest performance wins there is.

prompt: A sort is unexpectedly slow, and its comparator performs a database lookup. What is wrong?
optionA: The comparator is being called only once per item
optionB: The comparator runs n log n times, so the lookups dominate everything
optionC: The database simply cannot be queried during a sort operation
optionD: The sort algorithm chosen does not suit database data
correctAnswerText: The comparator runs n log n times, so the lookups dominate everything
explanation: A comparator is called a great many times, so anything expensive inside it is multiplied. Fetching the keys once and sorting those is the standard fix.

prompt: Code assumes a collection is sorted because it usually arrives that way, and occasionally produces wrong results. What is the real defect?
optionA: The collection has grown too large to remain ordered
optionB: An assumption about order that nothing enforces or checks
optionC: The sort algorithm being used is unstable
optionD: The comparator is inconsistent on some inputs
correctAnswerText: An assumption about order that nothing enforces or checks
explanation: An unstated precondition holds until it does not, and the failure appears far from its cause. Either sort it or assert the order, rather than relying on habit.

prompt: Both quicksort and merge sort are n log n typically. What is the real trade between them?
optionA: Quicksort works only on numbers and merge sort on any type
optionB: Quicksort is faster on every possible input, and merge sort is simply the older of the two
optionC: Merge sort is unstable while quicksort preserves ties
optionD: Quicksort sorts in place but has a quadratic worst case; merge sort guarantees n log n but needs extra memory
correctAnswerText: Quicksort sorts in place but has a quadratic worst case; merge sort guarantees n log n but needs extra memory
explanation: Space against worst-case guarantee. Merge sort is also the stable one of the pair, which is the opposite of the third option.

prompt: What is the strongest signal that sorting is the wrong tool for a problem?
optionA: The ordering rule involves more than one field
optionB: The collection contains more than ten thousand items
optionC: The items are objects rather than simple values
optionD: Only a few items from the collection are actually needed
correctAnswerText: Only a few items from the collection are actually needed
explanation: Sorting answers "what is the full order", so needing one item, or the top few, means paying for far more than the question required.

prompt: Sorting algorithms are studied although nobody writes one in production. What is the best justification?
optionA: Hand-written sorts reliably outperform library ones on real production data
optionB: They teach divide and conquer, cost analysis and trade-offs on a problem simple enough to hold in the head
optionC: Library sorts are often wrong and must be replaced
optionD: Interviews are the only place the knowledge is used
correctAnswerText: They teach divide and conquer, cost analysis and trade-offs on a problem simple enough to hold in the head
explanation: The subject is a vehicle for reasoning that transfers everywhere. The claim about library sorts being wrong or slow is false in almost every case.

prompt: The sorts used by Python and Java exploit runs of already-ordered items. What assumption does that reflect?
optionA: Real-world data is rarely in a random order
optionB: Comparison is more expensive than movement
optionC: Users prefer results that arrive gradually
optionD: Ordered runs are cheaper to store in memory
correctAnswerText: Real-world data is rarely in a random order
explanation: Records arrive by date, ids ascend, appended data is ordered. Detecting and merging existing runs makes the common case much faster than worst-case analysis predicts.

prompt: To detect duplicates in a large collection, why might a hash set beat sorting?
optionA: It preserves the original order of the collection
optionB: It detects duplicates that differ slightly in value
optionC: It uses less memory than an in-place sort
optionD: It answers in linear time, where sorting first costs n log n
correctAnswerText: It answers in linear time, where sorting first costs n log n
explanation: Sorting brings duplicates together as a side effect of a more expensive job. A set answers the question directly, at the cost of memory rather than time.

prompt: For twenty items, insertion sort often beats quicksort. What does that illustrate?
optionA: Quicksort is incorrect on small collections
optionB: Insertion sort has a better complexity than quicksort
optionC: Asymptotic complexity describes growth, not the cost at small sizes
optionD: Complexity analysis applies only to recursive algorithms
correctAnswerText: Asymptotic complexity describes growth, not the cost at small sizes
explanation: Constant factors and overhead dominate when n is small, which is exactly why library sorts switch algorithms below a threshold.

prompt: Relying on a library sort being stable is safe only if:
optionA: The same version of the language runtime is used absolutely everywhere
optionB: The collection contains no duplicate keys at all
optionC: The sort is called only once on any collection
optionD: The language guarantees it, rather than the current implementation happening to be stable
correctAnswerText: The language guarantees it, rather than the current implementation happening to be stable
explanation: Some languages guarantee stability and some do not. Depending on an unguaranteed property is a bug waiting for a runtime upgrade to expose it.

prompt: Sorting data spread across many machines, what becomes the dominant cost?
optionA: Choosing which sorting algorithm each individual machine runs
optionB: The number of comparisons each machine performs
optionC: The memory each machine needs for its own portion
optionD: Moving data between machines, rather than the comparisons themselves
correctAnswerText: Moving data between machines, rather than the comparisons themselves
explanation: At that scale the network dominates, which is why distributed sorts partition by key range so each machine can sort locally and the results simply concatenate.

prompt: Why do real quicksort implementations choose the pivot randomly or by median of three?
optionA: It makes the algorithm stable with respect to equal keys
optionB: It makes the quadratic worst case vanishingly unlikely on any particular input
optionC: It reduces the number of comparisons needed to below the n log n bound
optionD: It removes the need for recursion entirely
correctAnswerText: It makes the quadratic worst case vanishingly unlikely on any particular input
explanation: The worst case still exists but no longer corresponds to a predictable input such as sorted data — which also matters where an attacker could supply that input deliberately.

prompt: A collection is read in order constantly and changed occasionally. What is usually better than re-sorting after each change?
optionA: Sorting only the portion that has changed
optionB: Storing it unsorted and then sorting it again on every read
optionC: Sorting it on a timer rather than on every change
optionD: Keeping it ordered as items are inserted, so it is never unsorted
correctAnswerText: Keeping it ordered as items are inserted, so it is never unsorted
explanation: An insertion into an ordered structure costs far less than sorting everything again. That is what a balanced tree or a sorted index does, and it is why databases keep them.

prompt: What is normalisation trying to achieve?
optionA: The smallest possible number of tables
optionB: Each fact stored in exactly one place
optionC: The fastest possible query performance
optionD: Every column holding a numeric value
correctAnswerText: Each fact stored in exactly one place
explanation: One fact, one place. Fewer tables is usually the opposite of normalised, and query speed is frequently traded against it rather than gained from it.

prompt: What is an update anomaly?
optionA: Two users update the same row at the same time
optionB: An update runs more slowly than expected
optionC: One fact must be changed in many rows, and some are missed
optionD: An update fails because a constraint rejects it part way through
correctAnswerText: One fact must be changed in many rows, and some are missed
explanation: Duplicated data must be changed everywhere at once. Missing one leaves the database holding two answers to a single question, neither marked as wrong.

prompt: What is an insert anomaly?
optionA: Inserting a row unexpectedly changes another row
optionB: A fact cannot be recorded because unrelated data is missing
optionC: An insert is rejected because a row with that key already exists
optionD: An insert takes longer as the table grows
correctAnswerText: A fact cannot be recorded because unrelated data is missing
explanation: In a single orders table, a customer who has not ordered cannot be recorded at all. The table can only capture them as a side effect of something else.

prompt: What is a delete anomaly?
optionA: A deleted row reappears after the transaction commits
optionB: A delete is refused because rows in another table still reference it
optionC: Deleting rows makes subsequent queries slower
optionD: Removing one row destroys a fact that had nothing to do with it
correctAnswerText: Removing one row destroys a fact that had nothing to do with it
explanation: Deleting a customer's last order also erases the customer. Two unrelated facts sharing a row means losing one loses the other.

prompt: What does first normal form require?
optionA: Each table relates to exactly one other table
optionB: Each column has a different name from every other
optionC: Each column holds a single value, not a list
optionD: Each table has a numeric primary key
correctAnswerText: Each column holds a single value, not a list
explanation: No repeating groups and no comma-separated lists in a column. A phone_numbers column holding "9876, 9877" breaks it.

prompt: What does a primary key do?
optionA: Orders the rows within the table
optionB: Marks which column is searched most often
optionC: Identifies each row uniquely
optionD: Links the table to its parent table
correctAnswerText: Identifies each row uniquely
explanation: Unique identification. Linking to another table is a foreign key, and ordering is not something a key provides at all.

prompt: What is the main danger of storing the same fact in several places?
optionA: The database file becomes larger than necessary
optionB: Queries must read more rows than they otherwise would need to
optionC: The copies drift apart and the data contradicts itself
optionD: Backups take longer to complete
correctAnswerText: The copies drift apart and the data contradicts itself
explanation: Storage is cheap; disagreement is not. A database holding two different emails for one customer cannot say which is correct.

prompt: Which summary captures the first three normal forms?
optionA: Every column is a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key
optionB: Every table has fewer columns than it has rows
optionC: Every column is indexed and every key is numeric
optionD: Every table is joined to at least one other table through a declared foreign key
correctAnswerText: Every column is a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key
explanation: It gets you to third normal form without the formal vocabulary, which is why it is the version practitioners actually use.

prompt: What is denormalisation?
optionA: Removing constraints so that inserts succeed
optionB: Failing to normalise a schema in the first place
optionC: Splitting a large table into several smaller related ones
optionD: Deliberately duplicating data to make reads faster
correctAnswerText: Deliberately duplicating data to make reads faster
explanation: A deliberate trade, made after measuring, with something keeping the copies correct. Splitting tables is normalisation, which is the opposite.

prompt: What does a foreign key do?
optionA: Points at a row in another table and requires that it exists
optionB: Copies the referenced row into this table whenever it changes
optionC: Makes the column unique across the whole database
optionD: Speeds up joins by storing both rows together
correctAnswerText: Points at a row in another table and requires that it exists
explanation: It is a reference plus a guarantee the target exists. Nothing is copied, and it is what prevents rows pointing at records that have been removed.

prompt: A customers table has a column holding "9876543210, 9876543211". Which rule does this break?
optionA: Second normal form — the column depends on part of the key
optionB: Third normal form — the column depends on another column
optionC: None — a text column may hold any text
optionD: First normal form — a column must hold a single value
correctAnswerText: First normal form — a column must hold a single value
explanation: A list inside a column cannot be queried, constrained or indexed properly. Searching for one number means pattern matching, which is slow and gets partial matches wrong.

prompt: An orders table repeats the customer name and email on every order. What does this cause?
optionA: Two customers can no longer share an email address, even legitimately
optionB: Changing an email means updating every one of that customer's orders
optionC: The email column cannot be indexed
optionD: Orders can no longer be queried by customer
correctAnswerText: Changing an email means updating every one of that customer's orders
explanation: One fact spread across many rows must be changed in all of them. Missing one is how a database ends up holding two emails for one person.

prompt: What decides which columns should move into a separate table?
optionA: Whether they hold text or numbers
optionB: How often they are read by queries
optionC: Which thing they are facts about
optionD: How many distinct values they contain
correctAnswerText: Which thing they are facts about
explanation: A column describing the customer belongs with the customer, not the order. Subject is the question; access frequency belongs to a later, different decision.

prompt: An employees table holds department_id and department_name. Why is that a problem?
optionA: Names should never be stored in the same table as the identifiers they belong to
optionB: Two columns may not both refer to a department
optionC: The department name is a fact about the department, not about the employee
optionD: It is not a problem, because the two columns always agree
correctAnswerText: The department name is a fact about the department, not about the employee
explanation: It depends on the key only indirectly, through the department. Renaming a department then means updating every employee in it.

prompt: A book may have several authors and an author several books. How is this modelled?
optionA: A third table holding pairs of book and author identifiers
optionB: A foreign key from books to authors
optionC: Duplicate book rows, one for each author
optionD: An author_names column on the books table listing each contributor
correctAnswerText: A third table holding pairs of book and author identifiers
explanation: Neither side can hold a single reference, so the relationship becomes its own table. That table can also carry facts about the pairing, such as author order.

prompt: You suspect a duplicated customer name has drifted out of step. How do you find out?
optionA: Look at when each row was last updated
optionB: Compare the number of rows in the two tables against each other
optionC: Check whether the column allows null values
optionD: Count the rows where the two copies of the name disagree
correctAnswerText: Count the rows where the two copies of the name disagree
explanation: A count tells you both that it happened and how widely, which also indicates how long it has been going on. Timestamps rarely survive the kind of update that caused it.

prompt: What does normalising a schema cost?
optionA: The database uses considerably more storage
optionB: Constraints can no longer be enforced
optionC: Inserts become impossible without wrapping them in a transaction
optionD: Queries must join tables to reassemble information
correctAnswerText: Queries must join tables to reassemble information
explanation: The information is spread across tables, so reading it means joining. Normalisation usually reduces storage rather than increasing it.

prompt: An order line stores the price paid, although the product table already holds a price. Is that a normalisation error?
optionA: No, because prices are numbers rather than text
optionB: Yes, unless the two prices are guaranteed to stay equal
optionC: No — the price paid is a fact about the order, not about the product today
optionD: Yes — the price is duplicated and should be read from the product table instead
correctAnswerText: No — the price paid is a fact about the order, not about the product today
explanation: They are two different facts that happen to share a value at one moment. Joining to the product would silently rewrite every historical invoice when a price changed.

prompt: A table has several columns that are null for most rows. What does this often indicate?
optionA: The rows were inserted in the wrong order
optionB: The columns should be given default values instead of nulls
optionC: The table is holding two different kinds of thing
optionD: The table needs an additional index
correctAnswerText: The table is holding two different kinds of thing
explanation: Columns that apply to only some rows usually mean two entities have been merged into one table. Splitting them makes each set of columns required rather than optional.

prompt: When is denormalising defensible?
optionA: Whenever a table grows past a few million rows and its reads begin to slow down
optionB: Whenever a query needs more than two joins
optionC: At design time, to avoid joins later
optionD: After measuring a genuinely slow read, with something keeping the copy correct
correctAnswerText: After measuring a genuinely slow read, with something keeping the copy correct
explanation: It is an optimisation, so it follows measurement. Doing it at design time optimises a problem nobody has yet observed.

prompt: One table holds order_id, customer_name, customer_email, product_name, price. How should it be split?
optionA: Into orders and products only
optionB: Into customers, products, orders and order_items
optionC: Into customers and orders only
optionD: It should stay as one table with an index on order_id
correctAnswerText: Into customers, products, orders and order_items
explanation: Four subjects are present: a customer, a product, an order, and the fact that an order contains a product. Each becomes a table, and the last is where quantity and price paid belong.

prompt: A customer may have several phone numbers. What is the correct structure?
optionA: A phone column on the orders table instead
optionB: One phone column holding the numbers separated by commas
optionC: A phone_numbers table with one row per number, referencing the customer
optionD: Columns phone1, phone2 and phone3 on the customers table, left null if unused
correctAnswerText: A phone_numbers table with one row per number, referencing the customer
explanation: A fact that can repeat becomes its own table. Numbered columns impose an arbitrary limit and leave most of them null.

prompt: A join table pairs students with courses. What should its primary key be?
optionA: Both foreign keys together, so a pairing cannot be recorded twice
optionB: A new auto-generated identifier, since every table should have one
optionC: The student identifier alone
optionD: The course identifier alone
correctAnswerText: Both foreign keys together, so a pairing cannot be recorded twice
explanation: A composite key prevents duplicate enrolments. Either key alone would allow a student one course only, or a course one student.

prompt: A delivery must record where a parcel was actually sent, and customers move house. How?
optionA: Keep a single address table and update it in place
optionB: Join to the customer address table whenever the delivery is displayed or reprinted later
optionC: Store the delivery address on the delivery itself, not only a reference to the customer
optionD: Forbid customers from changing their address once set
correctAnswerText: Store the delivery address on the delivery itself, not only a reference to the customer
explanation: Where it went is a fact about that delivery. Joining to the current address would rewrite history every time somebody moves.

prompt: After normalising, what keeps the tables consistent with each other?
optionA: Foreign key constraints declared in the schema
optionB: Careful code review of every query that writes
optionC: Documentation describing the relationships
optionD: A scheduled job that checks the tables nightly
correctAnswerText: Foreign key constraints declared in the schema
explanation: Constraints apply to every write from every path, including the admin panel and the migration script written next year. The others depend on somebody remembering.

prompt: A single table holds both individual and business customers, with half the columns null for each. What is the usual fix?
optionA: Two completely unrelated tables with no shared columns
optionB: Nulls replaced with empty strings so that no column is ever left unpopulated
optionC: A shared customers table plus a table of the columns specific to each kind
optionD: One table with a type column and all the columns kept nullable
correctAnswerText: A shared customers table plus a table of the columns specific to each kind
explanation: The shared facts stay together and the specific ones move, so each column can be required where it applies. Filling nulls with blanks hides the problem rather than solving it.

prompt: Splitting a live table into two, in what order should the steps run?
optionA: Create the new table and drop the old columns in one transaction
optionB: Create the new table, copy the data, switch the reads, then drop the old columns
optionC: Switch the reads across first, and then create the table that those reads now expect
optionD: Drop the old columns, create the new table, then copy the data
correctAnswerText: Create the new table, copy the data, switch the reads, then drop the old columns
explanation: Each step leaves the system working, which is what allows it to be deployed without downtime and stopped part way if something is wrong.

prompt: How do you find rows referencing a parent that no longer exists?
optionA: Compare the row counts of the two tables
optionB: Inner join to the parent table and count the rows that come back from it
optionC: Left join to the parent and keep the rows where the parent side is null
optionD: Look for null values in the foreign key column
correctAnswerText: Left join to the parent and keep the rows where the parent side is null
explanation: An inner join silently drops exactly the rows you are looking for. A null foreign key is a different case — deliberately no parent, rather than a missing one.

prompt: An order_total column is added to avoid summing the line items. What must accompany it?
optionA: Something that recalculates it whenever a line item changes
optionB: An index on the new column
optionC: A comment in the schema explaining where the column comes from
optionD: A constraint that the total is greater than zero
correctAnswerText: Something that recalculates it whenever a line item changes
explanation: A cached value with nothing maintaining it drifts, and a total that disagrees with its own lines is worse than a slow query. A trigger, or one code path that owns both, is the usual answer.

prompt: A new required column is added to an existing table. In what order must it be done?
optionA: Delete the existing rows and re-insert them with the column populated
optionB: Make it required first so that no bad rows can be inserted meanwhile
optionC: Add it nullable, fill in the existing rows, then make it required
optionD: Add it as required, which fills existing rows with a default
correctAnswerText: Add it nullable, fill in the existing rows, then make it required
explanation: A required column cannot be added while rows violate it. The three-step order is the standard way to add any constraint to a table that already holds data.

prompt: Two screens show different email addresses for one customer. What is the most likely underlying cause?
optionA: One screen is reading from a stale cache
optionB: The email is stored in two tables and only one was updated
optionC: The customer has two accounts in the system
optionD: One screen is formatting the address differently from the other
correctAnswerText: The email is stored in two tables and only one was updated
explanation: Duplicated storage with a partial update is the classic update anomaly. The other explanations are possible but do not leave the database itself holding two answers.

prompt: The business wants to record a supplier who has not yet delivered anything, and the system cannot. What does that reveal?
optionA: The application form for adding a supplier on its own has not been built yet
optionB: The supplier column does not permit null values
optionC: Suppliers exist only as columns on deliveries, with no table of their own
optionD: The deliveries table is missing an index on supplier
correctAnswerText: Suppliers exist only as columns on deliveries, with no table of their own
explanation: An entity that can only be recorded as a side effect of another has no table. This is the insert anomaly, and it usually surfaces as a business request that seems oddly hard.

prompt: Last year's invoices change their totals after a product is repriced. What is the fault?
optionA: The invoice joins to the current product price instead of storing the price paid
optionB: The totals are being recalculated in the application layer each time they are shown
optionC: The product table is missing a history of its prices
optionD: The invoices were never saved after being generated
correctAnswerText: The invoice joins to the current product price instead of storing the price paid
explanation: This is normalisation applied to a fact that is historical rather than current. A price-history table would help but the invoice should hold what was actually charged.

prompt: An order_total column disagrees with the sum of the order lines on some orders. What has happened?
optionA: The total column has the wrong numeric type for the larger values
optionB: The order rows were inserted before their line items
optionC: The line items are being read from a stale replica
optionD: A code path changed the lines without updating the cached total
correctAnswerText: A code path changed the lines without updating the cached total
explanation: A derived value is only as reliable as every path that can invalidate it, and there is usually one nobody remembered. The query that counts disagreeing orders tells you how long it has been happening.

prompt: Two customer rows share an email address, which the business says is impossible. What is missing?
optionA: An index on the email column
optionB: A unique constraint on the email column
optionC: A check that the email is correctly formatted
optionD: A trigger that logs new customer rows
correctAnswerText: A unique constraint on the email column
explanation: A rule everybody believes but nothing enforces is a rule the data will eventually break. An index makes lookups fast without preventing anything.

prompt: A table has columns named field1, extra and notes2. What does that usually indicate?
optionA: The naming convention was changed part way through
optionB: The columns are reserved for future use
optionC: The table was generated automatically from a spreadsheet that nobody has since looked at
optionD: Things were added without a design decision, and their contents are now relied upon
correctAnswerText: Things were added without a design decision, and their contents are now relied upon
explanation: Names that describe nothing mean nobody decided what they hold, yet code now depends on them. Finding out what is actually in them is the first step and usually a surprise.

prompt: Deleting one order removed the customer as well. What was wrong?
optionA: The customer existed only inside the orders table, or the cascade was set the wrong way
optionB: The foreign key from orders to customers was never declared in the schema in the first place
optionC: The delete was run without a transaction
optionD: The customer row was already marked as inactive
correctAnswerText: The customer existed only inside the orders table, or the cascade was set the wrong way
explanation: Either the customer had no independent row, or a cascade was declared on a relationship where the child does not own the parent. Both lose data that nobody asked to delete.

prompt: Displaying one screen requires joining eleven tables. What should be considered?
optionA: Whether the joins should be replaced by several separate queries run in turn
optionB: Whether every table has been given an index
optionC: Whether the database supports that many joins efficiently
optionD: Whether some of those tables represent facts that never vary independently
correctAnswerText: Whether some of those tables represent facts that never vary independently
explanation: Splitting out something with a fixed one-to-one relationship adds a join and buys nothing. Eleven is a prompt to re-examine the model, not automatically a defect.

prompt: A city column holds "Mumbai", "mumbai", "Bombay" and "Mumbai " as separate values. What is the structural cause?
optionA: The column should have been given a longer maximum length
optionB: The column is missing a case-insensitive collation
optionC: The application is not trimming whitespace or normalising case on input
optionD: The city is free text rather than a reference to a table of cities
correctAnswerText: The city is free text rather than a reference to a table of cities
explanation: Trimming and collation treat the symptom. A reference to a cities table makes the invalid values unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

prompt: Two tables hold a customer's phone number and they differ. Which is correct?
optionA: The one in the table that the application happens to write to first when saving
optionB: The schema cannot say — that is precisely the damage duplication does
optionC: The one in the table with the foreign key
optionD: The one in the table updated most recently
correctAnswerText: The schema cannot say — that is precisely the damage duplication does
explanation: Without a designated single source, both are equally authoritative and the database holds a contradiction. Recency is a guess, and the write order is an implementation detail rather than a rule.

prompt: What single question best decides whether an apparently duplicated value is really a normalisation error?
optionA: If the original changes, must this copy change too?
optionB: Do the two values currently hold the same data?
optionC: Was the copy added before or after the original column?
optionD: Is the column indexed in both tables?
correctAnswerText: If the original changes, must this copy change too?
explanation: Yes means one fact in two places. No means two different facts that coincide today — a price paid and a price list, an address delivered to and an address now.

prompt: Why normalise first and denormalise later, rather than designing for reads from the start?
optionA: Denormalisation requires features many databases lack
optionB: A normalised schema cannot hold contradictory data, and only measurement shows what is actually slow
optionC: Denormalised schemas are harder to write queries against once the duplication has spread across many tables
optionD: Normalised schemas always perform better in practice
correctAnswerText: A normalised schema cannot hold contradictory data, and only measurement shows what is actually slow
explanation: Correctness is the property that is expensive to retrofit; speed can be added where it is needed. Designing for imagined load optimises a problem nobody has measured.

prompt: Reporting databases are often deliberately denormalised. Why is that acceptable there?
optionA: Analytics databases cannot perform joins
optionB: The data is too large for a fully normalised schema to be queried effectively
optionC: Reporting queries do not need accurate data
optionD: They are read-only copies, so duplicated values cannot drift out of step
correctAnswerText: They are read-only copies, so duplicated values cannot drift out of step
explanation: The danger of duplication is inconsistent updates, and a read-only copy rebuilt from the source has none. The trade that is reckless in an operational database is sound here.

prompt: Why is a normalisation problem so much more expensive to fix once a system is live?
optionA: Migrations cannot be run without taking the whole system offline for a while
optionB: Live databases cannot have their schemas altered
optionC: The application code cannot be changed after release
optionD: The data has already diverged, so somebody must decide what the truth was
correctAnswerText: The data has already diverged, so somebody must decide what the truth was
explanation: Restructuring is mechanical; reconciling contradictory rows is a business decision, one row at a time, with nothing in the database to say which copy was right.

prompt: Document databases often embed related data rather than referencing it. What does that trade?
optionA: Faster reads of a whole document, against updating every copy of an embedded fact
optionB: Correctness, which document databases cannot provide at all
optionC: Storage space, which embedding always increases substantially
optionD: Query flexibility, since data embedded in a document cannot be filtered or indexed separately
correctAnswerText: Faster reads of a whole document, against updating every copy of an embedded fact
explanation: It is the same trade as denormalising, made structurally. It suits data read as a unit and changed rarely, and it suits a frequently updated shared fact badly.

prompt: Most practitioners stop at third normal form. Why?
optionA: Going further makes the schema impossible to query
optionB: The higher forms apply only to distributed systems
optionC: It removes the anomalies that actually occur, and the higher forms address rarer cases
optionD: The higher forms are not supported by most relational database engines in common use today
correctAnswerText: It removes the anomalies that actually occur, and the higher forms address rarer cases
explanation: Third normal form is where the return diminishes sharply. The higher forms are real and occasionally matter, but the cases they address are uncommon in ordinary business data.

prompt: Why enforce a relationship with a foreign key rather than in application code?
optionA: Foreign keys produce clearer error messages for users than application checks ever do
optionB: Application validation is per code path, and there will be paths nobody remembers
optionC: Foreign keys make the related queries faster
optionD: Application code cannot check whether a row exists
correctAnswerText: Application validation is per code path, and there will be paths nobody remembers
explanation: The admin screen, the bulk import and next year's migration are all paths, and the constraint is the only thing present in all of them. It usually costs a little speed rather than gaining it.

prompt: What does a well-normalised schema communicate to somebody reading it for the first time?
optionA: What the system is about, and which rules the business actually holds
optionB: How much data the system is expected to hold
optionC: Which queries the system runs most often
optionD: How the application code that reads and writes those tables is organised
correctAnswerText: What the system is about, and which rules the business actually holds
explanation: Tables name the entities and constraints state the rules, so the schema is often the clearest statement of the domain anywhere in the system — and the one most likely to be current.

prompt: Which duplicated value is NOT a normalisation problem?
optionA: A customer name repeated on each of their orders
optionB: The tax rate applied to a historical invoice
optionC: A department name repeated on each employee row
optionD: A product description repeated on each order line
correctAnswerText: The tax rate applied to a historical invoice
explanation: The rate charged then must not change when the rate changes now, so it is a separate fact. The other three are single current facts copied across rows.

prompt: Why write the queries a schema must support before finalising the tables?
optionA: The questions expose facts the design cannot answer while it is still cheap to change
optionB: It produces documentation for the development team
optionC: Table names follow naturally from the queries
optionD: The queries determine which indexes and which foreign keys the schema will eventually need
correctAnswerText: The questions expose facts the design cannot answer while it is still cheap to change
explanation: Designing for the data you happen to have rather than the questions you will be asked is the commonest modelling mistake, and it surfaces only once the data exists.

prompt: What is a database transaction?
optionA: A record of every change made to the database over a period
optionB: A connection held open between the application and the database server
optionC: A group of operations that either all take effect or none do
optionD: A single statement that reads or writes exactly one row at a time
correctAnswerText: A group of operations that either all take effect or none do
explanation: All or nothing. The point is that no observer, and no crash, ever sees the half-finished state in between.

prompt: What does atomicity mean?
optionA: Each statement inside the transaction runs in the order it was written
optionB: The whole transaction succeeds or the whole transaction is undone
optionC: Committed changes survive a crash of the database server itself
optionD: Only one transaction may run against the database at any moment
correctAnswerText: The whole transaction succeeds or the whole transaction is undone
explanation: There is no partial outcome. Surviving a crash after commit is durability, and running alone is closer to isolation.

prompt: What does durability mean?
optionA: The change cannot be undone by any later transaction whatsoever
optionB: The transaction can be retried if it fails for any reason
optionC: Once committed, the change survives a crash
optionD: The data remains readable for as long as the table exists
correctAnswerText: Once committed, the change survives a crash
explanation: Commit is a promise. A later transaction may of course change the data again — durability is about crashes, not about permanence.

prompt: What does ROLLBACK do?
optionA: Undoes everything done since the transaction began
optionB: Undoes the most recent statement and leaves the rest in place
optionC: Restores the table to the state of the last backup taken
optionD: Cancels any transactions that are still waiting on a lock
correctAnswerText: Undoes everything done since the transaction began
explanation: Back to the state at BEGIN, in one step. It does not undo statement by statement, and it touches nothing outside this transaction.

prompt: What does isolation mean?
optionA: Tables touched by a transaction are hidden from other queries
optionB: Concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work
optionC: Each transaction runs on a separate connection to the database
optionD: Transactions are executed strictly one after another, never together
correctAnswerText: Concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work
explanation: Uncommitted work stays invisible. Databases run transactions concurrently and use isolation to make the result look as though they had not.

prompt: What is a lock for?
optionA: To prevent unauthorised users from reading a particular table or row
optionB: To keep a row in memory so that reading it again is fast
optionC: To mark a row as read-only until an administrator releases it
optionD: To stop two transactions interfering with the same data at once
correctAnswerText: To stop two transactions interfering with the same data at once
explanation: Locks are about concurrency, not permissions. They are taken and released by the database, usually without the application asking.

prompt: What is a deadlock?
optionA: A query that never completes because the table is too large to scan
optionB: Two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds
optionC: A row that has been locked and never released by its transaction
optionD: A transaction that has been waiting for a lock for a very long time
correctAnswerText: Two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds
explanation: A cycle of waiting that cannot resolve itself. The database detects it and kills one of the transactions, which is why the error arrives quickly.

prompt: What does consistency mean in ACID?
optionA: The database moves from one valid state to another valid state
optionB: Every table is kept in third normal form by the database engine
optionC: All users see identical data at exactly the same moment in time
optionD: The same query returns the same result every time it is executed
correctAnswerText: The database moves from one valid state to another valid state
explanation: Constraints that held before the transaction hold after it. The "everyone sees the same data" sense belongs to distributed systems, not to this letter.

prompt: What happens at COMMIT?
optionA: The changes are queued to be applied when the server is next idle
optionB: The changes are written to disk and the connection is then closed
optionC: The database checks the changes and applies them if they are valid
optionD: The changes become permanent and visible to everyone else
correctAnswerText: The changes become permanent and visible to everyone else
explanation: Permanent and visible, in one step. The connection stays open, and nothing is deferred — that is the promise commit makes.

prompt: Is a single UPDATE statement, run on its own, a transaction?
optionA: Only if it changes more than one row in the table
optionB: No — a transaction requires an explicit BEGIN statement first
optionC: Only if the table it is updating has constraints declared on it
optionD: Yes — the database wraps it in one automatically
correctAnswerText: Yes — the database wraps it in one automatically
explanation: Every statement runs inside a transaction, declared or not. That is why a single UPDATE touching a thousand rows never leaves half of them changed.

prompt: A transfer debits one account and credits another. What does wrapping it in a transaction prevent?
optionA: The balance being read while the transfer is still in progress
optionB: The transfer being applied twice if the request is retried
optionC: Two transfers from the same account running at the same time
optionD: Money leaving one account without arriving in the other
correctAnswerText: Money leaving one account without arriving in the other
explanation: Atomicity rules out the half-completed transfer. Concurrent transfers need isolation, and duplicate requests need an idempotency key — different problems.

prompt: What is a dirty read?
optionA: Reading a change that is later rolled back and never existed
optionB: Reading a row that another transaction is in the middle of deleting
optionC: Reading a row whose values fail the constraints declared on the table
optionD: Reading data that is out of date because a cache was not refreshed
correctAnswerText: Reading a change that is later rolled back and never existed
explanation: You act on a number that was never true. Most databases prevent it by default, which is why it is more often discussed than encountered.

prompt: Two requests read a counter of 10, each add 1 and write 11. What is this called?
optionA: A lost update — one increment vanished
optionB: A deadlock — the two requests blocked each other
optionC: A constraint violation — the counter holds the wrong value
optionD: A dirty read — one request read uncommitted data
correctAnswerText: A lost update — one increment vanished
explanation: Two increments went in and one came out. Nothing errored, nothing was logged, and the count is simply wrong from then on.

prompt: What decides where a transaction should begin and end?
optionA: How long the statements are expected to take to run
optionB: The number of statements that will be executed inside it
optionC: The set of changes that must not be left half-applied
optionD: Whether the statements touch more than one table
correctAnswerText: The set of changes that must not be left half-applied
explanation: The boundary follows the unit of work the business cares about. Statement count and table count are both beside the point.

prompt: Why is a long-running transaction a problem?
optionA: It holds locks, so other transactions queue behind it
optionB: It cannot be committed once it exceeds the connection timeout
optionC: It is more likely to be rolled back by the database automatically
optionD: It consumes more disk space than several shorter ones would
correctAnswerText: It holds locks, so other transactions queue behind it
explanation: Everything waiting on those rows waits for the whole duration. One slow transaction can therefore make an entire application appear to hang.

prompt: Why should a call to an external payment API not sit inside a transaction?
optionA: The database holds locks while waiting, and a rollback cannot undo the charge
optionB: Transactions are limited to statements written in SQL
optionC: External APIs cannot be called while a database connection has a transaction open
optionD: The API call would be rolled back along with the database changes
correctAnswerText: The database holds locks while waiting, and a rollback cannot undo the charge
explanation: Two separate harms: an unbounded wait holding locks, and an external effect the database has no power to reverse. ROLLBACK does not un-charge a card.

prompt: At READ COMMITTED, the usual default, what does a transaction see?
optionA: Everything other transactions have done, committed or not
optionB: Data committed by others, including changes made after it began
optionC: Only the data as it stood at the moment the transaction began
optionD: Its own changes only, with everything else frozen until it commits
correctAnswerText: Data committed by others, including changes made after it began
explanation: Uncommitted work is hidden, but newly committed work is not, so reading the same row twice can give two answers. Freezing the start state is REPEATABLE READ.

prompt: A statement inside a transaction throws an error. What must the code do?
optionA: Nothing — the database rolls the transaction back by itself
optionB: Commit what succeeded and log the statement that failed
optionC: Roll back, so the earlier statements do not remain applied
optionD: Retry the failed statement and carry on with the rest
correctAnswerText: Roll back, so the earlier statements do not remain applied
explanation: Leaving it open holds locks and may commit a partial change. Some drivers roll back on disconnect, but relying on that is relying on an accident.

prompt: Why is read-modify-write in application code dangerous?
optionA: The application may calculate the new value incorrectly
optionB: Another transaction can change the row between the read and the write
optionC: Reading and writing separately takes two round trips to the database instead of one
optionD: The database cannot index a column that is written this way
correctAnswerText: Another transaction can change the row between the read and the write
explanation: The gap between the two is where the other transaction fits. It is the commonest transaction bug in real systems and it never looks wrong when tested alone.

prompt: Your transaction is killed with a deadlock error. What is the normal response?
optionA: Report the failure to the user and take no further action for now
optionB: Retry it, since the conflicting transaction has now finished
optionC: Increase the lock timeout so it waits longer next time
optionD: Split the transaction so that it takes fewer locks
correctAnswerText: Retry it, since the conflicting transaction has now finished
explanation: Deadlocks are transient by nature, so a bounded retry usually succeeds. Taking locks in a consistent order is the fix when they become frequent.

prompt: What is the simplest correct way to increment a counter column?
optionA: SELECT the value, then UPDATE only if it has not changed meanwhile
optionB: UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1, letting the database do the arithmetic
optionC: Lock the whole table, read the value, write it back and unlock
optionD: SELECT the value, add one in code, then UPDATE with the result
correctAnswerText: UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1, letting the database do the arithmetic
explanation: One statement means no gap for another transaction to slip into. The compare-and-set version is also correct but needs retry logic to go with it.

prompt: A value must be read, checked against business rules, then written. How do you make that safe?
optionA: Run the read and the write as two statements inside the same explicit transaction block
optionB: Read the value, then verify it again immediately before writing it
optionC: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the transaction, so the row is locked while you decide
optionD: Set the isolation level to READ COMMITTED before the read
correctAnswerText: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the transaction, so the row is locked while you decide
explanation: Being in a transaction does not by itself stop another from changing the row at READ COMMITTED. FOR UPDATE is what holds it until you commit.

prompt: Placing an order writes an order row, writes its line items, decrements stock, and emails the customer. What belongs in the transaction?
optionA: The three database writes, with the email sent after the commit
optionB: Each of the four steps in its own separate transaction
optionC: All four steps, so that the email is not sent if anything at all fails
optionD: The order row only, with the rest written afterwards
correctAnswerText: The three database writes, with the email sent after the commit
explanation: The writes must not be left half-applied; the email cannot be rolled back and the SMTP wait would hold locks. After commit is the correct place.

prompt: How should transaction code be structured so a connection is never left open?
optionA: Wrap every statement in its own try/catch and continue past failures
optionB: Roll back at the start of the function in case one was left open
optionC: Rely on the connection pool to reclaim idle connections once a timeout has elapsed
optionD: Commit on success, roll back on error, release the connection in a finally block
correctAnswerText: Commit on success, roll back on error, release the connection in a finally block
explanation: The release must happen on every path, including the throw nobody anticipated. A pool timeout leaves locks held for its full duration first.

prompt: A form is loaded, edited for several minutes, then saved. How do you stop one user overwriting another?
optionA: Compare the timestamps and keep whichever save arrived most recently
optionB: Carry a version number and reject the save if the stored version has moved on
optionC: Lock the row when the form is opened and release it when it is saved
optionD: Save each field separately so that only the fields the user actually edited are written
correctAnswerText: Carry a version number and reject the save if the stored version has moved on
explanation: A lock held across user thinking time is a lock held until they go to lunch. The optimistic version detects the conflict at save and can tell the user about it.

prompt: Two operations both touch accounts A and B, in opposite orders. How do you stop them deadlocking?
optionA: Shorten the transactions so that the window for a conflict is much smaller
optionB: Always take the locks in the same order, for instance by ascending id
optionC: Put the two operations in a queue so they cannot overlap
optionD: Retry whichever transaction the database chooses to kill
correctAnswerText: Always take the locks in the same order, for instance by ascending id
explanation: A cycle needs opposing orders, so a consistent order makes it impossible rather than merely rare. Shortening and retrying reduce the pain without removing the cause.

prompt: A user double-clicks Pay and two identical requests arrive. What prevents a double charge?
optionA: A transaction around the payment, so only one can run at a time
optionB: Checking for a recent identical payment before inserting
optionC: A unique key on the request, so the second insert is rejected
optionD: Disabling the button in the browser after the first click
correctAnswerText: A unique key on the request, so the second insert is rejected
explanation: The database is the only place both requests must pass through. Checking first has the same read-modify-write gap the constraint closes; the disabled button helps but is not a guarantee.

prompt: A job must update a million rows. How should it be transacted?
optionA: In batches, each its own transaction, with the job able to resume
optionB: In one transaction, so the whole job can be rolled back cleanly on failure
optionC: One row per transaction, so that no lock is ever held for long
optionD: In one transaction, with a commit issued every few seconds
correctAnswerText: In batches, each its own transaction, with the job able to resume
explanation: A single million-row transaction holds locks for its whole duration and must undo everything if it fails near the end. Batches trade atomicity for resumability, deliberately.

prompt: Stock must never go negative. What enforces that most reliably?
optionA: A transaction around the read and the decrement together
optionB: Reading the stock and refusing the sale if it has already reached zero
optionC: A check constraint on the column, so no path can ever violate it
optionD: A background job that corrects any negative values it finds
correctAnswerText: A check constraint on the column, so no path can ever violate it
explanation: A rule in the schema applies to every path, including the admin screen and the import script. A check in one code path protects that one code path.

prompt: You add a retry around a transaction that can deadlock. What must the retry have?
optionA: A log entry written before each attempt begins
optionB: A longer timeout on each successive attempt
optionC: A fresh connection taken from the pool on each attempt
optionD: A limit on attempts and a growing delay between them
correctAnswerText: A limit on attempts and a growing delay between them
explanation: Unbounded immediate retries turn a transient conflict into sustained load on an already struggling database. Bounded attempts with backoff is the standard shape.

prompt: A view counter reads lower than the logged number of views, and only under load. What is happening?
optionA: The counter column is overflowing its numeric type under load
optionB: The counter is being read from a replica that lags behind the primary server
optionC: Increments are being read, added and written back, and some are being lost
optionD: Some requests are failing before they reach the counter update
correctAnswerText: Increments are being read, added and written back, and some are being lost
explanation: Only under load is the signature: concurrency is required to open the gap. A replica lag would show as a delay that catches up, not as a permanent shortfall.

prompt: Some orders exist with no line items at all. What does that suggest?
optionA: The line items were deleted by a later cleanup job
optionB: The orders were created directly through the admin interface instead
optionC: A foreign key is missing between the two tables
optionD: The two writes were not in one transaction and the second failed
correctAnswerText: The two writes were not in one transaction and the second failed
explanation: A half-applied unit of work is exactly what a missing boundary produces. A foreign key would not help here — nothing is pointing at a missing row, the rows simply were never written.

prompt: Requests all over the application start timing out at once, though the database is barely busy. What should you check first?
optionA: Whether the network between the application and database has degraded
optionB: Whether a query is missing an index and scanning a whole table
optionC: Whether one long transaction is holding locks everything else needs
optionD: Whether the database has run out of available connections
correctAnswerText: Whether one long transaction is holding locks everything else needs
explanation: Idle CPU with everything waiting points at blocking rather than work. A missing index would show as a busy database, which is the opposite symptom.

prompt: Deadlocks were rare and are now constant, with no code change. What most likely changed?
optionA: The lock timeout was lowered by a configuration change
