optionB: The database began detecting deadlocks that it had previously missed entirely
optionC: Traffic rose, so transactions that rarely overlapped now routinely do
optionD: An index was dropped, making the transactions slower
correctAnswerText: Traffic rose, so transactions that rarely overlapped now routinely do
explanation: The ordering fault was always there; volume made it likely rather than lucky. This is why deadlocks so often first appear on the day traffic grows.

prompt: Connections sit in state "idle in transaction" for minutes. What does that mean?
optionA: Code opened a transaction and neither committed nor rolled it back
optionB: The database is waiting for a slow query inside those transactions
optionC: The connection pool is holding connections open for reuse
optionD: Those transactions are blocked waiting on a lock held elsewhere
correctAnswerText: Code opened a transaction and neither committed nor rolled it back
explanation: Idle means the database is doing nothing and waiting on the application. Every lock those transactions took is still held while nobody is using them.

prompt: A few customers were charged twice. The payment call sits inside the transaction, which sometimes fails afterwards and retries. What went wrong?
optionA: The payment provider processed the same request twice without noticing
optionB: The transaction was not isolated from other payments
optionC: The rollback undid the database row but could not undo the charge
optionD: The transaction was committed twice by the retry logic
correctAnswerText: The rollback undid the database row but could not undo the charge
explanation: An external effect inside a transaction is outside the database's power to reverse, so the retry charges again. This is the concrete harm behind the rule about network calls.

prompt: A report sums two tables in separate queries and the totals sometimes disagree. Why?
optionA: A transfer committed between the two queries, so each saw a different moment
optionB: One query is missing rows because of a join condition that was written incorrectly
optionC: One of the two queries is reading from a stale replica
optionD: The two queries are rounding their results differently
correctAnswerText: A transfer committed between the two queries, so each saw a different moment
explanation: Two queries outside one transaction see two points in time. Running both inside a single transaction at REPEATABLE READ gives them one consistent snapshot.

prompt: A concurrency bug passes every test and fails in production. Why do the tests miss it?
optionA: The tests use a different isolation level from production
optionB: The test database holds much less data than production does
optionC: The tests roll back their changes at the end instead of committing them
optionD: The tests run operations one at a time, and the bug needs two at once
correctAnswerText: The tests run operations one at a time, and the bug needs two at once
explanation: Sequential tests cannot produce a gap that requires overlap. Catching these means a test that deliberately runs two transactions concurrently.

prompt: Stock went to minus three during a sale. The code checks stock before decrementing. What failed?
optionA: Several requests read the same positive stock before any of them wrote
optionB: The stock had not been updated after a previous delivery
optionC: The check was comparing against the wrong column
optionD: The decrement was applied more times than there were orders actually placed
correctAnswerText: Several requests read the same positive stock before any of them wrote
explanation: Check-then-act is read-modify-write wearing a different hat. A conditional update, or a check constraint, closes the gap the check leaves open.

prompt: Why are lost updates so much harder to notice than deadlocks?
optionA: They resolve themselves once the conflicting transaction has finally finished
optionB: They occur only on databases without transaction support at all
optionC: Nothing fails — the write succeeds and the wrong value is simply stored
optionD: They are logged at a level most applications do not capture
correctAnswerText: Nothing fails — the write succeeds and the wrong value is simply stored
explanation: A deadlock announces itself with an exception; a lost update is a successful write. It is usually found weeks later, by somebody who noticed a number looked wrong.

prompt: What single question best decides whether two writes belong in one transaction?
optionA: Would it be acceptable for the first to happen and the second not to?
optionB: Does the second write depend on a value the first one produced?
optionC: Do the two writes touch the same table as each other?
optionD: Will the two writes usually run within a short time of each other in practice?
correctAnswerText: Would it be acceptable for the first to happen and the second not to?
explanation: It asks about consequences rather than mechanics. Dependency and shared tables are common in a unit of work but neither defines one.

prompt: SERIALIZABLE removes every concurrency anomaly. Why is it not the default?
optionA: It prevents more than one connection from writing at a time
optionB: It cannot be combined with explicit locking in a transaction
optionC: It costs throughput, and adds failures the application must retry
optionD: It is not supported by most of the relational database engines in use
correctAnswerText: It costs throughput, and adds failures the application must retry
explanation: Correctness by default would be a reasonable choice, and some systems make it. The trade is real work: more serialisation failures, each of which the code must be written to retry.

prompt: What decides between optimistic and pessimistic locking?
optionA: Whether the application is single-threaded or handles requests concurrently
optionB: How many tables the operation needs to write to
optionC: How often conflicts actually occur, and how long the work is held open
optionD: Whether the database supports row-level locks natively
correctAnswerText: How often conflicts actually occur, and how long the work is held open
explanation: Rare conflicts and long think time favour detecting at save. Frequent conflicts on short operations favour holding the lock, since retrying constantly is worse than waiting briefly.

prompt: Why prefer a database constraint over a check in application code?
optionA: It can express rules that application code would be unable to express at all
optionB: It runs faster than the equivalent check in application code
optionC: It applies to every writer, and it cannot be raced the way a check can
optionD: It produces error messages that are easier for users to understand
correctAnswerText: It applies to every writer, and it cannot be raced the way a check can
explanation: Two separate advantages. The constraint is evaluated as part of the write itself, so there is no window between checking and acting, and no code path can skip it.

prompt: Two services own separate databases and a single action must change both. What does that cost?
optionA: Nothing, provided both services use transactions internally
optionB: Durability — committed changes may be lost if one service fails
optionC: Atomicity — the action must be made recoverable step by step instead
optionD: Isolation — the two services will read each other's uncommitted data
correctAnswerText: Atomicity — the action must be made recoverable step by step instead
explanation: One transaction cannot span two databases, so the guarantee becomes eventual and the application must carry compensating steps. It is the price of the boundary, paid knowingly.

prompt: How do you write a test that would actually catch a lost update?
optionA: Run the operation with the isolation level set to SERIALIZABLE throughout
optionB: Mock the database and assert the update statement was called
optionC: Run the operation repeatedly and check it succeeds every time
optionD: Run the operation many times concurrently and assert the final total
correctAnswerText: Run the operation many times concurrently and assert the final total
explanation: The assertion must be on the aggregate, not on each call, because every individual call succeeds. A hundred concurrent increments must leave exactly a hundred.

prompt: Why is "keep transactions short" such a consistently good rule?
optionA: The database can optimise short transactions more effectively
optionB: Duration multiplies every risk: locks held, conflicts met, work to undo
optionC: Short transactions are less likely to contain a programming error in them
optionD: Short transactions use fewer connections from the pool
correctAnswerText: Duration multiplies every risk: locks held, conflicts met, work to undo
explanation: One variable drives three separate harms at once, which is what makes the rule worth following without case-by-case analysis.

prompt: Which operation gains nothing from an explicit transaction?
optionA: Two updates that must both apply or neither apply
optionB: An insert into one table followed by an update to another
optionC: A single UPDATE against one row of one table
optionD: A read followed by a write that depends on what was read
correctAnswerText: A single UPDATE against one row of one table
explanation: It is already atomic — the database wrapped it. The other three each have a gap or a pair that an explicit boundary is there to close.

prompt: Which transaction mistake causes the most damage in real systems?
optionA: Choosing an isolation level weaker than the operation requires
optionB: Read-modify-write in application code, which loses data without any error
optionC: Forgetting to commit, which leaves the connection open indefinitely afterwards
optionD: Nesting one transaction inside another by mistake
correctAnswerText: Read-modify-write in application code, which loses data without any error
explanation: The others announce themselves — a hang, a slow query, an exception. This one succeeds quietly, so it can run for months before anyone notices the number is wrong.

prompt: What is the underlying point of transactions?
optionA: To group related statements together so they are easier to read
optionB: To let code be written as though nothing else were running at the same time
optionC: To let many users work against the database simultaneously
optionD: To make the database recover automatically after a crash of the server itself
correctAnswerText: To let code be written as though nothing else were running at the same time
explanation: They buy back the simple mental model that concurrency destroys. Understanding where that illusion stops holding is what the rest of this skill is about.

prompt: What does big-O notation describe?
optionA: How the work grows as the input grows
optionB: How many lines of code the algorithm is written in
optionC: How much memory the algorithm needs while it is running
optionD: How many seconds an algorithm takes to finish running
correctAnswerText: How the work grows as the input grows
explanation: Growth, not time. Seconds depend on the machine, the language and the day; growth is a property of the algorithm itself.

prompt: What does O(1) mean?
optionA: The algorithm finishes in under one second on any input
optionB: The algorithm touches only the first element of the input
optionC: The work does not change as the input grows
optionD: The algorithm performs exactly one operation in total
correctAnswerText: The work does not change as the input grows
explanation: Constant, not small. An O(1) operation may do a thousand things — the point is that it does the same thousand whether the input holds ten items or ten million.

prompt: What does O(n) mean?
optionA: The algorithm contains exactly one loop over the whole input
optionB: Ten times the input means roughly ten times the work
optionC: The algorithm must examine every element exactly once
optionD: The algorithm uses an amount of memory equal to the input size
correctAnswerText: Ten times the input means roughly ten times the work
explanation: Proportional growth. It does not require visiting each element exactly once, nor a single loop — two separate passes over the input are still O(n).

prompt: An algorithm is quadratic. What does that tell you about its growth?
optionA: The algorithm contains two loops written one after the other
optionB: Ten times the input means roughly a hundred times the work
optionC: The algorithm takes twice as long as a linear one would take
optionD: The algorithm needs twice the memory of a linear algorithm
correctAnswerText: Ten times the input means roughly a hundred times the work
explanation: The work grows with the square of the input. Two loops one after the other are still linear — it is nesting, not counting loops, that squares the work.

prompt: What does O(log n) mean in practice?
optionA: The work grows more slowly than the input but still in proportion to it
optionB: Doubling the input adds only one more step
optionC: The work depends on the logarithm of the largest value stored
optionD: The algorithm halves the input and processes both halves fully
correctAnswerText: Doubling the input adds only one more step
explanation: This is why binary search over a billion items takes about thirty steps. Each step discards half of what is left, so the input size barely matters.

prompt: Which ordering runs from least to most work as n grows large?
optionA: O(1), O(log n), O(n log n), O(n), O(n²)
optionB: O(log n), O(1), O(n log n), O(n), O(n²)
optionC: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)
optionD: O(1), O(n), O(log n), O(n²), O(n log n)
correctAnswerText: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)
explanation: The order worth knowing by heart. Note that n log n sits between n and n², which is why a good sort is affordable and a nested loop often is not.

prompt: Why is O(2n + 5) written as O(n)?
optionA: Adding constants would make the notation ambiguous
optionB: The constants are assumed to be one in every language
optionC: Constants stop mattering as the input grows large
optionD: Constants are too difficult to measure accurately in practice
correctAnswerText: Constants stop mattering as the input grows large
explanation: Big-O describes the shape of the curve, and constants do not change the shape. They matter enormously in real running time — they are just not what this notation is for.

prompt: When someone states a complexity without saying which case, which do they normally mean?
optionA: The case that occurs most often in production
optionB: The average case across typical inputs
optionC: The best case, since it is easiest to prove
optionD: The worst case
correctAnswerText: The worst case
explanation: Worst case is the default because it is the only one that gives a guarantee. Average case needs an assumption about the inputs, which is often wrong.

prompt: What does space complexity describe?
optionA: How much disk the program will occupy once it is installed
optionB: How the extra memory needed grows as the input grows
optionC: How large the input itself is when loaded into memory
optionD: How many variables the algorithm declares in its source
correctAnswerText: How the extra memory needed grows as the input grows
explanation: Extra memory, beyond the input. An algorithm that sorts in place is O(1) space even though the array it sorts may be enormous.

prompt: Where does O(n log n) most commonly appear?
optionA: In efficient general-purpose sorting
optionB: In searching a sorted array for one value
optionC: In comparing every pair of elements in a list
optionD: In looking a key up in a hash table
correctAnswerText: In efficient general-purpose sorting
explanation: Merge sort, heap sort and the sorts built into standard libraries. It is also the proven floor for any sort that works by comparing elements.

prompt: A single loop runs from 0 to n, doing constant work each time. What is its complexity?
optionA: O(1), because the body is constant
optionB: O(n²), because the loop repeats
optionC: O(n)
optionD: O(log n), because the counter grows
correctAnswerText: O(n)
explanation: Constant work repeated n times is n work. The body being O(1) is what makes the whole loop O(n) rather than something worse.

prompt: A loop over n contains another loop over n. What is the complexity?
optionA: O(2n), because there are two loops in total
optionB: O(n), because each loop on its own is linear
optionC: O(n²)
optionD: O(n log n), because the loops are nested
correctAnswerText: O(n²)
explanation: Nesting multiplies; sequencing adds. The inner loop runs n times for each of the outer loop's n iterations.

prompt: Two separate loops over n run one after the other. What is the complexity?
optionA: O(n)
optionB: O(n log n), because the work is doubled
optionC: O(2n), which is a distinct class from O(n)
optionD: O(n²), because there are two loops over n
correctAnswerText: O(n)
explanation: Sequential loops add, giving 2n, and the constant drops. This is the distinction people most often get wrong when reading unfamiliar code.

prompt: A loop starts at n and halves the counter each iteration until it reaches 1. What is the complexity?
optionA: O(n/2), which simplifies to O(n)
optionB: O(1), because it stops quickly on any input
optionC: O(n), because it still depends on n
optionD: O(log n)
correctAnswerText: O(log n)
explanation: Halving is the signature of a logarithm. Any loop that multiplies or divides its counter, rather than adding to it, is logarithmic.

prompt: An algorithm does O(n²) work and then O(n) work. What is its overall complexity?
optionA: O(n²) — the larger term dominates
optionB: O(n), because that is the last thing it does
optionC: O(n² + n), which must be stated in full
optionD: O(n³), because the two are combined
correctAnswerText: O(n²) — the larger term dominates
explanation: At large n the quadratic part swamps everything else, so the smaller term stops being worth stating.

prompt: What is the average complexity of looking a key up in a hash table?
optionA: O(log n), like a balanced tree
optionB: O(n), since the table must be scanned
optionC: O(n log n), because the keys are sorted first
explanation: The hash computes where to look rather than searching for it. The worst case is O(n) when every key collides, which is rare but not impossible.

prompt: What is the complexity of checking whether an unsorted list contains a value?
optionA: O(n²), because each element is compared to the others
optionB: O(log n), because the search can skip elements
optionC: O(1), because the check is a single operation
optionD: O(n) — every element may have to be examined
correctAnswerText: O(n) — every element may have to be examined
explanation: The value may be last or absent. It is written as one short call in most languages, which is exactly why it is so easy to hide inside a loop.

prompt: Can an O(n²) algorithm beat an O(n log n) one in practice?
optionA: Only when the input happens to be already sorted
optionB: Only if the O(n log n) implementation contains a bug
optionC: Yes, on small inputs, where the constants dominate
optionD: No, a lower complexity class is always faster
correctAnswerText: Yes, on small inputs, where the constants dominate
explanation: This is why real sort implementations switch to insertion sort below a threshold of a few dozen elements. Big-O describes large n and says nothing about small n.

prompt: Building a set of seen values to avoid a nested loop is an example of what?
optionA: Trading memory for speed
optionB: Reducing both time and space at once
optionC: Trading speed for memory
optionD: Reducing the constant factor without changing the class
correctAnswerText: Trading memory for speed
explanation: O(n) extra space buys a drop from O(n²) to O(n) time. It is the most common optimisation there is, and the one worth reaching for first.

prompt: Searching an unsorted list is O(n) in the worst case. What is the best case?
optionA: O(1), when the value is the first element examined
optionB: O(n²), if the list contains duplicate values
optionC: O(log n), when the list happens to be sorted
optionD: O(n), because the whole list is always scanned anyway
correctAnswerText: O(1), when the value is the first element examined
explanation: Best case is usually uninteresting precisely because it is so easy to achieve. It is the guarantee that matters, which is why worst case is the default.

prompt: You must find whether a list contains any duplicate. What is the best complexity achievable?
optionA: O(n) time with O(n) space, using a set of seen values
optionB: O(1) time, by checking the length of the list
optionC: O(n log n) time, which cannot be improved upon in theory
optionD: O(n²) time, comparing every pair of elements
correctAnswerText: O(n) time with O(n) space, using a set of seen values
explanation: One pass, adding each value to a set and checking membership first. Sorting first gives O(n log n) without extra space, which is the right answer when memory is tight.

prompt: You will search the same list a million times. What should you do first?
optionA: Search linearly each time, since the list does not change
optionB: Sort before each search so binary search can be used
optionC: Build a hash set once, making each search O(1)
optionD: Split the list into smaller lists and search each one
correctAnswerText: Build a hash set once, making each search O(1)
explanation: One O(n) setup amortised over a million O(1) lookups. Sorting once and binary searching is the alternative when order is also needed.

prompt: An O(n²) routine takes 1 second on 1,000 records. Roughly how long on 10,000?
optionA: About 20 seconds
optionB: About 1,000 seconds
optionC: About 10 seconds
optionD: About 100 seconds
correctAnswerText: About 100 seconds
explanation: Ten times the input squares to a hundred times the work. Being able to do this arithmetic in your head is most of the practical value of the notation.

prompt: A loop over n calls list.includes(x) on a list of n items each time. What is the complexity?
optionA: O(n), because there is only one visible loop
optionB: O(n²), because the lookup is itself O(n)
optionC: O(n log n), because the lookup is optimised internally
optionD: O(1), because includes is a single method call
correctAnswerText: O(n²), because the lookup is itself O(n)
explanation: The second loop is inside the library call. This is the commonest accidental quadratic in real code, and nothing in the source looks nested.

prompt: When is sorting a list first worth its O(n log n) cost?
optionA: Whenever the list is longer than a thousand elements
optionB: Whenever the values are numbers rather than text
optionC: When it turns later work from quadratic into linear
optionD: When the list will be displayed to a user afterwards
correctAnswerText: When it turns later work from quadratic into linear
explanation: Sorting is an investment, so it pays when it changes the class of what follows — finding duplicates, merging, or grouping adjacent equal values.

prompt: You must repeatedly insert at the front of a collection. Which choice avoids O(n) per insert?
optionA: A linked list, where inserting at the head is O(1)
optionB: A hash table, which has no notion of position
optionC: An array, which handles front insertion efficiently
optionD: A sorted array, which keeps insertion cheap
correctAnswerText: A linked list, where inserting at the head is O(1)
explanation: An array must shift every element right to make room. A linked list only rewrites one pointer, which is the whole reason the structure exists.

prompt: Building a long string by repeated concatenation in a loop is often quadratic. Why?
optionA: The loop must scan the string to find its end each time
optionB: Each concatenation copies the whole string built so far
optionC: String comparison inside the loop is itself linear
optionD: Each concatenation allocates memory that is never freed
correctAnswerText: Each concatenation copies the whole string built so far
explanation: Immutable strings mean every append builds a new one, copying everything. Joining a list of parts at the end is the linear alternative.

prompt: A recursive function calls itself n times deep. What is its space complexity?
optionA: O(1), because recursion allocates no extra memory
optionB: O(n), because each pending call occupies a stack frame
optionC: O(n²), because each frame holds its own copy of the input
optionD: O(log n), because the stack grows logarithmically
correctAnswerText: O(n), because each pending call occupies a stack frame
explanation: Every unfinished call keeps its frame. It is why a recursion deep enough overflows the stack where the equivalent loop would not.

prompt: Find two numbers in a list that add to a target. What is the best complexity?
optionA: O(n), storing each value seen and looking for the complement
optionB: O(n log n), which is the proven lower bound for this problem type
optionC: O(n²), checking every pair of values in turn
optionD: O(1), because only two values are being sought
correctAnswerText: O(n), storing each value seen and looking for the complement
explanation: For each value, ask whether target minus it has already been seen. One pass, one hash set — the same trade that fixes most quadratic loops.

prompt: An O(n²) routine runs on a list that is never longer than twenty. Should it be optimised?
optionA: No — at that size the simpler code is the better code
optionB: Yes, because quadratic algorithms should always be replaced
optionC: Yes, in case the list becomes much longer in the future
optionD: No, because twenty squared is still a small number of steps
correctAnswerText: No — at that size the simpler code is the better code
explanation: Four hundred operations is nothing, and clarity has real value. The judgement worth having is whether the bound on the size is guaranteed or merely assumed.

prompt: A page was instant with 500 records and takes 40 seconds with 5,000. What does that pattern indicate?
optionA: Something quadratic — ten times the data, a hundred times the time
optionB: A network call that has become slower under load
optionC: A missing cache, which would slow every request down proportionally
optionD: Memory exhaustion causing the system to swap to disk
correctAnswerText: Something quadratic — ten times the data, a hundred times the time
explanation: The ratio names the class. Ten times the data giving ten times the time would be linear and unremarkable; a hundred times points straight at a nested cost.

prompt: A report loads 500 orders, then queries the customer for each one. What is wrong?
optionA: The orders should have been loaded one at a time
optionB: The customer table is missing an index
optionC: The queries are being run in the wrong order
optionD: It issues 501 queries where two would do
correctAnswerText: It issues 501 queries where two would do
explanation: The classic N+1. Each query is fast, so nothing looks slow in isolation, and the total is five hundred round trips that a single join or one batched lookup replaces.

prompt: A profiler shows no single slow function, yet the whole job is slow. What should you suspect?
optionA: The profiler is sampling too infrequently to see the cause
optionB: Memory allocation is dominating without being attributed
optionC: A cheap operation being performed an enormous number of times
optionD: The slowness is in the operating system rather than in the code
correctAnswerText: A cheap operation being performed an enormous number of times
explanation: Complexity problems spread cost thinly rather than concentrating it. The question to ask a profiler is how many times something ran, not how long each call took.

prompt: Code maps over users and, for each, filters a list of all orders to find theirs. What is the complexity?
optionA: O(users + orders), because each list is visited once
optionB: O(users), because the filter is a single library call
optionC: O(users × orders), because the filter scans every order each time
optionD: O(orders log users), because filtering is optimised internally by the engine
correctAnswerText: O(users × orders), because the filter scans every order each time
explanation: It reads as two clean functional calls and is a nested loop. Grouping the orders by user id once first turns it linear.

prompt: Why do complexity problems so often reach production undetected?
optionA: Test suites deliberately exclude performance measurements
optionB: Developers do not run the code before they ship it
optionC: Development data is small, and the difference only appears at scale
optionD: Production hardware is usually slower than a modern developer machine
correctAnswerText: Development data is small, and the difference only appears at scale
explanation: On fifty seed records a quadratic and a linear routine are indistinguishable. The defect is present and correct-looking from the first day it is written.

prompt: A job crashes with an out-of-memory error only on the largest files. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The file format is inefficient and should be compressed
optionB: Garbage collection is not running frequently enough
optionC: The machine does not have enough memory installed for the task
optionD: The whole file is being loaded at once rather than streamed
correctAnswerText: The whole file is being loaded at once rather than streamed
explanation: O(n) space where O(1) was available. Processing line by line keeps memory flat however large the file grows, and is usually a small change.

prompt: A query slows down steadily as a table grows, in direct proportion. What does that suggest?
optionA: The database is running out of connections
optionB: A quadratic join between two growing tables
optionC: A full table scan, which is O(n) in the row count
optionD: The result set has become too large to transfer quickly
correctAnswerText: A full table scan, which is O(n) in the row count
explanation: Proportional growth is the signature of a scan. An index turns it into roughly O(log n), which is why the slowdown stops being noticeable.

prompt: A function recomputes the same expensive value on every call inside a loop. What is the fix?
optionA: Compute it once before the loop and reuse the result
optionB: Reduce the number of iterations the loop performs
optionC: Run the loop iterations in parallel across several threads
optionD: Make the expensive function itself run faster
correctAnswerText: Compute it once before the loop and reuse the result
explanation: Moving loop-invariant work out is the cheapest optimisation there is and changes the complexity class. The others attack the constant instead.

prompt: Code keeps an array of ten thousand ids and checks membership constantly. What is the root problem?
optionA: The membership checks should be batched together
optionB: The array holds too many elements to be searched at all
optionC: The data is in a structure whose strengths do not match its use
optionD: The ids should have been stored as numbers rather than as text strings
correctAnswerText: The data is in a structure whose strengths do not match its use
explanation: An array is for order and iteration; a set is for membership. Choosing the structure by what will be asked of it is most of what this skill is for.

prompt: Something is slow. What should you establish before changing any code?
optionA: How the time changes as the input grows
optionB: How much memory the process is currently using
optionC: Whether a faster machine would solve the problem
optionD: Which line of the code is executed most often
correctAnswerText: How the time changes as the input grows
explanation: Two measurements at two sizes tell you the class, which tells you whether to rewrite the algorithm or tune the constant. Guessing usually tunes the constant.

prompt: What does big-O deliberately refuse to tell you?
optionA: Whether one algorithm is faster than another on your actual data
optionB: How the work grows as the input becomes very large
optionC: Which of two algorithms scales better in the long run
optionD: Whether an algorithm will ever finish at all on very large inputs
correctAnswerText: Whether one algorithm is faster than another on your actual data
explanation: It discards exactly the constants that decide real running time. That is a feature — it makes the comparison machine-independent — and a limit worth stating out loud.

prompt: When is it right to knowingly write the higher-complexity version?
optionA: When nobody on the team understands the faster algorithm
optionB: When the input is bounded and the simpler code is clearer
optionC: When the deadline does not allow time for the better version
optionD: When the better version uses a library not already in use
correctAnswerText: When the input is bounded and the simpler code is clearer
explanation: Bounded input is the condition that makes it a real decision rather than an excuse. The bound should be guaranteed by something, not merely true today.

prompt: "Premature optimisation is the root of all evil." What does that NOT excuse?
optionA: Leaving a constant factor untuned until it is measured
optionB: Choosing a structure whose complexity is wrong for the job
optionC: Writing straightforward code before it has been profiled at all
optionD: Preferring clarity over cleverness in ordinary code
correctAnswerText: Choosing a structure whose complexity is wrong for the job
explanation: Picking the right structure is design, not optimisation, and it is nearly free at the time and expensive afterwards. The saying is about tuning, not about class.

prompt: Where does complexity analysis actually earn its keep in everyday work?
optionA: In choosing between two named sorting algorithms
optionB: In spotting the loop that quietly contains a second loop
optionC: In estimating how long a feature will take to build
optionD: In proving that a program is correct for all possible inputs
correctAnswerText: In spotting the loop that quietly contains a second loop
explanation: Almost nobody implements a sort. Nearly everybody writes a lookup inside a loop, and recognising it is the skill that pays.

prompt: Appending to a dynamic array is called amortised O(1). What does that mean?
optionA: Every append is constant time on every implementation
optionB: Most appends are cheap, and the occasional costly resize averages out
optionC: The cost is O(1) in the best case and O(n) on average
optionD: The cost is constant provided that the array has been pre-sized correctly
correctAnswerText: Most appends are cheap, and the occasional costly resize averages out
explanation: Doubling the capacity makes one append O(n) but pays for the n cheap ones before it. Amortised is a claim about a sequence, not about any single call.

prompt: Two algorithms are both O(n). What can still separate them by a large factor?
optionA: Only the size of the input each one is given
optionB: Only the programming language each one is written in
optionC: Constant costs per element, such as allocation or cache behaviour
optionD: Nothing at all — the same complexity class implies the same speed
correctAnswerText: Constant costs per element, such as allocation or cache behaviour
explanation: One linear pass touching memory in order can be many times faster than another that jumps about, and big-O cannot see the difference.

prompt: Why can no comparison-based sort beat O(n log n)?
optionA: Because the input must be read at least log n times
optionB: There are too many possible orderings to distinguish with fewer comparisons
optionC: Because comparisons themselves take logarithmic time to perform
optionD: Because every known sorting algorithm has been tested and none of them is faster
correctAnswerText: There are too many possible orderings to distinguish with fewer comparisons
explanation: It is a proof about information, not about implementations. Sorts that do beat it, like counting sort, work by not comparing at all.

prompt: Reviewing a pull request, what single question best exposes a complexity problem?
optionA: Does this code follow the conventions used elsewhere?
optionB: Has this code been measured against the previous version?
optionC: What is inside every loop, including the calls it makes?
optionD: How many loops does this change introduce in total?
correctAnswerText: What is inside every loop, including the calls it makes?
explanation: Visible nesting is easy to spot and rarely the culprit. The cost is almost always in a call whose own complexity the reader has to go and look up.

prompt: What makes "this list will never be large" a dangerous justification?
optionA: Nothing enforces it, and the code outlives the assumption
optionB: The compiler cannot optimise code that is written on that basis
optionC: Lists in modern systems are always large in practice
optionD: It is impossible to know how large a list will become
correctAnswerText: Nothing enforces it, and the code outlives the assumption
explanation: It is a reasonable decision and an unreasonable thing to leave unwritten. A comment stating the bound, or a check that enforces it, costs one line.

prompt: What is complexity analysis ultimately for?
optionA: Describing how much memory a program will need to run in total
optionB: Measuring how fast a program runs on a given machine
optionC: Proving which of two algorithms is the better one to use
optionD: Predicting how code will behave on data you have not got yet
correctAnswerText: Predicting how code will behave on data you have not got yet
explanation: It is the only tool that answers a question about the future without running anything, which is precisely when it is needed: before the data arrives.

prompt: What does a linear search do?
optionA: Computes where the value should be and looks only there
optionB: Checks each element in turn until it finds the value or runs out
optionC: Jumps to the middle and discards half of the data on each successive step
optionD: Sorts the data first and then locates the value directly
correctAnswerText: Checks each element in turn until it finds the value or runs out
explanation: The simplest possible search, and the only one that works on anything. The other three describe binary search, a sort-then-search, and a hash lookup.

prompt: What does a binary search do on each step?
optionA: Splits the data in two and searches both halves in turn
optionB: Divides the value being sought by two and looks again
optionC: Compares with the first element and then moves forward by one
optionD: Compares with the middle element and discards half the range
correctAnswerText: Compares with the middle element and discards half the range
explanation: One comparison removes half the remaining candidates. Searching both halves would defeat the purpose — the discard is what makes it logarithmic.

prompt: What does binary search require of its data?
optionA: It must already be sorted
optionB: It must contain no duplicate values
optionC: It must be stored in a linked structure
optionD: It must have a length that is a power of two
correctAnswerText: It must already be sorted
explanation: Sorted order is the only requirement, and it is absolute. Duplicates are fine, and so is any length.

prompt: What is the worst-case cost of a linear search over n items?
optionA: O(log n)
optionC: O(n)
optionD: O(n log n)
correctAnswerText: O(n)
explanation: The value may be the last element or absent entirely, so every item is examined. That is the case the cost is quoted for.

prompt: What is the worst-case cost of a binary search over n sorted items?
optionB: O(log n)
optionC: O(n)
optionD: O(n log n)
correctAnswerText: O(log n)
explanation: Each step halves what remains, so a billion items take about thirty comparisons. That number is worth carrying around.

prompt: What is the average cost of finding a key in a hash table?
optionA: O(log n)
optionC: O(n)
optionD: O(n log n)
explanation: The hash computes the location rather than searching for it. This is why a set is the usual answer when membership is all that is needed.

prompt: What should a search return when the value is not present?
optionA: The length of the collection that was searched
optionB: Zero, since no element was found at any index
optionC: The position closest to where the value would have been
optionD: A value that cannot be confused with a valid position
correctAnswerText: A value that cannot be confused with a valid position
explanation: Usually -1, or null, or a separate found flag. Returning 0 is the classic bug, because 0 is also a perfectly good index.

prompt: What is linear search's one real advantage?
optionA: It uses less memory than any other search method
optionB: It is faster than binary search on large collections
optionC: It works on any data, in any order, with no preparation
optionD: It can find several matching values where others cannot
correctAnswerText: It works on any data, in any order, with no preparation
explanation: No precondition at all. That is why it is right for small or unsorted data and for anything you will only look at once.

prompt: What is the best case for a linear search?
optionA: O(n), because every element is always checked
optionB: O(log n), when the data happens to be sorted
optionC: O(n/2), when the value is in the middle
optionD: O(1), when the value is the first element
correctAnswerText: O(1), when the value is the first element
explanation: A linear search stops as soon as it finds the value. It is the worst case that is quoted, because that is the one that gives a guarantee.

prompt: What does a database index do?
optionA: Keeps a sorted structure so rows can be found without a full scan
optionB: Copies the whole table into memory so that reads can avoid the disk entirely
optionC: Records which rows have been read most frequently
optionD: Compresses the table so that fewer bytes must be read
correctAnswerText: Keeps a sorted structure so rows can be found without a full scan
explanation: It is binary search applied to a table, maintained by the database. The cost is that every write must also update it.

prompt: What happens if binary search is run on unsorted data?
optionA: It returns a confident wrong answer, usually "not found"
optionB: It still works but takes linear time instead
optionC: It finds the value only if it happens to be in the middle
optionD: It raises an error because the precondition is violated
correctAnswerText: It returns a confident wrong answer, usually "not found"
explanation: Nothing checks the precondition, so it silently discards the half containing the value. Silence is what makes this bug expensive.

prompt: You will search an unsorted list exactly once. Should you sort it first and binary search?
optionA: No — sorting costs more than the single linear scan would
optionB: No, because binary search cannot handle duplicate values
optionC: Yes, because binary search is always faster than a linear scan
optionD: Yes, because sorted data is easier to work with later
correctAnswerText: No — sorting costs more than the single linear scan would
explanation: O(n log n) to sort, to save an O(n) scan. Sorting pays only when the searches are repeated enough to amortise it.

prompt: You will search the same list thousands of times. What changes?
optionA: Linear search becomes faster because the data is cached
optionB: The choice of search stops mattering at that scale
optionC: A one-off sort or hash set becomes clearly worth its cost
optionD: The list should be split up so that each search covers less data
correctAnswerText: A one-off sort or hash set becomes clearly worth its cost
explanation: Setup cost is paid once and divided across every search. This amortisation is the whole reason indexes exist.

prompt: Why is binary search a poor fit for a linked list, even a sorted one?
optionA: Reaching the middle element costs a walk from the start
optionB: Following pointers makes every comparison more expensive
optionC: The list has no length, so the range cannot be halved
optionD: Linked lists cannot be kept in sorted order at all
correctAnswerText: Reaching the middle element costs a walk from the start
explanation: Binary search assumes jumping to any index is free. Without random access the halving costs O(n) per step, which is worse than simply scanning.

prompt: A hash set gives O(1) membership. What can it not do?
optionA: Hold more items than will fit in a single array
optionB: Answer range questions, such as every value between two bounds
optionC: Store values that are strings rather than plain numbers, or objects
optionD: Report whether a particular value is present
correctAnswerText: Answer range questions, such as every value between two bounds
explanation: Hashing destroys order deliberately, which is what buys the constant time. Range queries need a sorted structure or a tree.

prompt: Roughly how many comparisons does a binary search need over a million sorted items?
optionA: About 500,000
optionB: About 20
optionC: About 100
optionD: About 1,000
correctAnswerText: About 20
explanation: Two to the twentieth is just over a million. The gap between twenty and a million is the whole argument for keeping data sorted.

prompt: A sorted list holds the value 7 five times. What does a plain binary search return?
optionA: All five positions, as a range
optionB: The last occurrence, since it narrows from the right
optionC: The first occurrence, since it searches from the left
optionD: One of them, with no guarantee which
correctAnswerText: One of them, with no guarantee which
explanation: It stops at whichever it lands on first. Finding the first or last occurrence needs a modified version that keeps searching after a match.

prompt: Why not simply index every column in a database table?
optionA: Indexes on unused columns cause queries to be misplanned
optionB: Indexed columns can no longer be updated after creation
optionC: Databases permit only a limited number of indexes per table
optionD: Every write must update every index, and they occupy space
correctAnswerText: Every write must update every index, and they occupy space
explanation: An index is a read optimisation paid for on every write. Indexing what is never searched is pure cost.

prompt: For a collection of ten items, which search should you write?
optionA: A hash lookup, because constant time is always preferable
optionB: Binary, because it is faster at every size
optionC: Linear, because at that size the simpler code is better
optionD: Binary, but only after checking the data is sorted
correctAnswerText: Linear, because at that size the simpler code is better
explanation: Ten comparisons is nothing, and the sorted precondition is a liability nobody is watching. Complexity arguments apply to large n.

prompt: Which inputs most often expose a bug in a hand-written binary search?
optionA: An empty list, a single element, and the first and last values
optionB: A list where every element happens to hold exactly the same value
optionC: A list of negative numbers rather than positive ones
optionD: A list containing several thousand elements
correctAnswerText: An empty list, a single element, and the first and last values
explanation: The boundaries are where the loop condition and the midpoint arithmetic go wrong. The middle of a large list is the case that already works.

prompt: For each of 10,000 users you must check membership in a 10,000-item list. What should you do?
optionA: Sort the list once and binary search it for each user
optionB: Split the list into chunks and scan the relevant chunk
optionC: Build a set from the list once, then check each user against it
optionD: Scan the list for each user, since it is only checked once each
correctAnswerText: Build a set from the list once, then check each user against it
explanation: One O(n) build turns 100 million comparisons into 10,000 constant-time lookups. Sorting and binary searching also works and is slower.

prompt: You need every record with a date between two bounds. What suits this?
optionA: A sorted structure, where the range is a contiguous run
optionB: A hash table, which finds any single key almost instantly
optionC: A set, which answers membership questions quickly
optionD: An unsorted list scanned once per query
correctAnswerText: A sorted structure, where the range is a contiguous run
explanation: Find the first date in range, then walk forward until you leave it. Hashing scatters those records, so a range becomes a full scan.

prompt: Why is low + (high - low) / 2 preferred over (low + high) / 2 for the midpoint?
optionA: It cannot overflow when both bounds are very large
optionB: It produces a different midpoint on odd-length ranges
optionC: It avoids a division, which is slower than subtraction
optionD: It handles the case where high is smaller than low
correctAnswerText: It cannot overflow when both bounds are very large
explanation: A famous bug that sat in published library code for years. Both forms are equivalent mathematically and only one survives large integers.

prompt: A binary search loops while low <= high. What goes wrong with low < high?
optionA: The midpoint calculation produces an invalid index
optionB: The loop runs one iteration too many on every search
optionC: A range that has narrowed to one element is never examined
optionD: Duplicate values cause the loop to repeat itself indefinitely
correctAnswerText: A range that has narrowed to one element is never examined
explanation: When low equals high there is still one candidate left. This is the off-by-one that makes a search fail only on single-element ranges.

prompt: Which column is worth indexing?
optionA: One that queries filter on often and writes touch rarely
optionB: One that is displayed on every screen in the application
optionC: One that is updated on almost every write
optionD: One that holds the largest values in the table
correctAnswerText: One that queries filter on often and writes touch rarely
explanation: Read often, written rarely, and selective enough to eliminate most rows. Indexing a heavily written column pays the cost without the benefit.

prompt: You keep an array sorted so binary search stays valid. What does an insert cost?
optionA: O(n log n), because the array must be sorted again
optionB: O(1), because the element is appended and the array resorted
optionC: O(log n), because the position is found by binary search
optionD: O(n), because the later elements must shift to make room
correctAnswerText: O(n), because the later elements must shift to make room
explanation: Finding where it goes is O(log n); putting it there is O(n). A tree or skip list keeps both operations logarithmic, which is why they exist.

prompt: How do you find the FIRST occurrence of a value in a sorted list with duplicates?
optionA: Search normally, then step backwards while the value repeats
optionB: Search normally, since the first match is always leftmost
optionC: Remove the duplicates first, then search the result
optionD: Record the match and keep searching the left half
correctAnswerText: Record the match and keep searching the left half
explanation: Keeping the binary search going preserves O(log n). Stepping backwards is correct but degrades to O(n) when the value repeats often.

prompt: What should a test suite for a search function cover first?
optionA: Repeated searches, to confirm that the performance is still acceptable
optionB: A large randomly generated list, checked against a known answer
optionC: Lists of several different data types
optionD: Empty input, one element, the first, the last, and an absent value
correctAnswerText: Empty input, one element, the first, the last, and an absent value
explanation: Those five catch nearly every real search bug because they are all boundaries. The large random list mostly exercises the case that already works.

prompt: You must repeatedly find objects by their id. What is the usual structure?
optionA: A list kept sorted by id and binary searched
optionB: Separate lists, one per range of ids
optionC: A list scanned linearly, comparing each id
optionD: A map from id to object, built once
correctAnswerText: A map from id to object, built once
explanation: Lookup by key is exactly what a map is for. Reaching for binary search here is solving with an algorithm what a structure already solves.

prompt: You build a lookup map at startup from data that later changes. What must accompany it?
optionA: Something that updates the map whenever the data changes
optionB: A periodic check that the map is still the right size
optionC: A lock so that reads cannot see it mid-update
optionD: A copy of the original data, kept for later comparison against it
correctAnswerText: Something that updates the map whenever the data changes
explanation: A cached index with nothing maintaining it answers yesterday's question confidently. This is the same trap as any other derived value.

prompt: A search reports "not found" for records that definitely exist, but only sometimes. What should you check first?
optionA: Whether the search function contains an off-by-one error somewhere
optionB: Whether the comparison is case-sensitive
optionC: Whether the data is still sorted when the search runs
optionD: Whether the records were deleted and then restored
correctAnswerText: Whether the data is still sorted when the search runs
explanation: Intermittent is the clue: an off-by-one fails consistently. Something is appending or updating without re-sorting, so the precondition holds until it does not.

prompt: A lookup takes twice as long each time the table doubles. What does that indicate?
optionA: A full scan — the search is not using an index
optionB: The query is returning twice as many rows
optionC: The table has outgrown the available memory
optionD: The index has become fragmented and needs rebuilding
correctAnswerText: A full scan — the search is not using an index
explanation: Proportional growth is the signature of a scan. An indexed lookup would grow logarithmically, which looks like no growth at all at these sizes.

prompt: An index exists on the column but the query still scans. What is a common cause?
optionA: The index was created after the rows were inserted
optionB: The table has too few rows for an index to exist
optionC: The query selects more columns than the index itself actually contains
optionD: The column is wrapped in a function, so the index cannot be used
correctAnswerText: The column is wrapped in a function, so the index cannot be used
explanation: LOWER(email) = ... cannot use an index on email, because the index stores the original values. A function-based index or storing it normalised fixes it.

prompt: A search over duplicates returns a different record on different runs. Why?
optionA: Nothing specifies which duplicate wins, so any is valid
optionB: The search function contains a race condition
optionC: The records are being reordered between the runs
optionD: The comparison function is behaving inconsistently between runs
correctAnswerText: Nothing specifies which duplicate wins, so any is valid
explanation: Binary search lands wherever the halving takes it. If which one matters, the requirement is first or last and the search must say so.

prompt: A hand-written binary search hangs on some inputs. What is the usual cause?
optionA: The comparison returns equal for two values that are actually quite different
optionB: The list is too large for the loop counter to hold
optionC: The recursion is too deep for the available stack
optionD: The bounds are not moving past the midpoint, so the range stops shrinking
correctAnswerText: The bounds are not moving past the midpoint, so the range stops shrinking
explanation: Setting low = mid instead of mid + 1 leaves the same range forever once two elements remain. The range must shrink on every path.

prompt: Hash lookups that were instant have become slow, with no code change. What is one explanation?
optionA: The keys have become longer and so take much more time to compare
optionB: The hash table has run out of the memory allocated to it
optionC: The keys are colliding heavily, degrading lookups towards linear
optionD: The table is being rebuilt on every lookup
correctAnswerText: The keys are colliding heavily, degrading lookups towards linear
explanation: O(1) is the average, not a guarantee. Keys sharing a pattern the hash handles badly collapse the table into a handful of long chains.

prompt: A report that joins two lists by scanning one for each element of the other is slow. What is the fix?
optionA: Index one list by key first, then look each element up directly
optionB: Run the outer loop in parallel across several separate worker threads
optionC: Sort both lists before running the existing scan
optionD: Load both lists into memory before starting the loop
correctAnswerText: Index one list by key first, then look each element up directly
explanation: O(n×m) becomes O(n+m) for the cost of one map. It is the same trade a database makes when it chooses a hash join over a nested loop.

prompt: Why do missing indexes so often survive into production?
optionA: Development databases do not support index creation
optionB: Query plans are not available outside production
optionC: A scan of a small development table is indistinguishable from an indexed lookup
optionD: Indexes are usually added by a separate database team much later on in the project
correctAnswerText: A scan of a small development table is indistinguishable from an indexed lookup
explanation: On two hundred seed rows everything is instant. The defect is fully present from the first day and only becomes visible when the data arrives.

prompt: A lookup map returns records that were deleted hours ago. What has happened?
optionA: The map was built once and nothing updates it on delete
optionB: The map is being read before it has finished being built
optionC: The records were deleted from a different table
optionD: The deletes were rolled back without anyone noticing
correctAnswerText: The map was built once and nothing updates it on delete
explanation: The index and its source have diverged. Every derived structure needs something that invalidates it, or it becomes a confident record of the past.

prompt: A lookup is slow. What single measurement most quickly identifies the cause?
optionA: How the time changes when the data size doubles
optionB: How much memory the process holds while searching
optionC: How many lookups are performed per second
optionD: How long a single lookup takes on average
correctAnswerText: How the time changes when the data size doubles
explanation: Unchanged means logarithmic, doubled means a scan, quadrupled means something nested. One comparison names the class and the fix follows.

prompt: In most production code, what is the more useful question than "which search algorithm"?
optionA: Why is anything being scanned at this point at all
optionB: How many elements the collection is expected to hold
optionC: Whether the search should be written recursively
optionD: Which of the two searches has the lower constant factor
correctAnswerText: Why is anything being scanned at this point at all
explanation: Almost nobody writes a binary search; nearly everybody writes a scan they did not notice. The fix is usually a map or an index, not a better loop.

prompt: What makes binary search's sorted precondition genuinely dangerous in a large codebase?
optionA: Nothing enforces it, and breaking it produces a wrong answer rather than an error
optionB: Sorting large collections is generally far too slow to be done defensively everywhere
optionC: Most languages do not provide a sort that is stable
optionD: The precondition cannot be expressed in code at all
correctAnswerText: Nothing enforces it, and breaking it produces a wrong answer rather than an error
explanation: A requirement held in somebody's head, in code that outlives them. An assertion in development, or a type that can only hold sorted data, makes it visible.

prompt: When should you write your own binary search rather than use the library one?
optionA: Whenever the data is held in a custom structure
optionB: Whenever the library version returns a result in an unfamiliar form
optionC: Almost never — a variant the library lacks is the only real reason
optionD: Whenever performance is important to the feature
correctAnswerText: Almost never — a variant the library lacks is the only real reason
explanation: It is famously easy to get wrong and was wrong in published libraries for years. Finding the first match or an insertion point is a legitimate reason.

prompt: If you will never implement it, why is binary search still worth understanding?
optionA: It demonstrates recursion better than other examples do
optionB: It is the fastest possible way to search any collection
optionC: It is the most commonly asked question in technical interviews today
optionD: It is how indexes, lookups and sorted structures work underneath
correctAnswerText: It is how indexes, lookups and sorted structures work underneath
explanation: Understanding it is understanding why an index helps, why it needs order, and why a write pays for a read. That transfers; the implementation does not.

prompt: What decides between a hash-based and a sorted structure?
optionA: Whether order and ranges are needed, or only exact lookups
optionB: Whether the keys are strings or numeric values
optionC: Which one the programming language happens to provide by default
optionD: How many items the collection is expected to hold
correctAnswerText: Whether order and ranges are needed, or only exact lookups
explanation: Hashing is faster and throws order away. If you will ever ask for a range, the sorted structure is worth its extra logarithm.

prompt: Why might a system with hard latency limits prefer a tree to a hash table?
optionA: A tree can hold key types that a hash table cannot
optionB: A tree uses less memory for the same number of stored keys overall
optionC: A tree guarantees O(log n); a hash table only averages O(1)
optionD: A tree is faster than a hash table on every lookup
correctAnswerText: A tree guarantees O(log n); a hash table only averages O(1)
explanation: A predictable logarithm can be better than a usually-constant with an occasional linear spike. Worst case is what a guarantee is made of.

prompt: What is the general principle behind every index, cache and lookup map?
optionA: Keep frequently used data physically close together
optionB: Avoid computing anything until it is actually needed
optionC: Pay once on write to make many reads cheap
optionD: Trade accuracy for speed where accuracy is not critical
correctAnswerText: Pay once on write to make many reads cheap
explanation: The same trade in every guise, which is why it is worth naming. It follows that an index on data written more often than read is a net loss.

prompt: Reviewing code, which pattern should most reliably make you stop?
optionA: A find, filter or contains call inside a loop
optionB: A loop that iterates over a collection once
optionC: A binary search written using recursion
optionD: A lookup map that is built at application startup
correctAnswerText: A find, filter or contains call inside a loop
explanation: Each reads as one operation and each is a scan. Two of them nested is the most common performance defect in application code.

prompt: What is the cost of adding indexes speculatively, before any query needs them?
optionA: Every write pays for them and no read benefits
optionB: The database refuses queries that could use several at once
optionC: Existing queries begin to use the wrong index
optionD: The table can no longer be altered once indexed
correctAnswerText: Every write pays for them and no read benefits
explanation: An unused index is pure overhead on every insert, update and delete. Indexes follow measured queries, in the same way that denormalising follows a measured read.

prompt: What is the single idea underneath every fast search?
optionA: Comparisons should be made as cheap as they can possibly be made
optionB: Data should be held in memory rather than read from disk
optionC: Structure imposed beforehand lets most of the data go unexamined
optionD: The most frequently sought values should be checked first
correctAnswerText: Structure imposed beforehand lets most of the data go unexamined
explanation: Sorted order, a hash, a tree, an index — all of them are work done early so that a later question can ignore almost everything.

prompt: What is recursion?
optionA: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller part of it
optionB: A loop that repeats until a condition is no longer satisfied
optionC: A function that calls several other functions in a fixed, predetermined sequence
optionD: A technique for storing results so they need not be recomputed
correctAnswerText: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller part of it
explanation: Self-reference on a smaller input. The last option describes memoisation, which is often used alongside recursion but is a different idea.

prompt: What is a base case?
optionA: The simplest possible input the function is expected to handle correctly
optionB: The first call made to the recursive function from outside
optionC: The value the function returns when its input is invalid
optionD: The condition under which the function returns without calling itself
correctAnswerText: The condition under which the function returns without calling itself
explanation: It is defined by the absence of a further call, which is what stops the recursion. Without one the function descends until the stack is exhausted.

prompt: What must every recursive call do to guarantee termination?
optionA: Pass a value smaller than the one it received
optionB: Reduce the input by exactly one each time
optionC: Move measurably closer to the base case
optionD: Return a value rather than calling itself again
correctAnswerText: Move measurably closer to the base case
explanation: Progress toward the base case, however it is measured — a shorter list, a shallower tree, a smaller number. Reducing by exactly one is one way, not the requirement.

prompt: What holds the state of a call that is waiting for its recursive call to return?
optionA: A frame on the call stack
optionB: A record in the heap allocated for it
optionC: A reserved area of the function's own memory
optionD: A queue maintained by the language runtime
correctAnswerText: A frame on the call stack
explanation: Each pending call keeps its own frame with its own local variables. The stack is finite, which is why depth is the limiting factor.

prompt: What causes a stack overflow?
optionA: Too many functions being defined in the same program
optionB: Recursion going deeper than the stack has room for
optionC: A function returning a value larger than the stack allows
optionD: A recursive function allocating too much memory per call
correctAnswerText: Recursion going deeper than the stack has room for
explanation: Depth, not width. A million sibling calls one after another is fine; a thousand nested ones may not be.

prompt: What kind of data is recursion most naturally suited to?
optionA: Data that arrives one item at a time from an external source
optionB: Data that is stored in a single flat array of fixed length
optionC: Data that contains more of itself, such as trees and nested structures
optionD: Data that must be processed in exactly the order in which it was received
correctAnswerText: Data that contains more of itself, such as trees and nested structures
explanation: A recursive shape is what makes a recursive function fit. A folder holds folders, a comment holds replies, an expression holds expressions.

prompt: A recursion reaches a depth of n. What is its space cost?
optionA: O(log n), because the stack grows slowly
optionB: O(n²), because each frame stores the whole input
optionC: O(1), because each call returns before the next begins
optionD: O(n), because n frames are held at once
correctAnswerText: O(n), because n frames are held at once
explanation: Every unfinished call occupies a frame simultaneously. This is the cost a loop does not pay, and the reason deep recursion crashes.

prompt: What makes a recursion tail-recursive?
optionA: The function calls itself only once per invocation
optionB: The base case is checked at the end rather than the start
optionC: The recursive call is the very last thing the function does
optionD: The function processes the last element of its input list first
correctAnswerText: The recursive call is the very last thing the function does
explanation: Nothing remains to be done after the call returns, so the frame need not be kept. Some languages exploit this; many, including JavaScript in practice, do not.

prompt: What is memoisation?
optionA: Caching the final answer so that the whole function only ever runs once
optionB: Rewriting a recursive function as an equivalent loop
optionC: Reducing the depth of a recursion by combining calls
optionD: Storing the result of a call so the same input is never computed twice
correctAnswerText: Storing the result of a call so the same input is never computed twice
explanation: One cache entry per distinct input. It is what turns an exponential recursion into a linear one without changing its shape.

prompt: What happens to a recursive function with no reachable base case?
optionA: It loops indefinitely without consuming any extra memory
optionB: It descends until the stack runs out and the program fails
optionC: It returns an undefined value after a fixed number of calls
optionD: The compiler refuses to accept it before it is ever run
correctAnswerText: It descends until the stack runs out and the program fails
explanation: Unlike an infinite loop, it consumes memory as it goes, so it fails rather than hanging. The crash is the useful part.

prompt: In what order do recursive calls finish?
optionA: They all finish together when the base case is reached
optionB: The first call finishes first, in the same order they were made
optionC: The order depends on how the language schedules the stack
optionD: The deepest finishes first, and the first call finishes last
correctAnswerText: The deepest finishes first, and the first call finishes last
explanation: Last in, first out, which is exactly what a stack does. It is why work placed after the recursive call happens on the way back up.

prompt: What changes if you print before the recursive call rather than after it?
optionA: Before prints only the base case value
optionB: Before prints top-down; after prints bottom-up, in reverse
optionC: After prints nothing at all, because the call never actually returns
optionD: Nothing — the output is identical either way
correctAnswerText: Before prints top-down; after prints bottom-up, in reverse
explanation: Work before the call happens on the way down, work after it on the way back. Reversing a list with recursion relies entirely on this.

prompt: A function calls itself twice per invocation, reducing n by one each time. How does the work grow?
optionA: Logarithmically, because the problem is being split in two
optionB: Linearly, because n decreases by one each call
optionC: Exponentially — roughly doubling with each increase in n
optionD: Quadratically, because there are two calls
correctAnswerText: Exponentially — roughly doubling with each increase in n
explanation: Two branches per level over n levels gives about 2^n calls. Naive Fibonacci is exactly this, which is why it is unusable past about forty.

prompt: Merge sort calls itself twice but HALVES the input each time. Why is that not exponential?
optionA: The halves are smaller, so each call returns immediately
optionB: Each level handles the same total data, and there are only log n levels
optionC: One of the two calls is discarded before it runs
optionD: The two calls are made one after the other rather than both at the same time
correctAnswerText: Each level handles the same total data, and there are only log n levels
explanation: Halving bounds the depth at log n, and the branching only keeps each level the same size. Reducing by one instead gives n levels and a disaster.

prompt: Why does memoisation turn naive Fibonacci from exponential into linear?
optionA: There are only n distinct inputs, so each is computed once
optionB: It removes one of the two recursive calls from the function entirely
optionC: It converts the recursion into an iterative loop
optionD: It reduces the depth of the recursion to log n
correctAnswerText: There are only n distinct inputs, so each is computed once
explanation: The exponential cost was recomputing the same subproblems endlessly. Bounding the work by the number of distinct inputs is the whole trick.

prompt: Can every recursion be rewritten as a loop?
optionA: Yes, though branching ones need an explicit stack to do it
optionB: No, a tree traversal cannot be expressed at all without recursion
optionC: Yes, and the loop version is always simpler to read
optionD: No, unless the recursion is already tail-recursive
correctAnswerText: Yes, though branching ones need an explicit stack to do it
explanation: The loop version manages by hand what the call stack was managing for you. For a tree that is usually more code, not less.

prompt: Roughly how deep can a typical recursion go before the stack runs out?
optionA: Thousands to tens of thousands of frames
optionB: Several million frames on any modern machine
optionC: It is unlimited, since the stack grows as needed
optionD: A few hundred frames at most
correctAnswerText: Thousands to tens of thousands of frames
explanation: Enough for a balanced tree over millions of nodes, and nowhere near enough for one recursive call per element of a large list.

prompt: Why is recursing over a flat list usually a poor choice?
optionA: A list has no base case that can be defined for it
optionB: Depth grows with the list, so a large one overflows the stack
optionC: Recursive functions cannot access list elements directly by index
optionD: Each call copies the list, which uses quadratic memory
correctAnswerText: Depth grows with the list, so a large one overflows the stack
explanation: One frame per element buys nothing a loop does not do more cheaply. The shape of the data is not recursive, so the function need not be.

prompt: What is the right way to reason about whether a recursion is correct?
optionA: Assume the recursive call works, and check the base case and the combination
optionB: Check that the depth never exceeds the available stack
optionC: Trace every level of calls by hand for a realistic input
optionD: Confirm that the function calls itself exactly once on every possible code branch
correctAnswerText: Assume the recursive call works, and check the base case and the combination
explanation: Tracing more than two levels defeats most people and proves nothing. Base case correct, plus one step correct given the rest, is the whole argument.

prompt: Why does writing a function tail-recursively often not prevent a stack overflow?
optionA: Tail calls are eliminated only when the depth is known in advance
optionB: The optimisation applies only to functions with one parameter
optionC: Tail recursion still keeps every frame by definition
optionD: Most mainstream runtimes do not eliminate tail calls
correctAnswerText: Most mainstream runtimes do not eliminate tail calls
explanation: It is an optimisation a runtime may perform, not a language guarantee. Writing tail-recursive code and assuming it is free is a common disappointment.

prompt: How do you total the sizes of every file in a folder tree of unknown depth?
optionA: Loop over the top-level entries and sum their sizes
optionB: Recurse into each subfolder and add what it returns
optionC: Count the folders, then multiply by the average file size
optionD: Flatten the tree into a list first, then loop over it
correctAnswerText: Recurse into each subfolder and add what it returns
explanation: Unknown depth is what rules out loops written in advance. Flattening works but needs its own traversal, which will itself be recursive.

prompt: What should the first lines of a recursive function normally do?
optionA: Make the recursive call and then hold on to its result
optionB: Validate that the input is of the expected type
optionC: Reduce the input in preparation for the next call
optionD: Check the base case and return before any other work
correctAnswerText: Check the base case and return before any other work
explanation: The guard clause comes first so nothing below it has to consider the empty or terminal case. It also makes the termination argument visible at a glance.

prompt: A recursion needs to build up a result across calls. What is the usual approach?
optionA: Pass the partial result down as a parameter, or combine on the way back
optionB: Store the partial result in a variable declared outside the function body
optionC: Return early as soon as the first result is available
optionD: Call the function twice and add the two results together
correctAnswerText: Pass the partial result down as a parameter, or combine on the way back
explanation: Both are clean and testable. A variable outside the function makes it stateful, so two concurrent uses interfere and a second call sees the first one's result.

prompt: You must find every value with a given key in a JSON document of arbitrary shape. What fits?
optionA: Three nested loops, which covers most realistic documents anyway
optionB: A loop over the top-level keys, checking each one
optionC: Recursion, descending into each object and array encountered
optionD: A regular expression run over the raw JSON text
correctAnswerText: Recursion, descending into each object and array encountered
explanation: Arbitrary nesting is the signature of a recursive problem. Fixed nesting depth is an assumption the next document will break.

prompt: When is memoisation the right fix for a slow recursion?
optionA: When the function is being called from inside a loop
optionB: When the same inputs recur across different branches of the call tree
optionC: Whenever the recursion goes deeper than about a few thousand stack frames
optionD: Whenever the function calls itself more than once
correctAnswerText: When the same inputs recur across different branches of the call tree
explanation: Overlapping subproblems is the precondition. Merge sort branches twice and memoising it gains nothing, because no two calls share an input.

prompt: A tree traversal overflows the stack on deep trees. What is the fix?
optionA: Memoise the function so fewer calls are made
optionB: Rewrite it as a loop with an explicit stack of pending nodes
optionC: Increase the recursion depth limit in the runtime configuration
optionD: Process the tree one level at a time, recursing on each
correctAnswerText: Rewrite it as a loop with an explicit stack of pending nodes
explanation: The pending work moves from the call stack to a data structure on the heap, which is far larger. Raising the limit postpones the problem rather than removing it.

prompt: Can a recursive function have more than one base case?
optionA: Yes — any input that returns without recursing is one
optionB: Only when the recursive calls are mutually recursive
optionC: Only if the function takes more than one parameter
optionD: No, a second base case makes termination impossible to prove
correctAnswerText: Yes — any input that returns without recursing is one
explanation: Fibonacci needs two, and a tree walk needs one for null and often one for a leaf. What matters is that every path reaches one of them.

prompt: What should you test first in a recursive function?
optionA: The performance, to confirm that it finishes in a reasonable time
optionB: Several inputs of the same size to confirm consistency
