optionC: The subclass cannot be compiled at all without the parent class being present
optionD: The parent and the subclass must live in the same source file
correctAnswerText: The subclass depends on the parent's internals, not just its interface
explanation: Protected members, call order, what the parent does internally — all of it becomes something the subclass can be broken by. Hence "the fragile base class".

prompt: What does "a class should have one reason to change" mean in practice?
optionA: A class should never be modified once it has been released
optionB: A class should contain no more than a handful of methods
optionC: Each class should only ever be changed by one developer at a time
optionD: One kind of requirement changing should affect only one class
correctAnswerText: One kind of requirement changing should affect only one class
explanation: A class that formats, validates and saves has three unrelated reasons to be edited, so three teams keep colliding in it.

prompt: What does making an object immutable buy you?
optionA: It cannot be put into an invalid state after it is constructed
optionB: It occupies rather less memory than a mutable equivalent would do
optionC: It can be inherited from more safely by other classes
optionD: It removes the need for the class to have a constructor
correctAnswerText: It cannot be put into an invalid state after it is constructed
explanation: Validate once and the guarantee holds forever, including across threads and when it is used as a key. It is encapsulation taken to its limit.

prompt: Three payment methods each need different processing. What is the cleanest design?
optionA: One class with a switch statement over the payment type
optionB: One interface with a process method, implemented three times
optionC: Three entirely unrelated classes, each called from its own branch
optionD: A base class holding all three behaviours behind flags
correctAnswerText: One interface with a process method, implemented three times
explanation: Adding a fourth method means adding one class rather than editing a conditional that may appear in several places.

prompt: An Order must always have at least one line. Where does that rule belong?
optionA: In the user interface, which is where the lines are actually added
optionB: In the service that saves the order to the database
optionC: In a validate method the caller is expected to call
optionD: In the constructor, so an invalid Order cannot exist at all
correctAnswerText: In the constructor, so an invalid Order cannot exist at all
explanation: A rule enforced at construction is a rule no code path can skip. A validate method is a rule somebody has to remember, which is a different guarantee.

prompt: Two classes need the same logging behaviour. What should you do?
optionA: Make one inherit from the other and share it
optionB: Give each one a logger object to use
optionC: Copy the logging code into both classes
optionD: Make both inherit from a LoggingBase class
correctAnswerText: Give each one a logger object to use
explanation: Shared code is not a reason to claim a family relationship. A logger passed in can also be swapped in a test, which a base class makes awkward.

prompt: A class creates its own database connection internally. Why is that a problem?
optionA: The connection will not be closed when the object is destroyed
optionB: The class will hold more state than it strictly needs to
optionC: Creating a connection is too slow to do inside a constructor
optionD: It cannot be tested or reused without a real database present
correctAnswerText: It cannot be tested or reused without a real database present
explanation: A dependency created inside cannot be replaced from outside. Passing it in costs one parameter and makes the class testable in isolation.

prompt: A class has grown to 800 lines. What is the best signal for how to split it?
optionA: Groups of methods that use the same subset of the fields
optionB: The order in which the methods happen to be written
optionC: Splitting it evenly so that each part is about the same size as the others
optionD: Separating the public methods from the private ones
correctAnswerText: Groups of methods that use the same subset of the fields
explanation: Methods clustering around different fields is usually two classes sharing a file. It is a structural signal rather than a judgement about length.

prompt: You must add a new report type without touching the existing ones. What makes that possible?
optionA: The report types already sit behind a common interface
optionB: The existing reports are covered by a full test suite
optionC: The report code is kept in a separate module from the rest
optionD: The new report is written to match the existing style
correctAnswerText: The report types already sit behind a common interface
explanation: Extension without modification needs a seam that was put there in advance. Tests tell you whether you broke something; the interface is what lets you avoid touching it.

prompt: You need to move a few related values around with no rules attached. What should you use?
optionA: A class with a constructor that validates every value
optionB: A full class with private fields and accessors for each
optionC: A simple record or data object, with no behaviour at all
optionD: Separate parameters passed to each function that needs them
correctAnswerText: A simple record or data object, with no behaviour at all
explanation: Where there is no invariant there is nothing to encapsulate, and the accessors are ceremony. Not every group of values wants to be a class.

prompt: What does a class named OrderManager usually indicate?
optionA: It follows a widely used and well-understood naming convention
optionB: It is the single entry point through which orders are accessed
optionC: Nobody decided what it is responsible for, so it accumulates
optionD: It manages the lifecycle of order objects in memory
correctAnswerText: Nobody decided what it is responsible for, so it accumulates
explanation: Manager, Helper, Util and Processor are names that exclude nothing, so nothing is ever out of place in them. They grow until somebody splits them.

prompt: Code reads an object's fields, calculates something and writes a field back. What does that suggest?
optionA: The object should expose fewer fields to its callers
optionB: The fields should be made public for convenience
optionC: The calculation belongs inside the object itself
optionD: The calculation should be moved into a utility class
correctAnswerText: The calculation belongs inside the object itself
explanation: Behaviour has drifted away from the data it depends on. Moving it in is what makes the object more than a bag of values.

prompt: What makes a class easy to test in isolation?
optionA: Its methods are short and each does only one thing
optionB: Its dependencies arrive from outside and can be substituted
optionC: It inherits from a base class that the tests are able to extend
optionD: It has no private methods that the tests cannot reach
correctAnswerText: Its dependencies arrive from outside and can be substituted
explanation: Substitutable dependencies are the whole of it. Short methods help you read the class; they do not help you run it without a database.

prompt: Square inherits from Rectangle. Setting the width of a Square also changes its height, and code that expected a Rectangle breaks. What is the lesson?
optionA: Square and Rectangle should both inherit from a common Shape base class
optionB: The width and height fields should have been made private
optionC: The setters should raise an error when used on a Square
optionD: Inheritance must preserve behaviour, not just real-world categories
correctAnswerText: Inheritance must preserve behaviour, not just real-world categories
explanation: A square is a rectangle in geometry and not in code, because it cannot be used everywhere a rectangle can. Substitutability is the real test.

prompt: Understanding one class means reading four ancestors. What has gone wrong?
optionA: The class simply has too many methods for its own level of abstraction
optionB: The ancestors should have been marked as abstract classes
optionC: The hierarchy is missing interfaces between its levels
optionD: Behaviour is scattered up the hierarchy, so no class can be read alone
correctAnswerText: Behaviour is scattered up the hierarchy, so no class can be read alone
explanation: Deep hierarchies distribute one behaviour across several files, and a change at the top reaches everything below it in ways nobody can see locally.

prompt: A small change to a base class breaks three subclasses in different ways. What does that reveal?
optionA: The subclasses should have overridden rather more of the parent methods
optionB: The subclasses were written by developers who have since left
optionC: The subclasses depend on how the parent works, not just what it does
optionD: The base class contains too much code for one class to hold
correctAnswerText: The subclasses depend on how the parent works, not just what it does
explanation: The fragile base class problem. The parent cannot be changed safely because its internals became part of the contract without anybody writing that down.

prompt: Every class is fields with getters and setters, and all the logic sits in service classes. What is the consequence?
optionA: The rules are scattered, so no object can guarantee anything about itself
optionB: The design cannot make use of inheritance at any level
optionC: The services become measurably slower because of all the extra method calls
optionD: The classes cannot be serialised or stored in a database
correctAnswerText: The rules are scattered, so no object can guarantee anything about itself
explanation: It works, and plenty of systems are built this way. What is lost is the guarantee: with setters open, the same rule must be re-checked everywhere.

prompt: A class inherits from another purely to reuse two of its methods, and inherits nine it must ignore. What is wrong?
optionA: The subclass should simply override the nine methods that it does not want
optionB: The two useful methods should have been made static instead
optionC: The parent class should have made the nine methods private
optionD: The relationship is not is-a, so the inherited surface is a liability
correctAnswerText: The relationship is not is-a, so the inherited surface is a liability
explanation: Every ignored method is still callable on the subclass, and callers will eventually call them. Composition takes the two and leaves the nine.

prompt: The same switch over a type field appears in six places. What is the underlying problem?
optionA: The type is being checked too often for good performance
optionB: The six switches should be extracted into a single function
optionC: Behaviour that varies by type is not living with the type
optionD: The type field should have been an enumeration rather than text
correctAnswerText: Behaviour that varies by type is not living with the type
explanation: Adding a seventh type means finding all six and remembering each one. Polymorphism makes the compiler do the finding.

prompt: An object must have init() called after construction or it misbehaves. What is the flaw?
optionA: The object cannot be reinitialised once it has been used
optionB: The init method is doing work that belongs in a service
optionC: It has a valid-looking state that is not actually usable
optionD: The constructor is taking too few parameters to be useful
correctAnswerText: It has a valid-looking state that is not actually usable
explanation: Two-phase construction means every caller must remember step two, and the type system will not remind them. Whatever init does belongs in the constructor.

prompt: A class keeps its list of items private but returns it directly from a getter. What has it given away?
optionA: Everything — callers can modify the list without the class knowing
optionB: Thread safety, but only if two threads read at once
optionC: Performance, since returning the list requires a copy
optionD: Nothing at all, because the field itself is still declared as private
correctAnswerText: Everything — callers can modify the list without the class knowing
explanation: Private is about the reference, not about what it points at. Returning a copy, or a read-only view, is what the private was meant to achieve.

prompt: One class is edited in almost every pull request. What does that tell you?
optionA: It is badly named and people cannot find the right alternative
optionB: It is the most important class in the system and so deserves the most attention
optionC: It needs more test coverage than the other classes have
optionD: It has taken on several responsibilities that change independently
correctAnswerText: It has taken on several responsibilities that change independently
explanation: Edit frequency is a measurable proxy for responsibility count, and it also predicts merge conflicts. Git history is a design review nobody had to write.

prompt: Two classes each hold a reference to the other and call into it. What does that usually mean?
optionA: One of them should inherit from the other instead
optionB: The boundary between them is in the wrong place
optionC: They should be merged into a single larger class
optionD: The references should be made weak to avoid a leak
correctAnswerText: The boundary between them is in the wrong place
explanation: Neither can be understood, tested or changed alone, so they are one unit pretending to be two. The fix is usually a third thing that owns the interaction.

prompt: Of the four pillars, which does the most work in a real codebase?
optionA: Abstraction — hiding detail is what allows a system to be understood
optionB: Polymorphism — it is what distinguishes objects from plain functions
optionC: Encapsulation — a guarantee about state is what everything else rests on
optionD: Inheritance — reusing behaviour is what makes really large systems possible
correctAnswerText: Encapsulation — a guarantee about state is what everything else rests on
explanation: An object that cannot be put into an invalid state is worth more than any hierarchy. Inheritance is the one most taught and the one most often regretted.

prompt: When is inheritance genuinely the right tool?
optionA: When every subclass can be used wherever the parent can, without exception
optionB: When a framework or library requires a particular base class
optionC: When several classes would otherwise end up duplicating the very same methods
optionD: When the classes form a natural category in the problem domain
correctAnswerText: When every subclass can be used wherever the parent can, without exception
explanation: Substitutability with no exceptions. "Natural category" is what produces the square and the rectangle, and duplication is what composition is for.

prompt: When is a class the wrong shape for the problem?
optionA: When there is no state to protect and a function would do
optionB: When the language also supports functional programming
optionC: When the code will be used by only one other module
optionD: When the problem involves fewer than three related values
correctAnswerText: When there is no state to protect and a function would do
explanation: A class with no fields and one method is a function with ceremony. Objects earn their cost by owning state; without state there is nothing to own.

prompt: What is a good object-oriented design actually optimising for?
optionA: How closely the classes mirror objects in the real world
optionB: How cheaply the system can be changed when requirements move
optionC: How quickly the program runs once it has been compiled
optionD: How few lines of code are needed in order to express the behaviour
correctAnswerText: How cheaply the system can be changed when requirements move
explanation: Every trade in this subject is about the second change and the tenth, not the first. Mirroring the real world is a heuristic that sometimes helps and often misleads.

prompt: What does an unnecessary layer of abstraction cost?
optionA: The program runs measurably more slowly at every single call site involved
optionB: The compiler is unable to check the code as thoroughly
optionC: The abstraction cannot be removed once it has been added
optionD: A reader must follow more indirection to find where anything happens
correctAnswerText: A reader must follow more indirection to find where anything happens
explanation: Interfaces with exactly one implementation are the usual case. Abstraction is worth paying for when a second implementation exists, or is genuinely imminent.

prompt: A class is very hard to write a unit test for. What is that usually telling you?
optionA: The testing framework is not well suited to this kind of code
optionB: The class is complex enough to need integration tests instead
optionC: The test should be written against its interface rather than the class
optionD: It has too many responsibilities or dependencies it creates itself
correctAnswerText: It has too many responsibilities or dependencies it creates itself
explanation: Testability is a design property, not a testing property. Difficulty writing the test is the most honest design feedback available.

prompt: Reviewing a new class, what single question is most revealing?
optionA: Could this class be written with fewer dependencies?
optionB: Does this class follow the same style as all of the others do?
optionC: How many lines and methods does this class contain?
optionD: What can this object promise that is true of it at all times?
correctAnswerText: What can this object promise that is true of it at all times?
explanation: If the answer is nothing, it is a data holder and should stop pretending otherwise. If it is something, the review becomes whether the code actually enforces it.

prompt: Why is "model the real world" unreliable advice?
optionA: Real-world models produce too many classes to manage
optionB: The real world changes rather faster than the software modelling it can be updated
optionC: Real-world categories do not predict which code can substitute for which
optionD: Most business problems have no real-world objects to model
correctAnswerText: Real-world categories do not predict which code can substitute for which
explanation: It is how Square ends up under Rectangle and Manager ends up under Employee. The question is always what can stand in for what, not what is a kind of what.

prompt: Why is a wrong inheritance hierarchy so expensive to correct later?
optionA: Tests written against subclasses will all need rewriting
optionB: Every subclass depends on it, so the change is never local
optionC: The hierarchy will have been documented in several different places
optionD: Most languages do not allow a class to change its parent
correctAnswerText: Every subclass depends on it, so the change is never local
explanation: Composition can be changed one class at a time; a hierarchy has to be unpicked all at once. That asymmetry is the strongest argument for preferring composition.

prompt: What is object orientation ultimately trying to achieve?
optionA: Representing the concepts of the problem domain as code
optionB: Confining what any one piece of code can break to a small, known area
optionC: Allowing behaviour to be reused across a great many different classes
optionD: Reducing the total amount of code that has to be written
correctAnswerText: Confining what any one piece of code can break to a small, known area
explanation: Every pillar serves that: encapsulation bounds what can be touched, interfaces bound what is depended on, polymorphism bounds what a change must reach.

prompt: What does __init__ do?
optionA: Runs once when the class itself is first defined
optionB: Sets up a newly created object before anyone uses it
optionC: Imports the module that the class has been written in
optionD: Creates and returns the new object when the class is called
correctAnswerText: Sets up a newly created object before anyone uses it
explanation: It initialises; __new__ is what actually creates. That is why __init__ returns nothing and assigns to self instead.

prompt: What is self in a Python method?
optionA: A reference to the object that called the current method
optionB: A reserved keyword that refers to the class the method has been defined in
optionC: A reserved name that Python treats specially inside methods
optionD: The instance the method was called on, passed in as the first argument
correctAnswerText: The instance the method was called on, passed in as the first argument
explanation: An ordinary parameter with a conventional name — you could call it anything. Python passes the instance explicitly where most languages hide it.

prompt: What does a single leading underscore on an attribute mean?
optionA: The attribute is excluded when the object is copied
optionB: The attribute is private and cannot be read from outside
optionC: A convention signalling "internal", enforced by nothing
optionD: The attribute is read-only once it has been assigned
correctAnswerText: A convention signalling "internal", enforced by nothing
explanation: It is a message to the reader, not a rule for the runtime. Any code can read and write it exactly as before.

prompt: What does super() give you?
optionA: A copy of the parent object held inside this one
optionB: The direct parent class of the current class
optionC: The class that originally defined the method being called
optionD: The next class in the method resolution order
correctAnswerText: The next class in the method resolution order
explanation: Not the parent — the next one along the MRO, which with multiple inheritance may be a sibling. The distinction only shows up when it matters.

prompt: What is a class attribute?
optionA: An attribute that is assigned to self inside the __init__ method
optionB: An attribute that may only be read, never written to
optionC: A value that each instance receives its own copy of
optionD: A value defined on the class itself and shared by every instance
correctAnswerText: A value defined on the class itself and shared by every instance
explanation: Defined in the class body rather than on self. Shared is the key word, and it is where a surprising number of bugs begin.

prompt: What are methods like __str__ and __len__ for?
optionA: Defining methods that run automatically at fixed points in time
optionB: Marking out methods that Python should treat as private to the class itself
optionC: Letting your objects work with Python's built-in syntax and functions
optionD: Providing documentation that tools can read from the class
correctAnswerText: Letting your objects work with Python's built-in syntax and functions
explanation: Define __len__ and len() works on your object; define __eq__ and == does. They are the hooks that make a class feel native.

prompt: What does the @property decorator do?
optionA: Makes a method readable as though it were a plain attribute
optionB: Registers an attribute so it appears when the object is printed
optionC: Marks an attribute so that it cannot be changed once set
optionD: Declares a value that belongs to the class rather than instances
correctAnswerText: Makes a method readable as though it were a plain attribute
explanation: It means a field can later become computed without any caller changing, which is why Python does not need getters everywhere from the start.

prompt: What does @classmethod receive as its first argument?
optionA: The instance the method was called on
optionB: Nothing — it takes only the arguments given
optionC: The module in which the class was defined
optionD: The class itself, conventionally named cls
correctAnswerText: The class itself, conventionally named cls
explanation: Getting the class is what makes it useful for alternative constructors, since it works correctly for a subclass too.

prompt: What does @dataclass do?
optionA: Prevents the class from having any methods of its own
optionB: Writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from the declared fields
optionC: Makes every attribute of the class immutable by default
optionD: Stores the object's data in a dictionary rather than attributes
correctAnswerText: Writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from the declared fields
explanation: It removes the boilerplate that made simple Python classes tedious. frozen=True adds immutability, which is a separate choice.

prompt: What is duck typing?
optionA: Declaring the expected type of every parameter in a function
optionB: Converting an object automatically into whichever type happens to be required
optionC: Accepting any object that has the methods you need, whatever its type
optionD: Checking an object's type before calling any method on it
correctAnswerText: Accepting any object that has the methods you need, whatever its type
explanation: Python asks what an object can do rather than what it is. It is why explicit interfaces are far less central here than in Java or C#.

prompt: What does a double leading underscore actually do?
optionA: Renames the attribute to include the class name, avoiding collisions
optionB: Removes the attribute from the object's dictionary entirely
optionC: Makes the attribute genuinely inaccessible from anywhere outside the class
optionD: Prevents subclasses from reading or overriding the attribute
correctAnswerText: Renames the attribute to include the class name, avoiding collisions
explanation: __x becomes _ClassName__x, which is reachable by anyone who knows the rule. It exists to stop subclasses clashing, not to enforce privacy.

prompt: When is a default argument value evaluated?
optionA: Once, when the function is defined
optionB: Every time the function is called without that argument
optionC: Once per instance, when the object is constructed
optionD: Every time the function is called, regardless of arguments
correctAnswerText: Once, when the function is defined
explanation: This single fact explains the mutable default trap completely. A list written as a default is one list, shared by every call forever.

prompt: A class defines items = [] in its body. What happens when one instance appends to it?
optionA: Only that one instance sees it, since assignment creates a copy
optionB: Python raises an error for modifying a class attribute
optionC: The instance gets its own copy the first time it appends
optionD: Every instance sees the new item, because the list is shared
correctAnswerText: Every instance sees the new item, because the list is shared
explanation: Appending mutates the one shared list. Assigning with self.items = [] would create an instance attribute, which is why the two look deceptively similar.

prompt: Where does Python look when you read obj.x?
optionA: The ancestors first, so the base class always wins
optionB: The class first, then the instance that was created from it
optionC: The instance first, then the class, then its ancestors
optionD: Only the instance — class attributes need the class name
correctAnswerText: The instance first, then the class, then its ancestors
explanation: Instance shadows class. It is why assigning to self.x hides a class attribute of the same name for that object only.

prompt: What happens if you define two methods with the same name in one class?
optionA: Python chooses between them based on the arguments given
optionB: Both are kept and tried in the order they were written
optionC: Python raises an error when the class is defined
optionD: The second silently replaces the first
correctAnswerText: The second silently replaces the first
explanation: A class body is executed, so the second assignment wins. Python has no overloading; default and keyword arguments cover the same ground.

prompt: Why do Python classes usually not start with getters and setters?
optionA: Attributes in Python are already protected from being changed from outside
optionB: Python does not allow methods to be named get_ or set_
optionC: Getters and setters make attribute access measurably slower
optionD: A plain attribute can become a property later without callers changing
correctAnswerText: A plain attribute can become a property later without callers changing
explanation: The upgrade path is free, so the boilerplate buys nothing in advance. In a language without properties you must add them up front or break callers later.

prompt: Why is checking isinstance() everywhere considered unpythonic?
optionA: It produces error messages that are hard for callers to read
optionB: It rejects objects that would have worked perfectly well
optionC: It is significantly slower than calling the method directly
optionD: It does not work correctly with classes that use inheritance
correctAnswerText: It rejects objects that would have worked perfectly well
explanation: A test double, a wrapper or a new implementation all fail the check while satisfying the requirement. The relevant question is what the object can do.

prompt: Python allows multiple inheritance. What resolves which method is used?
optionA: The method resolution order, computed from the class hierarchy
optionB: The first parent listed, always, with the rest used only for their fields
optionC: The order in which the parent classes were first imported
optionD: The parent that defines the method with the most arguments
correctAnswerText: The method resolution order, computed from the class hierarchy
explanation: A linearisation of the whole hierarchy, visible as ClassName.__mro__. It is deterministic, and it is also why super() is not simply "the parent".

prompt: You define __eq__ on a class. What else must you consider?
optionA: __str__, so that equal objects print in the same way
optionB: __hash__, or the objects can no longer be used in sets and dicts
optionC: __len__, so that equality can compare their sizes
optionD: __init__, so that objects which are equal get constructed identically
correctAnswerText: __hash__, or the objects can no longer be used in sets and dicts
explanation: Python sets __hash__ to None when you define __eq__, making instances unhashable. Equal objects must hash equally, so the two belong together.

prompt: In Python, what can you do with a class that you cannot in many other languages?
optionA: Define it inside another class to keep it private
optionB: Call its methods without creating any instance of it
optionC: Pass it around as a value, store it, and create it at runtime
optionD: Change which parent class it inherits from after it has been defined
correctAnswerText: Pass it around as a value, store it, and create it at runtime
explanation: Classes are ordinary objects, which is what makes registries, factories and decorators so natural here and so ceremonious elsewhere.

prompt: How do you write a parameter that should default to an empty list?
optionA: Default it to an empty tuple and convert it to a list
optionB: Default it to None and create the list inside the function
optionC: Declare it without a default and require the caller to pass one
optionD: Default it to an empty list, which Python copies per call
correctAnswerText: Default it to None and create the list inside the function
explanation: The None sentinel is the standard idiom and exists entirely because defaults are evaluated once. An empty tuple works but says less about intent.

prompt: An existing public attribute now needs validation on assignment. What do you do?
optionA: Move the validation into the constructor and freeze the attribute
optionB: Rename it with an underscore and add explicit get and set methods
optionC: Make it a property with a setter that validates, changing no callers
optionD: Validate it in every single place that currently assigns to the attribute
correctAnswerText: Make it a property with a setter that validates, changing no callers
explanation: This is precisely what properties are for: the syntax at the call site is unchanged while the behaviour behind it becomes whatever you need.

prompt: You want a second way to construct a class, from a dictionary. What is the idiom?
optionA: An optional dictionary parameter on the existing __init__
optionB: A module-level function that builds and returns the object
optionC: A second __init__ that accepts a dictionary instead
optionD: A @classmethod named from_dict that returns cls(...)
correctAnswerText: A @classmethod named from_dict that returns cls(...)
explanation: Using cls rather than the class name means a subclass gets its own type back. The overloaded __init__ is not available, since Python has no overloading.

prompt: A dataclass needs a field defaulting to an empty list. How is it declared?
optionA: With a plain default of [], which the dataclass then handles safely for you
optionB: With field(default_factory=list), which builds a new one per instance
optionC: With a default of None, checked inside __post_init__
optionD: Without a default, so every caller must supply the list
correctAnswerText: With field(default_factory=list), which builds a new one per instance
explanation: Dataclasses refuse a mutable default outright, which is one of the few places Python protects you from this trap rather than letting it through.

prompt: Which dunder method is most worth adding to a class you will debug?
optionA: __eq__, because it is needed to compare objects in tests
optionB: __str__, because it is what the users of the program will actually see
optionC: __repr__, because it is what appears in logs and the debugger
optionD: __len__, because it shows how much data the object holds
correctAnswerText: __repr__, because it is what appears in logs and the debugger
explanation: Without it you get a memory address, and a list of ten objects tells you nothing at all. __str__ falls back to __repr__ but not the other way round.

prompt: A subclass defines __init__. What must it usually do?
optionA: Avoid assigning to any attribute the parent also assigns to
optionB: Redefine every single attribute that the parent class would have assigned
optionC: Call super().__init__() so the parent can set up its own state
optionD: Nothing — Python calls the parent constructor automatically
correctAnswerText: Call super().__init__() so the parent can set up its own state
explanation: Python does not chain constructors for you. Forgetting the call leaves the parent's attributes missing, and the failure appears much later.

prompt: You want subclasses to be required to implement a method. What enforces that?
optionA: An abstract base class with @abstractmethod
optionB: A type annotation declaring the method on the parent
optionC: A comment in the base class stating the requirement
optionD: A method in the parent that raises NotImplementedError
correctAnswerText: An abstract base class with @abstractmethod
explanation: ABCs fail at instantiation, before anything runs. Raising NotImplementedError also works and fails only when that method is finally called.

prompt: A class creates its own HTTP client inside __init__. How do you make it testable?
optionA: Move the client creation into a separate method to override
optionB: Patch the client module in every test that uses the class
optionC: Add a flag that switches the class into a test mode
optionD: Accept the client as a parameter, defaulting to a real one
correctAnswerText: Accept the client as a parameter, defaulting to a real one
explanation: One parameter, one default, and duck typing means the test can pass anything with the right methods. Patching works and couples the test to the import path.

prompt: A class has no attributes and one method. What should it be?
optionA: A class with a classmethod instead
optionB: A dataclass with no declared fields
optionC: A function in a module
optionD: A class with a @staticmethod on it
correctAnswerText: A function in a module
explanation: Python has first-class functions and real modules, so a stateless class is ceremony borrowed from languages that have neither.

prompt: A class holds a resource that must always be released. What should it provide?
optionA: __enter__ and __exit__, so it can be used with a with statement
optionB: A timer that releases the resource after a fixed period
optionC: A __del__ method that releases it when the object is garbage collected
optionD: A close method that callers are documented to call
correctAnswerText: __enter__ and __exit__, so it can be used with a with statement
explanation: with guarantees cleanup on every path, including an exception. __del__ runs at an unpredictable time and may not run at all.

prompt: A function with a list default returns results from previous calls as well. Why?
optionA: The caller is passing the same list object in each time
optionB: The list is being held alive by a reference somewhere else
optionC: The default list was created once and is shared by every call
optionD: The function is quietly caching its results without being asked to
correctAnswerText: The default list was created once and is shared by every call
explanation: Defaults are evaluated at definition, so there is exactly one list for the life of the process. It looks correct and fails only once it has been called twice.

prompt: Adding an item to one object's list makes it appear on every object. What is the cause?
optionA: The list is being stored in a module-level variable
optionB: The list is a class attribute, not assigned per instance in __init__
optionC: The append method modifies the existing list in place rather than copying it
optionD: The objects were created by copying rather than constructing
correctAnswerText: The list is a class attribute, not assigned per instance in __init__
explanation: One list on the class, shared by all. Assigning self.items = [] in __init__ gives each instance its own, and the two spellings look almost identical.

prompt: A subclass raises AttributeError for an attribute the parent sets. What was forgotten?
optionA: The subclass __init__ never called super().__init__()
optionB: The subclass overrode the attribute with a method
optionC: The parent class was never imported into the subclass module
optionD: The parent attribute was given a double underscore name
correctAnswerText: The subclass __init__ never called super().__init__()
explanation: Python does not chain constructors automatically, so defining __init__ in the subclass silently replaces the parent's setup entirely.

prompt: A developer used __balance to make a field private, and other code is still changing it. How?
optionA: Name mangling only renames it; _ClassName__balance still reaches it
optionB: The field was also assigned somewhere else without the leading underscores
optionC: Subclasses of the class are able to bypass the mangling
optionD: Python removes the mangling when the module is imported
correctAnswerText: Name mangling only renames it; _ClassName__balance still reaches it
explanation: Mangling exists to prevent accidental collisions between a class and its subclasses. Treating it as an access control is importing an assumption from another language.

prompt: After adding __eq__, objects can no longer be put in a set. Why?
optionA: Sets require __lt__ as well in order to order their contents
optionB: The __eq__ method is returning some value that is not actually a boolean
optionC: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None unless you define it too
optionD: Objects with custom equality are never allowed in a set
correctAnswerText: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None unless you define it too
explanation: Python removes the default hash because it was based on identity and would now contradict your equality. Equal objects must hash equally.

prompt: A method appears to have no effect, and the class defines it twice. What is happening?
optionA: The later definition replaced the earlier one silently
optionB: The first definition runs and the second is ignored
optionC: Python is calling the version inherited from the parent
optionD: The two definitions are being merged into a single method
correctAnswerText: The later definition replaced the earlier one silently
explanation: The class body is executed top to bottom, so the second assignment wins with no warning at all. Linters catch it; the language does not.

prompt: An object used as a dict key cannot be found after one of its fields changed. Why?
optionA: The comparison now fails because the fields are different
optionB: Its hash changed, so the lookup goes to a different bucket
optionC: The dictionary was rebuilt without that entry being copied
optionD: Dictionaries do not permit objects to be used as keys
correctAnswerText: Its hash changed, so the lookup goes to a different bucket
explanation: It is present and unreachable at the same time. This is why frozen dataclasses and tuples make far safer keys than mutable objects.

prompt: Changing a class attribute updates some instances but not others. What explains it?
optionA: The class attribute is being cached on first read per instance
optionB: The attribute is mutable and each instance copied it
optionC: The instances that did not change had assigned their own value
optionD: Only instances created after the change see the new value
correctAnswerText: The instances that did not change had assigned their own value
explanation: Assigning to self.x creates an instance attribute that shadows the class one from then on. Reading looks identical; writing does not.

prompt: A class releases its file handle in __del__, and handles are leaking. Why?
optionA: File handles cannot be closed from inside __del__ at all
optionB: __del__ is never called on any object whose methods raised an exception
optionC: __del__ only runs when the interpreter is shutting down
optionD: __del__ runs when the object is collected, which may be late or never
correctAnswerText: __del__ runs when the object is collected, which may be late or never
explanation: Reference cycles and interpreter shutdown both make it unreliable. A context manager releases deterministically, which is what the guarantee requires.

prompt: What do the mutable default and the shared class attribute have in common?
optionA: Both are rejected outright by the interpreter when the module is first loaded
optionB: Both only occur in classes that use multiple inheritance
optionC: Both work on the first call and fail only once state has accumulated
optionD: Both are caught by type checkers before the code is run
correctAnswerText: Both work on the first call and fail only once state has accumulated
explanation: A single-call test passes, and so does review. They need a second call, or a second instance, and neither is usually present when the code is written.

prompt: Python enforces no real privacy. What does it rely on instead?
optionA: Tooling that simply prevents any access to underscore-prefixed attributes
optionB: Type checkers that reject access to internal attributes
optionC: Documentation that lists which attributes may be used
optionD: A convention that readers respect, and the consequences if they do not
correctAnswerText: A convention that readers respect, and the consequences if they do not
explanation: "We are all consenting adults." It puts the weight on clear naming and shared discipline rather than on a compiler.

prompt: Why are classes needed less often in Python than in Java?
optionA: Python cannot express inheritance as precisely as Java can
optionB: Python programs are usually rather smaller and simpler than Java ones
optionC: Functions, modules and dictionaries are all first-class already
optionD: Python classes are slower than the equivalent functions
correctAnswerText: Functions, modules and dictionaries are all first-class already
explanation: In Java a function must live in a class, so classes appear where there is no object. Python has no such requirement, so a class should mean something.

prompt: What does duck typing cost?
optionA: Performance, since the method must be looked up each time
optionB: Classes cannot be reused across different modules safely
optionC: Objects must be checked with isinstance before each and every call
optionD: The contract is implicit, so a mismatch surfaces at runtime
correctAnswerText: The contract is implicit, so a mismatch surfaces at runtime
explanation: Flexibility bought with a later failure. Type hints and protocols recover much of the safety without giving the flexibility back up.

prompt: What decides between a dataclass and a hand-written class?
optionA: Whether the type will be inherited from by other classes
optionB: How many separate fields the type is expected to contain in total
optionC: Whether the fields need to be serialised to JSON later
optionD: Whether the type mainly holds values or mainly enforces rules
correctAnswerText: Whether the type mainly holds values or mainly enforces rules
explanation: Dataclasses remove boilerplate from value types. A type with real invariants usually wants a constructor that can refuse, which is a different job.

prompt: Python permits multiple inheritance. Why is it still used sparingly?
optionA: It prevents the class from being used with duck typing
optionB: It is significantly slower than ordinary single inheritance is at runtime
optionC: Which implementation runs depends on an order few people can predict
optionD: Most Python versions do not support it consistently
correctAnswerText: Which implementation runs depends on an order few people can predict
explanation: The MRO is deterministic and not obvious, so behaviour depends on a base-class order that reads as arbitrary. Narrow mixins are the case that stays manageable.

prompt: Why does Python make you write self explicitly?
optionA: It allows a method to be called without any instance of the class existing
optionB: It lets the interpreter optimise how methods are dispatched
optionC: A method is just a function, and the instance is just its first argument
optionD: It makes the code easier for beginners to read and follow
correctAnswerText: A method is just a function, and the instance is just its first argument
explanation: There is no special method machinery to learn — which is also why a function can be attached to a class, and why decorators work on methods unchanged.

prompt: Reviewing a Python class, which check catches the most real bugs?
optionA: Whether the class defines __str__ as well as __repr__
optionB: Any mutable value used as a default or defined in the class body
optionC: Whether every attribute has a leading underscore where appropriate
optionD: Whether the class could have been written as a dataclass
correctAnswerText: Any mutable value used as a default or defined in the class body
explanation: Both shared-state traps have the same shape and the same signature in the source. Once you can see that shape, you find them by scanning.

prompt: What does Python's property mechanism let you defer?
optionA: Deciding which attributes should be visible to callers
optionB: Deciding whether an attribute needs logic behind it
optionC: Deciding whether the class should be immutable
optionD: Deciding what type each attribute is allowed to hold
correctAnswerText: Deciding whether an attribute needs logic behind it
explanation: Start with a plain attribute and add behaviour when a requirement appears. Deciding later, at no cost, is a genuinely unusual property of the language.

prompt: What does Python code written in a Java style typically look like?
optionA: Modules that import a great many other modules
optionB: Heavy use of dictionaries in place of proper objects
optionC: Very long functions, with hardly any classes defined anywhere at all
optionD: Getters and setters everywhere, deep hierarchies, stateless classes
correctAnswerText: Getters and setters everywhere, deep hierarchies, stateless classes
explanation: It works, and it carries ceremony that solves problems Python does not have. Recognising it is what lets a team write Python rather than translate.

prompt: What is the underlying difference between Python OOP and the Java model?
optionA: Python objects are faster to create than Java objects are
optionB: Python supports inheritance where Java supports interfaces
optionC: Python trusts the programmer where Java constrains them
optionD: Python classes cannot hold state that Java classes can hold
correctAnswerText: Python trusts the programmer where Java constrains them
explanation: No enforced privacy, no overloading, no required interfaces, no mandatory class for a function. More freedom and more responsibility, in equal measure.

prompt: Who is clean code written for?
optionA: The user, who experiences the result of well-structured code
optionB: The reviewer, who has to approve the change before it ships
optionC: The compiler, which produces rather better output from clearer code
optionD: The next person who has to change it, including you in six months
correctAnswerText: The next person who has to change it, including you in six months
explanation: Code is read many more times than it is written. Every rule in this subject is ultimately about that reader.

prompt: What makes a variable name good?
optionA: It is short enough to keep lines within the width limit
optionB: It includes the type of the value it is holding
optionC: It says what the value means, so the code needs no explanation
optionD: It follows the naming convention used by the rest of the whole file
correctAnswerText: It says what the value means, so the code needs no explanation
explanation: Meaning first. Conventions matter and are a much smaller effect; encoding the type is a habit from languages that could not show it to you.

prompt: What does "a function should do one thing" mean?
optionA: It should contain no more than one loop or conditional
optionB: It should return one value rather than several
optionC: It should be callable from only one place in the codebase
optionD: Everything it does should be at the same level of detail
correctAnswerText: Everything it does should be at the same level of detail
explanation: Mixing "validate the order" with "increment a counter" is two levels in one place. The count of statements is not the measure.

prompt: What should a comment explain?
optionA: What each line of the code does
optionB: How the code should be used by callers
optionC: Why the code is the way it is
optionD: Who wrote the code and when
correctAnswerText: Why the code is the way it is
explanation: The code already says what. Why it was done this way, and what was tried and rejected, is the thing that cannot be recovered by reading it.

prompt: What does "don't repeat yourself" actually mean?
optionA: Each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place
optionB: No two functions should contain identical lines of code
optionC: A function should never be called from more than one other place
optionD: Every value should be defined as a constant before use
correctAnswerText: Each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place
explanation: It is about knowledge, not text. Two identical lines that encode two unrelated rules are not duplication and should not be merged.

prompt: What is a magic number?
optionA: A literal value in the code whose meaning is not stated anywhere
optionB: A value that has been chosen by trial and error rather than reasoning
optionC: A number that must be recalculated whenever the data changes
optionD: A constant that is used in more than one module at once
correctAnswerText: A literal value in the code whose meaning is not stated anywhere
explanation: The problem is unexplained, not literal. `if (age >= 18)` is clear; `if (x >= 18)` in a discount calculation is not.

prompt: Why is clever code usually a problem?
optionA: It is more likely to contain an outright logical error
optionB: It takes longer to understand than it saved in writing
optionC: It cannot be optimised effectively by the compiler
optionD: It uses language features that are not widely supported
correctAnswerText: It takes longer to understand than it saved in writing
explanation: The cost is paid by every future reader, repeatedly, and the saving was paid once. Occasionally the cleverness is genuinely necessary, and then it needs a comment.

prompt: What is a guard clause?
optionA: An early return that handles a special case before the main logic
optionB: A wrapper that catches exceptions before they escape
optionC: A check that protects a resource from concurrent access
optionD: A condition that validates the arguments a function has been given
correctAnswerText: An early return that handles a special case before the main logic
explanation: It removes a level of nesting for every case it handles. Deeply nested conditionals usually turn out to be a stack of guards written the other way up.

prompt: What is a hidden side effect?
optionA: A function that modifies one of the arguments it was given
optionB: A function whose result depends on the current time
optionC: A function changing something its name gives no hint of
optionD: A function that writes to a log while doing its work
correctAnswerText: A function changing something its name gives no hint of
explanation: getUser() that also updates a last-seen timestamp. The problem is the gap between the name and the behaviour, not the effect itself.

prompt: Why does consistency matter even when the convention is not the best one?
optionA: It allows automated tools to reformat the code safely
optionB: Consistent code is significantly faster to execute
optionC: A reader can rely on a pattern instead of checking each case
optionD: Mixed conventions can prevent the code from compiling cleanly at all
correctAnswerText: A reader can rely on a pattern instead of checking each case
explanation: Surprise is the cost. Two conventions in one file means the reader must work out which applies here, every time.

prompt: A line needs a comment to explain what it does. What should you try first?
optionA: Extract it into a well-named function or variable
optionB: Move the comment above the whole block instead
optionC: Add a test that demonstrates what the line achieves
optionD: Rewrite the line using simpler language constructs
correctAnswerText: Extract it into a well-named function or variable
explanation: A name travels with the code and a comment can drift away from it. Where the name can carry the meaning, it is the more durable place to put it.

prompt: Why is a comment that describes what the code does a liability?
optionA: The code changes and the comment does not, so it starts lying
optionB: It duplicates information that the type system already provides
optionC: It makes the file longer and harder to scan quickly
optionD: It suggests the author did not trust the reader
correctAnswerText: The code changes and the comment does not, so it starts lying
explanation: Nothing checks a comment. A wrong one is worse than none, because the reader believes it and stops reading the code.

prompt: What is the real reason to keep functions short?
optionA: A reader can hold the whole thing in their head at once
optionB: Short functions are easier for the compiler to inline
optionC: Shorter functions are more likely to be reused elsewhere
optionD: Line count is the metric most tools measure quality by
correctAnswerText: A reader can hold the whole thing in their head at once
explanation: The limit is comprehension, not lines. A forty-line function with no branches can be far easier to follow than fifteen lines of nested conditions.

prompt: What goes wrong when unrelated duplicate code is merged into one function?
optionA: Callers can no longer be tested independently of one another at all
optionB: The function becomes too long for anyone to understand
optionC: The two uses diverge and the shared function fills with flags
optionD: The duplicated code reappears elsewhere in the codebase
correctAnswerText: The two uses diverge and the shared function fills with flags
explanation: Coupling two things that were only coincidentally alike. "A wrong abstraction is more expensive than duplication" is about exactly this.

prompt: A function takes seven parameters. What does that usually indicate?
optionA: The function should be turned into a class method
optionB: It is doing several things, or some parameters belong together
optionC: The language lacks a way to express default values
optionD: It has been written to be as widely reusable as it possibly can be
correctAnswerText: It is doing several things, or some parameters belong together
explanation: Parameters that always travel together are usually one concept without a name. It is also where positional arguments start being passed in the wrong order.

prompt: Why is a boolean parameter that switches behaviour a warning sign?
optionA: The parameter will eventually need a third possible value
optionB: The function is two functions, and the call site says nothing
optionC: It makes the function harder to call from other languages
optionD: Booleans cannot express any more than two possible behaviours
correctAnswerText: The function is two functions, and the call site says nothing
explanation: save(order, true) tells a reader nothing at all. Two named functions are clearer at every call site and usually simpler inside.

prompt: What does "a function should either do something or answer something" mean?
optionA: A function that returns a value should not also change state
optionB: A function should not both read and write the same variable
optionC: A function should have either parameters or a return value
optionD: A function should not call other functions that change state
correctAnswerText: A function that returns a value should not also change state
explanation: Command-query separation. It means a call can be read safely without checking whether the act of reading changed anything.

prompt: Why should commented-out code be deleted?
optionA: Editors may accidentally uncomment it during a refactor
optionB: It counts towards the line limits set by code quality tools
optionC: Version control already has it, and nobody dares remove it later
optionD: It slows down the file being parsed by the language runtime itself
correctAnswerText: Version control already has it, and nobody dares remove it later
explanation: It is a question the reader cannot answer: is this coming back? Git knows, and git is not afraid to forget.

prompt: What is wrong with an empty catch block?
optionA: It hides the exception type from any tooling that reads the code
optionB: It prevents the function from returning a meaningful value
optionC: It makes the code slower because exceptions are expensive
optionD: The failure happens and nothing anywhere records that it did
correctAnswerText: The failure happens and nothing anywhere records that it did
explanation: The system carries on in a state nobody chose, and the symptom appears somewhere else entirely. Catching in order to ignore is a decision that should be written down.

prompt: Why do the same standards apply to test code?
optionA: Test frameworks require a consistent style in order to run correctly
optionB: Unreadable tests get deleted rather than fixed when they fail
optionC: Tests are executed as often as the code they are testing
optionD: Tests are the first thing a new developer is asked to read
correctAnswerText: Unreadable tests get deleted rather than fixed when they fail
explanation: A test nobody understands is a test nobody trusts, and an untrusted failing test gets commented out. That is how a suite dies.

prompt: A function has four levels of nested if statements. What is the first thing to try?
optionA: Combine the conditions into one using logical operators
optionB: Add comments at each level explaining the condition
optionC: Extract the innermost block into its own function
optionD: Invert the conditions and return early from each one
correctAnswerText: Invert the conditions and return early from each one
explanation: Guard clauses flatten it without changing the logic, and usually reveal that the real work is three lines. Extraction helps afterwards if it is still deep.

prompt: A condition spans three lines of && and ||. How do you make it readable?
optionA: Split it into separate nested if statements, one for each operand
optionB: Add a comment above explaining the whole condition
optionC: Assign its parts to named booleans that state what each means
optionD: Reformat it so each operand sits on its own line
correctAnswerText: Assign its parts to named booleans that state what each means
explanation: isEligible and hasValidPayment tell the reader why, not just what. Nesting it makes the shape worse, and a comment can go stale.

prompt: The value 2592000 appears in a timeout calculation. What should you do?
optionA: Name it, for example THIRTY_DAYS_IN_SECONDS
optionB: Replace it with an expression such as 30 * 24 * 60 * 60
optionC: Add a comment beside it explaining what it represents
optionD: Move it into a configuration file for the environment
correctAnswerText: Name it, for example THIRTY_DAYS_IN_SECONDS
explanation: The name is the durable fix, and the arithmetic form is a decent second. A comment works until somebody changes the number and not the comment.

prompt: Four parameters are always passed together to several functions. What does that suggest?
optionA: The functions should be combined into a single function
optionB: The functions should accept them in a different order
optionC: They are one concept that has not been given a name yet
optionD: The parameters should be made into global configuration
correctAnswerText: They are one concept that has not been given a name yet
explanation: street, city, postcode and country are an Address. Naming it shortens every signature and gives validation somewhere to live.

prompt: You are about to restructure a messy function with no tests. What comes first?
optionA: Split it into smaller functions one piece at a time
optionB: Write tests that capture what it currently does
optionC: Rename the variables so the logic becomes clearer
optionD: Document the current behaviour in a comment block
correctAnswerText: Write tests that capture what it currently does
explanation: Refactoring means changing structure without changing behaviour, and without tests you cannot claim the second half. Capture the current behaviour, bugs included.

prompt: getUser() also writes a last-accessed timestamp. What should change?
optionA: The function should return whether the write succeeded
optionB: The timestamp write should be wrapped in a transaction
optionC: Either the name, or the behaviour — they must agree
optionD: The write should be moved into the database layer
correctAnswerText: Either the name, or the behaviour — they must agree
explanation: A get that writes will eventually be called in a loop, or in a read-only context, by someone who trusted the name. Either is a legitimate fix; disagreeing is not.

prompt: You catch an error you genuinely cannot handle here. What should you do?
optionA: Convert it into a null result the caller can check for
optionB: Let it propagate, or rethrow it with more context attached
optionC: Log it and return a default value so the caller continues
optionD: Retry the operation a fixed number of times before giving up
correctAnswerText: Let it propagate, or rethrow it with more context attached
explanation: Returning a default makes a failure look like a success, and the damage appears somewhere unrelated. Adding context on the way up is what makes the log useful.

prompt: Where should a variable be declared?
optionA: As close to where it is used as the language permits
optionB: At the top of the function, with the others
optionC: Wherever it makes the indentation most consistent
optionD: Outside the function, if more than one function needs it
correctAnswerText: As close to where it is used as the language permits
explanation: The reader then holds fewer things at once, and the variable cannot be misused before it means anything. Declaring everything at the top is a habit from older languages.

prompt: You are fixing a bug in a badly written file. What is the sensible scope of cleanup?
optionA: The part you had to understand anyway, and no more
optionB: Nothing — cleanup belongs in a separate dedicated change
optionC: Every file that the one you are editing depends upon
optionD: The whole file, since you are already working in it
correctAnswerText: The part you had to understand anyway, and no more
explanation: Keeps the diff reviewable and the fix easy to revert, while the file still improves. Rewriting the file buries the bug fix inside three hundred unrelated lines.

prompt: A function calls sendInvoice() and also manipulates a string index. What is wrong?
optionA: The function is doing too much work to be tested
optionB: Two levels of detail are mixed in the same function
optionC: String manipulation belongs in a utility module
optionD: The function name cannot possibly describe both of the operations
correctAnswerText: Two levels of detail are mixed in the same function
explanation: A reader shifts from business steps to character arithmetic and back. Extracting the low-level part restores one consistent altitude.

prompt: A team avoids touching one module and works around it instead. What does that tell you?
optionA: Nobody can predict what a change there will break
optionB: The module needs to be rewritten from scratch
optionC: The module is the most important part of the system
optionD: The module was written by somebody who has left
correctAnswerText: Nobody can predict what a change there will break
explanation: Fear is the most reliable signal of unclear code, and the workarounds are themselves a growing cost. Characterisation tests are how the fear gets reduced.

prompt: One small rule change requires edits in eleven files. What does that indicate?
optionA: The change was larger than it first appeared to be
optionB: The knowledge is duplicated rather than owned in one place
optionC: The codebase is well modularised into properly separate concerns
optionD: The files should be merged into a single module
correctAnswerText: The knowledge is duplicated rather than owned in one place
explanation: This is what DRY is actually about. The eleventh file is the one somebody misses, and then the system holds two versions of one rule.

prompt: A comment says the function retries three times; the code retries five. Which do you trust?
optionA: The code — but the disagreement is itself worth investigating
optionB: Neither, until the original author can be consulted
optionC: The code, and the comment should simply be deleted
optionD: The comment, since it records what the intended behaviour was
correctAnswerText: The code — but the disagreement is itself worth investigating
explanation: The code is what runs. But someone chose three deliberately once, and finding out why may reveal that five is the bug rather than the comment.

prompt: A shared function has grown four boolean parameters, each used by one caller. What happened?
optionA: The function has taken on too many responsibilities over time
optionB: The callers should have written their own versions instead
optionC: Things that were only superficially alike were merged
optionD: The parameters should have been combined into one object
correctAnswerText: Things that were only superficially alike were merged
explanation: Each flag is a caller saying "not quite". Inlining it back into the callers and re-splitting on what is genuinely shared is usually the cheapest route out.

prompt: Data is missing in production and no error was ever logged. What should you look for?
optionA: A database query that returned fewer rows than expected
optionB: A permission check that rejected the operation quietly
optionC: A catch block that discards the exception and continues
optionD: A network call that timed out without being retried
correctAnswerText: A catch block that discards the exception and continues
explanation: The absence of any log is the clue. Something decided this failure was not worth mentioning, and it was almost certainly written as a quick fix.

prompt: New developers take months to become productive. What is the most likely structural cause?
optionA: The system is genuinely much larger than most other systems are
optionB: The team is not allocating enough time to mentoring
optionC: The onboarding documentation has not been kept current
optionD: The code does not explain itself, so knowledge lives in people
correctAnswerText: The code does not explain itself, so knowledge lives in people
explanation: Documentation goes stale; code that reads clearly does not. Onboarding time is a measurable proxy for how much the codebase explains itself.

prompt: Failing tests are increasingly skipped rather than fixed. What does that reveal?
optionA: The build takes too long for developers to wait for
optionB: The tests are running against outdated test fixtures
optionC: The tests were written by a team that no longer exists
optionD: Nobody trusts them enough to believe a failure is real
correctAnswerText: Nobody trusts them enough to believe a failure is real
explanation: Flaky or unreadable tests train a team to ignore red. Once skipping is normal the suite has stopped being a safety net and become a chore.

prompt: Following one request means opening nine files, each of which delegates onwards. What is the problem?
optionA: Layers were added for flexibility nobody turned out to need
optionB: The files should be renamed to show their relationships
optionC: The delegation should be replaced with inheritance
optionD: The system is correctly separated into properly distinct concerns
correctAnswerText: Layers were added for flexibility nobody turned out to need
explanation: Clean code is often taught as "more layers", and this is the result. An interface with one implementation is indirection charged with no benefit.

prompt: One codebase uses three different patterns for the same task. What is the cost?
optionA: New code cannot be added without somebody choosing a fourth pattern
optionB: Every reader must work out which applies before they can act
optionC: The application runs more slowly because of the variation
optionD: The build tooling cannot be configured consistently
correctAnswerText: Every reader must work out which applies before they can act
explanation: It also means a newcomer cannot tell which is preferred, so they pick one at random and the count goes to four.

prompt: You want evidence that a codebase is hard to work in. What is the most useful measure?
optionA: How long a small change takes, and how often it breaks something
optionB: The number of style warnings the linter currently reports
optionC: The average length of all the functions across the whole repository
optionD: The ratio of comment lines to lines of executable code
correctAnswerText: How long a small change takes, and how often it breaks something
explanation: Cost of change is what all of this is about, and it is the only one that survives an argument. The others measure style, which correlates weakly.

prompt: Which single habit improves a codebase most for the least risk?
optionA: Extracting shared code into common utilities
optionB: Keeping every function under twenty lines
optionC: Adding comments to anything non-obvious
optionD: Naming things accurately
correctAnswerText: Naming things accurately
explanation: A rename cannot break behaviour, removes the need for comments, and makes wrong calls look wrong. Extraction is the one on that list that can do real harm.

prompt: When is it right to break a clean-code rule?
optionA: When following it would defeat the purpose the rule exists for
optionB: When the team agrees the rule is not worth following here
optionC: When the deadline does not allow enough time to follow it properly
optionD: When the code in question is not expected to change again
correctAnswerText: When following it would defeat the purpose the rule exists for
explanation: Splitting a clear function to satisfy a line limit makes it harder to read, which was the whole point. The purpose outranks the rule every time.

prompt: When is duplication the better choice?
optionA: When the two copies are in different modules of the system
optionB: When extracting it would require adding a new parameter
optionC: When the two copies may need to change independently later
optionD: When the duplicated block is shorter than about five lines
correctAnswerText: When the two copies may need to change independently later
explanation: Coincidental similarity is not shared knowledge. Duplication is cheap to fix later; the wrong abstraction has to be unpicked from every caller.

prompt: Which comment is genuinely worth writing?
optionA: One describing what a complicated block of code does
optionB: One recording why an obvious-looking approach was rejected
optionC: One listing the parameters and what each of them means
optionD: One naming the developer who most recently modified the function
correctAnswerText: One recording why an obvious-looking approach was rejected
explanation: It stops the next person spending a day rediscovering it. Nothing in the code can carry that, which is exactly the test for a useful comment.

prompt: What does over-applying clean-code rules produce?
optionA: Indirection that hides the logic instead of clarifying it
optionB: A codebase that cannot be extended with new features
optionC: Files that are far too small for the tools to analyse properly
optionD: Code that runs measurably more slowly than before
correctAnswerText: Indirection that hides the logic instead of clarifying it
explanation: Six three-line functions calling each other can be far harder to follow than one twenty-line function. Extraction has a cost, and it is paid in tracing.

prompt: What should a human reviewer spend their attention on?
optionA: Whether the imports are ordered the same way as elsewhere
optionB: Whether the lines exceed the configured maximum length
optionC: Whether the formatting matches the project conventions
optionD: Whether the names and structure will make sense in a year
correctAnswerText: Whether the names and structure will make sense in a year
explanation: The other three are a formatter's job and should never reach a person. Human attention is scarce and belongs on the judgement calls.

prompt: What does the phrase "technical debt" get right, and what does it hide?
optionA: It is accurate enough for code quality but not for architectural decisions
optionB: It suggests the debt can be repaid, when in practice it cannot be
optionC: It describes the cost accurately but understates how fast it grows
optionD: It names the interest correctly, but implies the borrowing was deliberate
correctAnswerText: It names the interest correctly, but implies the borrowing was deliberate
explanation: A knowing shortcut is debt. Most mess is not borrowed at all — nobody chose it, so there is no plan to repay and no record of the decision.

prompt: Why is rewriting a messy module usually worse than improving it gradually?
optionA: Rewrites take longer than the estimate given for them
optionB: The old module will continue to be used during the rewrite
optionC: The mess encodes years of fixes nobody has written down
optionD: The team will not agree on the design for the new version
correctAnswerText: The mess encodes years of fixes nobody has written down
explanation: Every strange branch is probably a bug somebody hit. A rewrite discards the bug fixes along with the mess and rediscovers them one incident at a time.

prompt: What is the argument for clean code that a manager should accept?
optionA: It lowers the cost of every future change to the system
optionB: It makes the development team more satisfied with their work
optionC: It reduces the number of bugs released into production
optionD: It allows the code to be reused in other projects later
correctAnswerText: It lowers the cost of every future change to the system
explanation: It is an economic argument, not an aesthetic one. The others are real effects and none of them survives contact with a deadline as well as this one does.

prompt: What is the single test of whether code is clean?
optionA: Would an experienced developer consider it elegant?
optionB: Can someone unfamiliar with it change it safely and quickly?
optionC: Does it follow the style guide that the whole team has agreed on?
optionD: Is every function small and every name descriptive?
correctAnswerText: Can someone unfamiliar with it change it safely and quickly?
explanation: Everything else is a proxy for it. Where a rule and that question disagree, the question wins, and that is the whole of the judgement this skill asks for.

prompt: What does a join do?
optionA: Copies the columns of one table into the other table on a permanent basis
optionB: Filters a table down to the rows that match another table
optionC: Appends the rows of one table to the end of another table
optionD: Combines rows from two tables using a condition that relates them
correctAnswerText: Combines rows from two tables using a condition that relates them
explanation: Rows are matched and combined side by side. Stacking rows vertically is UNION, which is a different operation entirely.

prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return?
optionA: Rows from the left table that have no match on the right
optionB: Only rows that have a match on both sides
optionC: All rows from the left table, matched where possible
optionD: All rows from both tables, with gaps filled by NULL
correctAnswerText: Only rows that have a match on both sides
explanation: Unmatched rows on either side disappear without comment. That silence is what makes it the commonest cause of missing data in a report.

prompt: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
optionA: The left table rows that turn out to have no match on the right side
optionB: Every row from the left table, with NULLs where there is no match
optionC: Every row from both tables, whether matched or not
optionD: Only the left table rows that have a match on the right
correctAnswerText: Every row from the left table, with NULLs where there is no match
explanation: The left side is preserved whatever happens. That is what makes it the right choice for "every customer, and their orders if any".

prompt: What does the ON clause specify?
optionA: The order in which the two tables should be read
optionB: Which columns should appear in the result of the query
optionC: How a row on one side is matched to a row on the other
optionD: Which rows should be excluded from the final result
correctAnswerText: How a row on one side is matched to a row on the other
explanation: It is the matching rule. Excluding rows afterwards is WHERE, and the difference between the two is where most join bugs live.

prompt: What does a CROSS JOIN produce?
optionA: One row for each table, containing their combined columns
optionB: The rows of each table that share a common column
optionC: Only the rows that appear in both of the tables
optionD: Every row of one table paired with every row of the other
correctAnswerText: Every row of one table paired with every row of the other
explanation: A thousand rows joined to a thousand rows gives a million. It is occasionally what you want and far more often what a missing ON clause gave you.

prompt: What does a FULL OUTER JOIN return?
optionA: Every row from both sides, with NULLs wherever there is no match
optionB: Every row from both sides that has a match on the other
optionC: Every possible pairing of the rows in the two tables
optionD: Every row from the left side, plus the right rows that matched it
correctAnswerText: Every row from both sides, with NULLs wherever there is no match
explanation: Nothing is lost from either side. It is mostly used for reconciliation — finding what exists in one system and not the other.

prompt: Which columns do you normally join on?
