optionA: The generated tables cannot easily be modified by hand afterwards at all
optionB: The schema inherits the application's shape rather than the data's
optionC: The framework will not create any indexes at all
optionD: The schema will be regenerated every time the app starts
correctAnswerText: The schema inherits the application's shape rather than the data's
explanation: Generated schemas frequently have no constraints beyond keys, because the objects did not express any. The schema then guarantees almost nothing.

prompt: What is a well-designed schema ultimately giving you?
optionA: Queries that run faster than they otherwise would
optionB: A structure that mirrors the business as it is today
optionC: Facts you can rely on without having to check them
optionD: Less storage used for the same quantity of data
correctAnswerText: Facts you can rely on without having to check them
explanation: Every order has a customer; no balance is negative; no email appears twice. Those are things the application never has to verify, because they cannot be false.

prompt: What is an API?
optionA: A server that stores data on behalf of other programs
optionB: A library of functions that a program can call directly
optionC: An agreed way for one program to ask another for something
optionD: A website that returns raw data instead of returning a rendered page
correctAnswerText: An agreed way for one program to ask another for something
explanation: An agreement about requests and responses. A web API is one kind; the word covers any published interface between two pieces of software.

prompt: What does it mean to call an API a contract?
optionA: A legal agreement governs how the API may be used
optionB: The provider guarantees that the service will always remain available
optionC: Both sides rely on the agreed shape, so changing it breaks callers
optionD: The caller must register before they are allowed to use it
correctAnswerText: Both sides rely on the agreed shape, so changing it breaks callers
explanation: The shape is the promise. It is why removing a field is a breaking change even when nothing in your own code uses it.

prompt: What do the 4xx and 5xx status ranges mean?
optionA: 4xx the data was invalid, 5xx the data was missing
optionB: 4xx means the request failed, 5xx means it was refused
optionC: 4xx the caller did something wrong, 5xx the server did
optionD: 4xx a temporary problem, 5xx a permanent problem
correctAnswerText: 4xx the caller did something wrong, 5xx the server did
explanation: Whose fault it was, which decides whether retrying can help. Retrying a 400 will fail identically forever.

prompt: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
optionA: 401 means the endpoint needs auth, 403 means it does not exist
optionB: 401 means the password was wrong, 403 means the account is locked
optionC: 401 means we do not know who you are, 403 means you may not
optionD: 401 means the token expired, 403 means no token was sent
correctAnswerText: 401 means we do not know who you are, 403 means you may not
explanation: Unauthenticated against unauthorised. A 401 means logging in might help; a 403 means it will not.

prompt: What does the Content-Type header say?
optionA: What format the body is in, so the receiver can parse it
optionB: How large the body of the message is in bytes
optionC: Which particular endpoint the request is intended to reach
optionD: Which version of the API the caller expects
correctAnswerText: What format the body is in, so the receiver can parse it
explanation: Without it the receiver is guessing. Sending JSON while declaring form data is a common cause of a body arriving empty.

prompt: What is the main difference between an API key and a bearer token?
optionA: A key is sent in the body and a token in the headers
optionB: A key is encrypted and a token is sent in plain text
optionC: A key usually identifies an application; a token usually a session
optionD: A key never expires at all, whereas a token is always fairly short-lived
correctAnswerText: A key usually identifies an application; a token usually a session
explanation: Keys tend to be long-lived and per-integration; tokens tend to be short-lived and per-login. Neither is encrypted by itself — that is what TLS is for.

prompt: What does it mean for a request to be idempotent?
optionA: It can only be sent once before the token expires
optionB: It cannot change any data held on the server
optionC: It returns exactly the same response every time it is called
optionD: Making it twice leaves the same result as making it once
correctAnswerText: Making it twice leaves the same result as making it once
explanation: It is about the effect, not the response. A DELETE that returns 404 the second time is still idempotent, because the end state is the same.

prompt: Why do APIs apply rate limits?
optionA: To reduce the amount of data stored on the server
optionB: To prevent callers from reading data they should not
optionC: To stop one caller degrading the service for everyone else
optionD: To ensure that callers pay properly for the requests they make
correctAnswerText: To stop one caller degrading the service for everyone else
explanation: Protection of a shared resource. 429 is the status that says so, and it usually carries a header telling you when to try again.

prompt: Why do APIs carry a version?
optionA: So the provider can charge differently for any of the newer features
optionB: So old data can be distinguished from newer data
optionC: So a breaking change can ship without breaking existing callers
optionD: So callers can tell how recently the API was updated
correctAnswerText: So a breaking change can ship without breaking existing callers
explanation: It lets two contracts exist at once while callers migrate. Without it, any breaking change breaks everyone on the day it ships.

prompt: Why must an outgoing API call have a timeout?
optionA: Without one your own request can hang for as long as theirs does
optionB: Without one the connection cannot be reused later
optionC: Timeouts are the way a caller cancels a request it has already sent
optionD: The remote server requires a timeout to be declared
correctAnswerText: Without one your own request can hang for as long as theirs does
explanation: Their slow day becomes your outage. A default of "wait forever" is the default in more HTTP clients than people expect.

prompt: Why does returning 200 with an error message inside cause problems?
optionA: The caller cannot tell which field holds the error
optionB: Browsers will refuse to display the response
optionC: The response body becomes larger than it needs to be
optionD: Every caller and proxy treats it as a success
correctAnswerText: Every caller and proxy treats it as a success
explanation: Monitoring, retries and client libraries all key on the status. A 200 that means failure has to be special-cased by every single caller.

prompt: What should an error response contain?
optionA: A suggested correction the caller should apply
optionB: A stack trace so the caller can see what happened
optionC: The original request, so that the caller can compare it
optionD: A stable code to branch on, and a message for a human
correctAnswerText: A stable code to branch on, and a message for a human
explanation: Code for machines, message for people. Callers who have to match on message text break the day somebody improves the wording.

prompt: Which change to a response is safe for existing callers?
optionA: Adding a new field alongside the existing ones
optionB: Changing a field from being a string to a number
optionC: Removing a field that appears to be unused
optionD: Renaming a field to something clearer
correctAnswerText: Adding a new field alongside the existing ones
explanation: Additive changes are ignored by callers who do not know about them. The other three all break somebody, and you cannot ask who.

prompt: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent by convention?
optionA: DELETE
optionB: GET
optionC: POST
optionD: PUT
correctAnswerText: POST
explanation: POST creates something each time, so two identical POSTs make two records. This is why a retried payment needs an idempotency key.

prompt: Which failures are worth retrying?
optionA: Timeouts, connection errors and 5xx responses
optionB: Only responses that explicitly ask you to retry
optionC: Any response that is not a 200 status
optionD: 4xx responses, since the request may be corrected
correctAnswerText: Timeouts, connection errors and 5xx responses
explanation: Transient failures may succeed on a second attempt; a 400 will fail identically forever. 429 is the 4xx exception, and it says when.

prompt: Why must an API secret never be embedded in a mobile app or front-end?
optionA: Anyone can extract it from the shipped code
optionB: Client code cannot send custom headers securely
optionC: Secrets expire faster when used from a client
optionD: The secret will be too long to store on a device
correctAnswerText: Anyone can extract it from the shipped code
explanation: Minified, compiled or obfuscated, it is still there to be read. Anything the client holds is public, which is why the call goes via your own server.

prompt: Why do list endpoints paginate?
optionA: Pagination is required by the HTTP specification
optionB: An unbounded response can exhaust memory at both ends
optionC: It allows the server to cache each page separately
optionD: Callers are unable to process more than a page at once
correctAnswerText: An unbounded response can exhaust memory at both ends
explanation: A list that is fine today has a hundred thousand rows in two years. An endpoint with no limit is a defect waiting for the data to arrive.

prompt: What is CORS actually doing?
optionA: Encrypting any requests that happen to travel between two different domains anywhere
optionB: Preventing a server from being called by unknown clients
optionC: Checking that the caller has permission to read the data
optionD: Letting a server say which other origins a browser may share responses with
correctAnswerText: Letting a server say which other origins a browser may share responses with
explanation: It is a browser rule, enforced by the browser. A server-to-server call, or curl, is entirely unaffected by it.

prompt: The front end validates every field. Why must the API validate too?
optionA: The two validations may disagree about the rules
optionB: Front-end validation runs far too late in the request cycle
optionC: Browsers may disable validation for accessibility
optionD: The API can be called without going through your front end
correctAnswerText: The API can be called without going through your front end
explanation: curl, a script, a mobile build from last year, an attacker. Client validation is a convenience for the user, never a control.

prompt: What makes API documentation trustworthy?
optionA: It is reviewed before each release goes out
optionB: It is written by the team that built the API
optionC: It is generated from, or verified against, the running code
optionD: It includes at least one example request for every endpoint
correctAnswerText: It is generated from, or verified against, the running code
explanation: Hand-written docs drift, and a wrong document is worse than none because it is believed. A generated schema cannot disagree with the code.

prompt: You are adding retries to an API call. What shape should they take?
optionA: Retries at a fixed interval for as long as it takes
optionB: One single retry, sent at the same time as the first request
optionC: Immediate retries until the call eventually succeeds
optionD: A small number of attempts with a growing delay between them
correctAnswerText: A small number of attempts with a growing delay between them
explanation: Immediate unbounded retries turn their bad minute into their bad hour, and yours. Bounded attempts with backoff, ideally with jitter.

prompt: A payment POST times out and you do not know whether it succeeded. What makes retrying safe?
optionA: A delay long enough for the first request to finish
optionB: A GET afterwards to check whether the payment already exists
optionC: An idempotency key the server uses to recognise the repeat
optionD: A flag telling the server that this is a retry
correctAnswerText: An idempotency key the server uses to recognise the repeat
explanation: A timeout tells you nothing about whether the work happened. The key lets the server answer "I have already done this one".

prompt: An API you depend on returns 503. What should your code do?
optionA: Return a 200 with empty data so the page still renders
optionB: Log the failure and then return the last cached value silently
optionC: Retry immediately until a successful response arrives
optionD: Retry with backoff, and degrade gracefully if it keeps failing
correctAnswerText: Retry with backoff, and degrade gracefully if it keeps failing
explanation: Degrading is a decision to make explicitly — a cached value with no indication it is stale is a lie the user cannot detect.

prompt: You must remove a field from a published API. What is the process?
optionA: Remove it in a new version and then delete the old version straight away at once
optionB: Remove it and fix any callers that report a problem
optionC: Keep returning it as null so that nothing breaks
optionD: Announce it, measure who still uses it, then remove it after a period
correctAnswerText: Announce it, measure who still uses it, then remove it after a period
explanation: Measurement is the part people skip, and it is the part that tells you whether the deadline is safe. Returning null often breaks callers just as badly.

prompt: How should you choose a timeout for an outgoing call?
optionA: Whatever default the HTTP client library provides
optionB: The same value for every call the application makes
optionC: As long as is possible, so that even the very slowest responses still succeed
optionD: From its measured response times, and what your own caller can wait
correctAnswerText: From its measured response times, and what your own caller can wait
explanation: It has to fit inside your own deadline, or you time out anyway having achieved nothing. Many clients default to no timeout at all.

prompt: Where should an API key live in your own service?
optionA: In configuration or a secret store, never in the repository
optionB: In the database, so it can be rotated without a deploy
optionC: In a constants file that has been excluded from version control
optionD: In an environment file committed alongside the code
correctAnswerText: In configuration or a secret store, never in the repository
explanation: A secret committed once is in the history forever, and rotating it is then the only real fix. Config or a secret manager keeps it out entirely.

prompt: You must fetch every page of a paginated endpoint. What must the loop have?
optionA: Parallel requests for every one of the pages at the same time
optionB: A retry on each page before moving to the next
optionC: A fixed page count taken from the first response
optionD: A stopping condition and a bound on total pages fetched
correctAnswerText: A stopping condition and a bound on total pages fetched
explanation: A pagination loop with no bound is an infinite loop waiting for an API quirk — a cursor that repeats, or a next link that always appears.

prompt: Why check the shape of a response from an API you do not control?
optionA: The response may contain executable code that has to be carefully stripped out first
optionB: Responses are not guaranteed to arrive in the right order
optionC: The provider may return data belonging to another caller
optionD: It can change without warning, and a missing field crashes far from the cause
correctAnswerText: It can change without warning, and a missing field crashes far from the cause
explanation: Failing at the boundary with a clear message beats a null reference three layers in. It is the same argument as validating input.

prompt: How should you test code that calls a third-party API?
optionA: Against a mock only, since the API itself is not your own code
optionB: Against a stub for logic, plus a real call run periodically
optionC: Against the live API on every test run
optionD: By skipping those paths and testing them manually
correctAnswerText: Against a stub for logic, plus a real call run periodically
explanation: Stubs are fast and cannot notice the contract changing. A periodic real call is what tells you the provider altered something.

prompt: You receive a 429. What should your client do?
optionA: Retry immediately, since the limit may already have been reset
optionB: Open more connections so the requests are spread out
optionC: Treat it as a permanent failure and stop calling
optionD: Wait for the period the response indicates, then try again
correctAnswerText: Wait for the period the response indicates, then try again
explanation: Retry-After is usually there and is usually ignored. Retrying immediately extends the block and may get you throttled harder.

prompt: A few customers were charged twice, and the logs show one timeout each. What happened?
optionA: The transaction was committed and then rolled back
optionB: The customers must have submitted the payment form twice over entirely by themselves
optionC: The request succeeded but the response was lost, and the retry charged again
optionD: The payment provider processed each request twice
correctAnswerText: The request succeeded but the response was lost, and the retry charged again
explanation: A timeout means you do not know, and the default assumption "it failed" is wrong half the time. An idempotency key removes the guess.

prompt: A call works in curl and fails in the browser with no useful error. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The browser is sending the request off to a different URL
optionB: The API rejects requests that originate from browsers
optionC: The browser cannot parse the response body correctly
optionD: CORS — the browser is refusing to hand over the response
correctAnswerText: CORS — the browser is refusing to hand over the response
explanation: The request usually reached the server and succeeded; the browser then withheld the response. The server log showing a 200 is the confusing part.

prompt: One slow third-party API has taken your whole service down. How?
optionA: The third party returned some responses that crashed your own parser
optionB: Requests waiting on it exhausted the connection or thread pool
optionC: Your service retried until it ran out of memory
optionD: The slow responses filled the available disk with logs
correctAnswerText: Requests waiting on it exhausted the connection or thread pool
explanation: Every waiting request holds a resource, so an unbounded wait converts their slowness into your outage. Timeouts and a circuit breaker are the containment.

prompt: A field you rely on started arriving as null, with no announcement. What should you do first?
optionA: Check the provider's changelog and confirm the current contract
optionB: Add a sensible default value and then carry on without investigating
optionC: Report it as an outage and wait for it to be fixed
optionD: Retry the request until the field is populated again
correctAnswerText: Check the provider's changelog and confirm the current contract
explanation: Deprecated and now empty, renamed, or conditional on something you stopped sending. Guessing a default hides the change and locks in the wrong behaviour.

prompt: Calls work for an hour after each deploy and then return 401. What is happening?
optionA: The token is being fetched once at startup and never refreshed
optionB: The provider is rate limiting after an hour of traffic
optionC: The service keeps on losing its network connection periodically
optionD: The API key is being rotated by the provider hourly
correctAnswerText: The token is being fetched once at startup and never refreshed
explanation: The hour is the token lifetime and the deploy is what refreshes it. Refresh-on-401 or refresh-before-expiry is the fix.

prompt: A brief provider outage became a long one once your clients started retrying. Why?
optionA: The retries were sent to a different endpoint by mistake
optionB: Each retry opened a connection that was never closed
optionC: Immediate retries multiplied the load exactly when it was struggling
optionD: The provider blocked all of your traffic after the very first failures
correctAnswerText: Immediate retries multiplied the load exactly when it was struggling
explanation: A retry storm. Everyone retries at once, the recovering service is knocked down again, and the cycle repeats — which is what jitter is for.

prompt: An import brings in exactly 100 records every time, though there are thousands. What is wrong?
optionA: The records after the first hundred are invalid
optionB: The provider is limiting this account to just 100 records
optionC: Only the first page is being read and pagination ignored
optionD: The import is timing out after the first batch
correctAnswerText: Only the first page is being read and pagination ignored
explanation: A round number equal to a common default page size is the giveaway. It succeeds every time, which is why nobody looks at it.

prompt: Your monitoring shows a 100% success rate while users report failures. What should you check?
optionA: Whether the monitoring is sampling too few requests
optionB: Whether the users are calling a different environment
optionC: Whether errors are being returned inside a 200 response
optionD: Whether the failures happen before the request is even sent
correctAnswerText: Whether errors are being returned inside a 200 response
explanation: Monitoring counts status codes, so an error wrapped in a 200 is invisible to it. The dashboard is green and the system is not.

prompt: An endpoint fails only for some customers, always the same ones. Where do you look?
optionA: At whether they are using an older client version
optionB: At the time of day at which they make the call
optionC: At what is different about their data or their permissions
optionD: At the network route between them and the service itself somewhere
correctAnswerText: At what is different about their data or their permissions
explanation: Consistent-by-caller rules out anything transient. A missing optional field, a name with an apostrophe, a permission nobody tested without.

prompt: An integration is failing and you cannot tell which side is at fault. What establishes it fastest?
optionA: Comparing the code with the last working version
optionB: Adding more logging and waiting for it to happen again
optionC: Asking the provider whether anything has changed
optionD: Replaying the exact request outside your application
correctAnswerText: Replaying the exact request outside your application
explanation: curl with the same headers and body either reproduces it, which makes it theirs or the request's, or does not, which makes it yours.

prompt: What makes a published API harder to change than internal code?
optionA: External callers are often on older versions of your software
optionB: Changes require approval from the callers themselves
optionC: You cannot find out who depends on it, or make them change
optionD: The API is usually built on a slower release cycle
correctAnswerText: You cannot find out who depends on it, or make them change
explanation: Internal code can be refactored because you can see every caller. Every published API decision is closer to permanent than it looks.

prompt: What is the general rule for evolving an API safely?
optionA: Add, never remove or repurpose
optionB: Change only what no caller is currently using
optionC: Keep the number of endpoints as small as possible
optionD: Version every change, however small it is
correctAnswerText: Add, never remove or repurpose
explanation: New fields and new endpoints are invisible to existing callers. Repurposing is the sneaky one — the shape survives and the meaning does not.

prompt: What does a network call do that a local function call never does?
optionA: Return a value of an unexpected type
optionB: Take longer than you expected it to
optionC: Throw an exception you have to handle
optionD: Succeed while you are told it failed
correctAnswerText: Succeed while you are told it failed
explanation: A lost response is indistinguishable from a failed request, and no amount of error handling resolves it. That uncertainty is what idempotency exists for.

prompt: A dependency is down. What decides whether you fail or degrade?
optionA: Whether the call was a read or else a write operation
optionB: Whether the dependency is internal or external
optionC: How long the dependency is expected to be down
optionD: Whether a partial answer is better or worse than none
correctAnswerText: Whether a partial answer is better or worse than none
explanation: Recommendations missing is fine; a balance shown as zero is not. The decision is about the meaning of the data, so it cannot be made once globally.

prompt: How much detail should an error response give?
optionA: As little as possible, so nothing is ever revealed
optionB: Whatever the underlying exception happened to contain
optionC: Enough to correct the request, never enough to map the system
optionD: As much as is possible, so that callers can diagnose it themselves
correctAnswerText: Enough to correct the request, never enough to map the system
explanation: "Email is not a valid address" helps; a stack trace naming your tables and framework versions helps somebody else. A reference id bridges the two.

prompt: Why is "every outgoing call has a timeout" worth treating as an absolute rule?
optionA: Providers require callers to set an explicit timeout
optionB: Timeouts make the application measurably faster overall
optionC: A single unbounded wait can take down an entire service
optionD: Without one the connection cannot be pooled or reused
correctAnswerText: A single unbounded wait can take down an entire service
explanation: The failure is disproportionate to the mistake, and it is one line to prevent. Rules earn absolute status by that ratio.

prompt: Reviewing code that calls an external API, what should you check first?
optionA: What happens when it is slow, fails, or returns something unexpected
optionB: Whether the endpoint URL is being stored in the application configuration
optionC: Whether the call is made asynchronously
optionD: Whether the response is being parsed efficiently
correctAnswerText: What happens when it is slow, fails, or returns something unexpected
explanation: The happy path almost always works, and every one of those three is invisible until production. Most integration code only handles the first.

prompt: What follows from "anything the client holds is public"?
optionA: Client code should be obfuscated before it is shipped
optionB: Client and server should share the same validation code
optionC: Clients should hold as little data as they possibly can
optionD: Every rule that matters must be enforced on the server
correctAnswerText: Every rule that matters must be enforced on the server
explanation: Hidden buttons, client-side price calculations and front-end-only validation are all the same mistake. The server is the only place a rule can hold.

prompt: What does keeping an old API version running cost?
optionA: The server must hold twice as much data in storage
optionB: The older version gradually becomes a security risk over time
optionC: Callers become confused about which version to use
optionD: Every change must be made and tested against both versions
correctAnswerText: Every change must be made and tested against both versions
explanation: Versions are cheap to create and expensive to keep, which is why the retirement plan should exist before the version does.

prompt: What is the single idea that most API discipline comes down to?
optionA: The other side is not under your control and may do anything
optionB: Documentation is more important than implementation
optionC: Requests should be kept as small and as fast as they possibly can be
optionD: Every endpoint should do exactly one thing well
correctAnswerText: The other side is not under your control and may do anything
explanation: Validate their input, check their responses, time out their calls, never trust their client. Every rule in this file is that one sentence applied somewhere.

prompt: In REST, what does a URL identify?
optionA: A function in the server's codebase
optionB: A thing, or a collection of things
optionC: A screen in the application that calls it
optionD: An action the server should perform
correctAnswerText: A thing, or a collection of things
explanation: Nouns in the URL, verbs in the method. That single split is most of what distinguishes REST from an RPC endpoint with slashes in it.

prompt: What does GET mean?
optionA: Fetch something and mark it as read
optionB: Retrieve a resource using query parameters
optionC: Request data without needing authentication
optionD: Read something, changing nothing
correctAnswerText: Read something, changing nothing
explanation: Safe: no side effects. It is why a browser, a proxy or a crawler may repeat it freely, and why a GET that deletes something is a real hazard.

prompt: What distinguishes POST from PUT?
optionA: POST is used by forms and PUT by programs
optionB: POST creates something new; PUT replaces a known resource
optionC: POST always sends a body, whereas PUT sends only query parameters
optionD: POST requires authentication and PUT does not
correctAnswerText: POST creates something new; PUT replaces a known resource
explanation: The consequence is that PUT is idempotent and POST is not: two identical POSTs make two records, two identical PUTs leave one.

prompt: What does PATCH do that PUT does not?
optionA: Creates the resource when it does not already exist
optionB: Applies the change only if the resource has not already moved
optionC: Changes only the fields supplied, leaving the rest alone
optionD: Updates a resource without needing its identifier
correctAnswerText: Changes only the fields supplied, leaving the rest alone
explanation: PUT replaces the whole resource, so a missing field means "remove this". Sending a partial body to PUT is a common way to erase data.

prompt: What is the conventional URL shape for one user and for all users?
optionA: /users for the collection and /users/42 for one
optionB: /user/all for the collection and /user/42 for one
optionC: /getUsers for the collection and /getUser/42 for one
optionD: /users?all=true for the collection and /users?id=42 for one
correctAnswerText: /users for the collection and /users/42 for one
explanation: Plural collection, identifier appended for a member. Predictable enough that a caller can guess the second URL from the first.

prompt: What does it mean for a REST API to be stateless?
optionA: Each request opens up a brand new connection to the server
optionB: Responses are never cached by the client
optionC: Each request carries everything needed to serve it
optionD: The server does not store any data at all
correctAnswerText: Each request carries everything needed to serve it
explanation: No conversation is remembered between calls, so any server in a pool can answer any request. The data is stored; the session is not.

prompt: What should a successful POST that creates something return?
optionA: 201, with the new resource or a link to it
optionB: 202, because the resource now exists on the server
optionC: 204, since the caller already knows what it sent
optionD: 200, with a message confirming the creation
correctAnswerText: 201, with the new resource or a link to it
explanation: 201 says created and carries the identifier the caller does not yet have. 202 means accepted for later processing, which is a different promise.

prompt: What does /users/42/orders represent?
optionA: The orders belonging to user 42
optionB: An order whose identifier is 42
optionC: The user 42 and their order details together
optionD: A request to add an order for user 42
correctAnswerText: The orders belonging to user 42
explanation: Nesting expresses ownership. What is done to that collection is decided by the method, not by the path.

prompt: What do query parameters belong to?
optionA: Identifying which resource is being requested
optionB: Filtering, sorting and paging a collection
optionC: Passing the credentials for the request
optionD: Carrying the data for a create or update
correctAnswerText: Filtering, sorting and paging a collection
explanation: The path says which collection; the query says which slice of it. Credentials belong in a header and payloads belong in the body.

prompt: What does 404 mean in a REST API?
optionA: The request was malformed and could not be read
optionB: The endpoint has been removed in this version
optionC: The resource at that URL does not exist
optionD: The caller is not permitted to see that resource
correctAnswerText: The resource at that URL does not exist
explanation: No such thing at that address. It is also sometimes returned deliberately instead of 403, so that the URL does not confirm what exists.

prompt: What is the main practical benefit of following REST conventions?
optionA: The server code becomes simpler to write and maintain
optionB: The API will perform noticeably better than a non-REST equivalent
optionC: The API can then be documented automatically by tools
optionD: A caller who has used one REST API can guess how yours behaves
correctAnswerText: A caller who has used one REST API can guess how yours behaves
explanation: Guessability is the return, and it is why consistency matters more than any individual choice. An unusual but consistent scheme beats a mixture.

prompt: What is actually lost by using /deleteUser?id=42 with a GET?
optionA: Query parameters cannot hold an identifier reliably
optionB: The request is then unable to carry a body with any additional data
optionC: The URL becomes longer than it strictly needs to be
optionD: Anything may repeat a GET, so it can be triggered accidentally
correctAnswerText: Anything may repeat a GET, so it can be triggered accidentally
explanation: Crawlers, prefetchers and browser history all repeat GETs. A destructive GET has taken down real systems, which is why safety is a property and not a style.

prompt: Which methods are idempotent?
optionA: All of them, by definition of HTTP
optionB: GET, PUT and DELETE, but not POST
optionC: GET and POST, but not PUT or DELETE
optionD: Only GET, since it changes nothing
correctAnswerText: GET, PUT and DELETE, but not POST
explanation: Repeating them leaves the same state. It is what lets a client library retry a failed PUT safely and refuse to retry a POST.

prompt: A POST is rejected because a required field is missing. What should it return?
optionA: 404, because the resource could not be created
optionB: 500, because the request could not be completed
optionC: 200, with a flag indicating that it failed
optionD: 400, with details of which field was wrong
correctAnswerText: 400, with details of which field was wrong
explanation: The caller can fix it, so it is a 4xx. A 500 tells them to retry something that will fail identically every time.

prompt: Why is /users/42/orders/7/items/3/reviews a poor URL?
optionA: Nesting more than twice is forbidden by the standard
optionB: The deep path adds nothing once the item has its own identifier
optionC: URLs are limited in length by most web servers
optionD: Each level of the path requires a separate database query to resolve
correctAnswerText: The deep path adds nothing once the item has its own identifier
explanation: If a review has a unique id, /reviews/3 identifies it completely. One level of nesting shows ownership; four makes every caller rebuild a chain they do not need.

prompt: Why can a GET be cached when a POST cannot?
optionA: A GET request has no body at all, so there is much less data to store
optionB: Caches are only able to store responses under 1MB
optionC: A GET is safe, so repeating it or skipping it changes nothing
optionD: A POST is always authenticated and a GET is not
correctAnswerText: A GET is safe, so repeating it or skipping it changes nothing
explanation: The whole caching layer of the web rests on GET being safe. Putting a state change behind a GET quietly opts out of it.

prompt: Why should a collection endpoint have a default page size?
optionA: It allows each page to be cached independently
optionB: The HTTP standard requires a limit on response size
optionC: The collection will eventually be larger than anyone expects
optionD: Callers are simply unable to request more than one page at a time
correctAnswerText: The collection will eventually be larger than anyone expects
explanation: An endpoint returning everything is fine on day one and a memory problem in two years, at both ends. The default is what makes it safe by omission.

prompt: Why should every endpoint use the same response and error shape?
optionA: The server can then serialise responses more efficiently
optionB: It is required for the API to be considered RESTful
optionC: Callers can write one handler instead of one per endpoint
optionD: Consistent shapes compress better when sent over the wire
correctAnswerText: Callers can write one handler instead of one per endpoint
explanation: Every inconsistency becomes a special case in every client. It is the same argument as naming conventions, applied across a network boundary.

prompt: Why do operations like "transfer money" fit REST awkwardly?
optionA: They are actions across resources rather than changes to one
optionB: They require rather more than one request in order to complete safely
optionC: They involve two users rather than one resource owner
optionD: They cannot be expressed without a custom HTTP method
correctAnswerText: They are actions across resources rather than changes to one
explanation: Two accounts change together and neither is the resource. Modelling the transfer itself as a resource is the usual escape, and it is a real design choice.

prompt: Where is an API version most commonly placed?
optionA: In a query parameter on every request
optionB: In the URL path, such as /v1/users
optionC: In the name of the domain being called
optionD: In the body of each request that is sent
correctAnswerText: In the URL path, such as /v1/users
explanation: Visible, easy to route and easy to log. A header is arguably purer and is harder to test by hand, which is why the path usually wins.

prompt: What is the standard set of endpoints for managing articles?
optionA: POST on /createArticle, /updateArticle and /deleteArticle
optionB: GET on /articles with an action parameter naming the operation wanted
optionC: POST on /articles for every operation, with a type in the body
optionD: GET and POST on /articles; GET, PUT and DELETE on /articles/:id
correctAnswerText: GET and POST on /articles; GET, PUT and DELETE on /articles/:id
explanation: Two URLs and five methods cover the whole lifecycle. A caller who knows the pattern needs no documentation to use it.

prompt: You need an endpoint to cancel an order. What is the cleanest design?
optionA: POST /orders/42/cancellations, or PATCH the order's status
optionB: POST /cancelOrder with the order id in the body
optionC: DELETE /orders/42, since cancelling removes the order
optionD: GET /orders/42/cancel, since it is quite a simple operation
correctAnswerText: POST /orders/42/cancellations, or PATCH the order's status
explanation: Either the cancellation is a thing that gets created, or the status is a field that changes. DELETE is wrong because a cancelled order still exists.

prompt: What should a paginated response include besides the items?
optionA: The time at which the page was generated
optionB: Enough information to request the next page
optionC: The total number of pages in the collection
optionD: The parameters that were used in the request
correctAnswerText: Enough information to request the next page
explanation: A cursor or a next link is the minimum. A total count is useful and can be expensive to compute, so it is a decision rather than a default.

prompt: A search needs more criteria than fit comfortably in a query string. What do you do?
optionA: POST the criteria to a search endpoint, accepting it is not cacheable
optionB: Split the search across several sequential GET requests
optionC: Encode the whole of the criteria object into one single query parameter
optionD: Store the criteria first, then GET the result by its id
correctAnswerText: POST the criteria to a search endpoint, accepting it is not cacheable
explanation: A deliberate exception. The cost is losing GET caching and safety, and it is worth paying when the alternative is an unreadable URL near its length limit.

prompt: What should DELETE return when the resource was already gone?
optionA: 204, since the desired end state has been reached
optionB: 500, because the operation could not be performed
optionC: 400, because the caller sent an invalid identifier
optionD: 200, with a message saying nothing was deleted
correctAnswerText: 204, since the desired end state has been reached
explanation: This is idempotency in practice: the caller wanted it gone and it is gone. Returning 404 is also defensible and makes retries harder to write.

prompt: A client wants to change only a user's email. Which method?
optionA: POST, sending the email to a sub-resource
optionB: PATCH, sending just the email field
optionC: PUT, sending the whole user with the email changed
optionD: PUT, sending just the email field
correctAnswerText: PATCH, sending just the email field
explanation: The last option is also correct and requires the client to hold the whole user. PUT with a partial body is the dangerous one, because the omitted fields mean "remove".

prompt: A client must update 500 records. What is the sensible design?
optionA: One PUT on the collection replacing all the records
optionB: 500 individual PATCH requests sent in parallel
optionC: A single PATCH with an array, returning one overall status
optionD: A batch endpoint that reports the outcome of each item
correctAnswerText: A batch endpoint that reports the outcome of each item
explanation: Batches partially fail, so one overall status cannot express the result. Per-item outcomes let the client retry only what failed.

prompt: What matters most when choosing between /users and /user?
optionA: That whichever you choose is used everywhere without exception
optionB: That the shortest form is used to keep URLs brief
optionC: That the plural form is always used, as the usual convention prefers
optionD: That the name matches the database table exactly
correctAnswerText: That whichever you choose is used everywhere without exception
explanation: Plural is the convention and worth following. A mixture is worse than either, because the caller has to remember which endpoints are which.

prompt: How is authentication carried in a stateless REST API?
optionA: A token or key sent with every single request
optionB: An identifier supplied once and cached by the server
optionC: A connection kept open for the duration of the session
optionD: A session established by a login call and remembered
correctAnswerText: A token or key sent with every single request
explanation: Every request stands alone, so it carries its own proof. That is what lets any server in a pool answer it without shared session state.

prompt: A submitted form has three invalid fields. What should the response do?
optionA: Report the first invalid field and stop there
optionB: Report all three at once, each identified by field
optionC: Return a 200 with the fields that were accepted
optionD: Return a single message saying the input was invalid
correctAnswerText: Report all three at once, each identified by field
explanation: One at a time means three round trips and a user fixing errors one by one. The field name is what lets the client attach each message to its input.

prompt: Records started disappearing after a crawler indexed an internal admin page. What was wrong?
optionA: Delete links were GET requests, which the crawler followed
optionB: The admin page was accidentally exposed to the public internet
optionC: The crawler was authenticated as an administrator by mistake
optionD: The crawler submitted the forms that were on the page
correctAnswerText: Delete links were GET requests, which the crawler followed
explanation: A famous class of incident. Anything that repeats GETs — a crawler, a prefetcher, a browser restoring tabs — will trigger every side effect behind one.

prompt: After a client updated a user's name, their phone number was blank. What happened?
optionA: The client sent the phone number as an empty string
optionB: The update was applied to the wrong user record
optionC: The phone number field was renamed in the same release
optionD: A PUT was sent with only the changed field in the body
correctAnswerText: A PUT was sent with only the changed field in the body
explanation: PUT means "make it exactly this", so anything absent is removed. It succeeds, returns 200, and quietly erases whatever the client did not send.

prompt: Users see old data after an update, and only some of them. What should you check?
optionA: Whether the update was actually written to a different database
optionB: Whether those users are authenticated differently
optionC: Whether the update returned an error that was ignored
optionD: Whether a cache between them and the server is serving the GET
correctAnswerText: Whether a cache between them and the server is serving the GET
explanation: Browser, CDN or proxy — GETs are cacheable by design. Affecting only some users points at a cache, because not everyone shares one.

prompt: Client code has a different error handler for nearly every endpoint. What does that reveal?
optionA: The API returns errors in a different shape from each endpoint
optionB: The error handling was never refactored after the first release
optionC: The client was written by several different developers
optionD: The endpoints are owned by different backend services
correctAnswerText: The API returns errors in a different shape from each endpoint
explanation: The client is compensating for the server. It is the clearest measurable symptom of an API that grew without a convention.

prompt: Duplicate records appear when the network is unreliable. Which method is involved?
optionA: PUT, because repeating it overwrites the first record
optionB: DELETE, because repeating it removes too much
optionC: GET, because repeating it returns stale data
optionD: POST, because repeating it creates a second record
correctAnswerText: POST, because repeating it creates a second record
explanation: POST is the only common method that is not idempotent, so it is the only one where a retry can duplicate. An idempotency key is what closes it.

prompt: A screen makes 200 API calls to render a list of 200 items. What is the design problem?
optionA: The client is not making its requests in parallel
optionB: The endpoints are too slow for that number of calls
optionC: The client is repeatedly failing to cache any of the responses it receives
optionD: The list endpoint returns ids only, so each item is fetched separately
correctAnswerText: The list endpoint returns ids only, so each item is fetched separately
explanation: The N+1 problem at the network layer, where each call costs a round trip. Returning the needed fields, or supporting an expand parameter, fixes it.

prompt: An API returns 200 for everything, with a success flag in the body. What breaks?
optionA: The ability to return a response body at all
optionB: The ordering in which responses are received
optionC: The caching behaviour of whichever browser the client happens to be using
optionD: Monitoring, retries and every client library that reads the status
correctAnswerText: Monitoring, retries and every client library that reads the status
explanation: Every layer between client and server reads the status and nothing reads your flag. It is a decision that makes the API unusual in a way that costs everyone.

prompt: A filter works for small selections and fails silently for large ones. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The database query is quietly timing out on the larger selection
optionB: The response is too large for the client to parse
optionC: The URL has exceeded a length limit somewhere in the chain
optionD: The filter parameter is being truncated by the framework
correctAnswerText: The URL has exceeded a length limit somewhere in the chain
explanation: Servers and proxies cap URL length, often around 2,000 characters, and the failure is frequently unhelpful. It is the usual argument for a POSTed search.

prompt: A field was renamed and several mobile clients broke. What was missed?
optionA: Old app versions keep running, so the change needed to be additive
optionB: The rename should have been announced to the app team
optionC: The mobile apps should have been forced to update first
optionD: The mobile clients should each have handled the missing field themselves
correctAnswerText: Old app versions keep running, so the change needed to be additive
explanation: Mobile is the sharpest case: you cannot make people update, so last year's build is still calling. The only safe change is to add the new name and keep the old.

prompt: An endpoint that was instant now times out for the largest customers. What was missing from the start?
optionA: A cache in front of the endpoint for repeat calls
optionB: A timeout on the database query it performs
optionC: A default limit on how many records it returns
optionD: An index on the column the endpoint filters by
correctAnswerText: A default limit on how many records it returns
explanation: Correct from day one and wrong as soon as one customer had fifty thousand records. An endpoint with no bound is a defect waiting for the data.

prompt: Why is putting the verb in the method rather than the URL more than a style preference?
optionA: The method is validated by the web framework entirely automatically
optionB: URLs with verbs cannot be versioned consistently
optionC: URLs containing verbs are harder for people to read
optionD: Infrastructure between client and server acts on the method
correctAnswerText: Infrastructure between client and server acts on the method
explanation: Caches, proxies, retry logic and browsers all read it. Naming an action in the path throws away information that machines you do not control were going to use.

prompt: When should you break REST conventions deliberately?
optionA: When the operation genuinely is not a change to one resource
optionB: When the client is one you also control yourself
optionC: When performance would be better with a different shape
optionD: When the team finds the conventions rather inconvenient to follow
correctAnswerText: When the operation genuinely is not a change to one resource
explanation: A POSTed search or a batch endpoint is an honest exception. Contorting a transfer into a PUT to stay pure serves nobody, and neither does abandoning the model wholesale.

prompt: An API uses a non-standard but consistent convention. Should you follow it or fix it?
optionA: Fix it only in the endpoints you are adding yourself
optionB: Follow it, but document the exceptions you introduce
optionC: Fix it, since the standards exist in order to be followed everywhere
optionD: Follow it — a mixture is worse for callers than either alone
correctAnswerText: Follow it — a mixture is worse for callers than either alone
explanation: Predictability is the product. Fixing it means migrating everything at once or living with two schemes, and the second is what usually happens.

prompt: What changes when an API is internal rather than public?
optionA: Authentication is no longer required on the endpoints
optionB: You can see every caller, so changes become negotiable
optionC: Conventions stop mattering because the team knows the API
optionD: Versioning becomes unnecessary for any change
correctAnswerText: You can see every caller, so changes become negotiable
explanation: Knowing the callers is what makes a breaking change a coordination problem rather than an impossible one. It does not make the conventions less useful.

prompt: Pure resource endpoints can force a client into many calls. What is the trade?
optionA: Simpler server code against simpler client code
optionB: Fewer round trips against endpoints shaped for one screen
optionC: Faster responses against responses that are easier to cache
optionD: Smaller payloads against fewer authentication checks
correctAnswerText: Fewer round trips against endpoints shaped for one screen
explanation: An endpoint built for a screen becomes a maintenance burden when the screen changes. An expand parameter is the usual compromise, and GraphQL is the other answer.

prompt: Why use standard status codes rather than your own scheme?
optionA: Standard codes are transmitted more efficiently
optionB: Everything between the client and server already understands them
optionC: Custom codes cannot be logged by most servers
optionD: Custom codes are simply not permitted by the HTTP specification itself
correctAnswerText: Everything between the client and server already understands them
explanation: Load balancers retry 503s, caches respect 404s, client libraries throw on 4xx. A private scheme opts out of all of it for no gain.

prompt: Reviewing a new endpoint, which question is most revealing?
optionA: Has the endpoint been added to the documentation?
optionB: Is the response body as small as it really could reasonably be made?
optionC: Does the endpoint follow the project naming convention?
optionD: What happens if this is called twice, and is the URL guessable?
correctAnswerText: What happens if this is called twice, and is the URL guessable?
explanation: The first half catches the non-idempotent retry; the second catches the verb in the path. Two questions that between them cover most of what goes wrong.

prompt: Why is a URL harder to change than the code behind it?
optionA: Search engines will already have indexed the original address by then
optionB: URLs are recorded in the logs of every request made
optionC: Routing configuration is harder to modify than code
optionD: It is in callers you cannot see, and in clients you cannot update
correctAnswerText: It is in callers you cannot see, and in clients you cannot update
explanation: Hardcoded in a mobile build from last year, in a partner's integration, in somebody's script. The implementation behind it can be rewritten freely.

prompt: When is REST the wrong model for an interface?
optionA: When the domain is operations and events rather than things
optionB: When the client and the server are written in different languages
optionC: When the API will be called more than a certain number of times
optionD: When the data does not fit into a relational database
correctAnswerText: When the domain is operations and events rather than things
explanation: A workflow engine or a streaming feed is not a set of resources. Forcing it into nouns produces a model nobody can predict, which was the only reason for the nouns.

prompt: What is REST fundamentally buying you?
optionA: A design that performs better than the alternatives
optionB: A caller can predict your API from having used other ones
optionC: A guarantee that the API can always be changed safely later
optionD: A structure that maps directly onto database tables
correctAnswerText: A caller can predict your API from having used other ones
explanation: Every rule here serves that prediction. When a rule stops making the API more predictable, following it has stopped being the point.

prompt: What is SQL injection?
optionA: Sending so many queries that the database eventually becomes overloaded
optionB: User input being treated as part of the query instead of a value
optionC: Inserting rows into a table that should have been read-only
optionD: Reading data from a database you are not authorised to see
correctAnswerText: User input being treated as part of the query instead of a value
explanation: Data crossing into instructions. The other options describe real problems that are not this one, and that this defence would not prevent.

prompt: What is cross-site scripting?
optionA: Attacker content being rendered as script in another user's browser
optionB: An attacker intercepting the scripts as they travel across the network
optionC: A site making requests to another site without permission
optionD: Scripts from one domain reading cookies set by another
correctAnswerText: Attacker content being rendered as script in another user's browser
explanation: The same failure as SQL injection, in HTML rather than SQL: data became instructions. The victim is another user rather than the database.

prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
optionA: Checking a password, against checking a token
optionB: Logging in, against staying logged in afterwards
optionC: Who you are, against what you are allowed to do
optionD: Verifying a user, against verifying a device
correctAnswerText: Who you are, against what you are allowed to do
explanation: Two separate checks, and forgetting the second is the commonest access-control bug: a logged-in user reaching somebody else's data.

prompt: How should passwords be stored?
optionA: Stored as written, in a database that is itself encrypted
optionB: Hashed with a fast algorithm such as SHA-256
optionC: Encrypted, so they can be decrypted if a user forgets
optionD: Hashed with a slow algorithm designed for passwords
correctAnswerText: Hashed with a slow algorithm designed for passwords
explanation: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2. Slowness is the feature: it makes guessing expensive, which a fast hash does not.

prompt: What does HTTPS protect?
optionA: The application from having its code stolen
optionB: The server from ever receiving any malicious requests at all
optionC: Data while it is stored in the database
optionD: Data while it travels between the browser and the server
correctAnswerText: Data while it travels between the browser and the server
explanation: In transit only. A site on HTTPS can still have SQL injection, weak passwords and broken access control — the padlock says nothing about any of them.

prompt: What does least privilege mean?
optionA: Users should be given as few accounts as possible
optionB: Every account has only the access its job requires
optionC: Administrative access should be shared between people
optionD: New users start with no access until they request it
correctAnswerText: Every account has only the access its job requires
explanation: It bounds the damage when something is compromised. An application whose database user cannot DROP TABLE survives an injection far better.

prompt: Why must secrets never be committed to a repository?
optionA: Version control systems log every value that is read
optionB: Secrets become invalid once they are written to a file
optionC: They stay in the history even after being deleted
optionD: Repositories are not encrypted while they are stored
correctAnswerText: They stay in the history even after being deleted
explanation: Deleting the line does not remove it from the history, and the repository may have been cloned already. Rotating the secret is the only real remedy.

prompt: What is an insecure direct object reference?
optionA: Allowing an object to be modified by two different users at once
optionB: Referring to an object that has already been deleted
optionC: Exposing internal database ids in a public API
optionD: Changing an id in a URL and getting somebody else's record
correctAnswerText: Changing an id in a URL and getting somebody else's record
explanation: The server authenticated the user and never checked whether that record was theirs. Exposing ids is only a problem when this check is missing.

prompt: Why do outdated dependencies matter for security?
optionA: Old libraries run more slowly than current versions
optionB: Published vulnerabilities tell attackers exactly what to try
optionC: Older code was written long before security was properly understood
optionD: Outdated packages are removed from public registries
correctAnswerText: Published vulnerabilities tell attackers exactly what to try
explanation: A fix being published is also an announcement of what was broken. Anyone can then scan for systems that have not applied it.

prompt: Why can the client never be trusted?
optionA: Everything it sends can be changed before it arrives
optionB: Browsers may be several versions out of date
optionC: Client code runs rather more slowly than server code does
optionD: Users may not have JavaScript enabled at all
correctAnswerText: Everything it sends can be changed before it arrives
explanation: A request is just text, and anyone can send one with curl. The browser is a convenience for honest users, never a control on dishonest ones.

prompt: Why does a parameterised query stop SQL injection completely?
optionA: The value is encrypted while it travels to the database
optionB: The database automatically escapes any dangerous characters found in the value
optionC: The driver rejects values containing SQL keywords
optionD: The query is parsed before the value arrives, so it cannot become syntax
correctAnswerText: The query is parsed before the value arrives, so it cannot become syntax
explanation: Structure and data travel separately, so no value can change the shape of the statement. That is why it works where escaping only mostly works.

prompt: Why is blocking dangerous characters a weak defence?
optionA: Character filters cannot be applied to numeric input
optionB: Blocking those characters makes the whole application measurably slower to run
optionC: Legitimate users rarely type any dangerous characters
optionD: You must anticipate every encoding; the attacker needs one you missed
correctAnswerText: You must anticipate every encoding; the attacker needs one you missed
explanation: An asymmetric fight you have to win every time. It also rejects O'Brien and any password with a quote in it.

prompt: Should XSS be prevented when data is stored or when it is displayed?
optionA: Neither — the browser prevents it automatically
optionB: When it is displayed, because the safe form depends on the context
optionC: When it is stored, so that the database only ever holds safe values
optionD: Both, so that the data is escaped twice over
correctAnswerText: When it is displayed, because the safe form depends on the context
explanation: HTML, an attribute, a URL and JavaScript all need different escaping. Escaping on the way in mangles the data and still gets one context wrong.

prompt: What does a salt achieve?
optionA: The password is made longer before it is hashed
optionB: The hash becomes impossible to reverse by any method
optionC: The hashing then takes much longer, which slows a determined attacker down
optionD: Identical passwords hash differently, so one crack does not break many
correctAnswerText: Identical passwords hash differently, so one crack does not break many
explanation: It defeats precomputed tables and stops a single result covering every user who chose the same password. Slowness is a separate property.

prompt: A user is logged in and requests /invoices/993. What must the server check?
optionA: That the id is a number within the expected range
optionB: That the user is logged in and the session is valid
optionC: That invoice 993 belongs to this particular user
optionD: That the invoice exists and has not been deleted
correctAnswerText: That invoice 993 belongs to this particular user
explanation: Authentication is already done; this is the authorisation half. Skipping it is broken access control, and it is consistently among the most common flaws found.

prompt: A delete button is hidden from non-admins. Is the delete endpoint protected?
optionA: Yes, provided the button is removed server-side
optionB: Only if the endpoint is also hidden from the documentation
optionC: No — anyone can call the endpoint directly
optionD: Yes, since the button is the only way to reach it
correctAnswerText: No — anyone can call the endpoint directly
explanation: Hiding a control changes what a user sees, not what the server accepts. Every endpoint needs its own check, whatever the interface shows.

prompt: Why should stack traces never be returned to users?
optionA: They are far too long for most clients to display properly
optionB: They make the application appear unprofessional
optionC: They may contain the user's own personal data
optionD: They reveal the framework, structure and versions in use
correctAnswerText: They reveal the framework, structure and versions in use
explanation: A map of what to attack: library versions with known vulnerabilities, file paths, table names. A reference id gives support the same information privately.

prompt: Why should a failed login say "email or password is incorrect" rather than which?
optionA: Saying which confirms whether that email has an account
optionB: Users find the combined message rather easier to understand
optionC: The specific message takes longer to generate
optionD: The specific message would need to be translated
correctAnswerText: Saying which confirms whether that email has an account
explanation: Otherwise the login form becomes a tool for checking who is registered. Response timing can leak the same thing, which is why the check is done either way.

prompt: How does cross-site request forgery work?
optionA: An attacker guesses your session identifier by brute force alone
optionB: An attacker steals your session cookie and replays it
optionC: Another site makes your browser send a request with your cookies
optionD: A script on your page sends data to an attacker's server
correctAnswerText: Another site makes your browser send a request with your cookies
explanation: The browser attaches your cookies to any request to that site, whoever caused it. The attacker never sees the response — they only need the effect.

prompt: What does defence in depth mean?
optionA: Every single layer of the application should be tested separately
optionB: The most important data should be protected most strongly
optionC: Security should be reviewed in depth before each release
optionD: No single failure should be enough to compromise the system
correctAnswerText: No single failure should be enough to compromise the system
explanation: Assume any one control will fail, because eventually one does. Least privilege is this applied to accounts.

prompt: A search builds its WHERE clause from optional user filters. How do you keep it safe?
optionA: Run the query as a database user with read-only access
optionB: Build the structure in code and pass every value as a parameter
optionC: Escape each of the values before putting it into the query string
optionD: Reject any value that contains a SQL keyword or quote
correctAnswerText: Build the structure in code and pass every value as a parameter
explanation: Structure from your code, values as parameters. The read-only user is a good idea and is a second layer, not a substitute for the first.

prompt: A sort column comes from the user and cannot be a query parameter. What do you do?
optionA: Match it against a fixed list of permitted column names
optionB: Strip any characters that are not letters or underscores
optionC: Escape it carefully before inserting it into the query
optionD: Wrap it in quotes so the database treats it as a value
correctAnswerText: Match it against a fixed list of permitted column names
explanation: Where parameters cannot reach, an allowlist can. It is one of the few places a blocklist tempts people, and one of the few where the safe set is genuinely small.

prompt: Your framework escapes output by default. When does XSS still occur?
optionA: When the same value is displayed in more than one place
optionB: When code deliberately bypasses it to render raw HTML
optionC: When the page is rendered on the server rather than the client
optionD: When the user input contains characters the framework misses
correctAnswerText: When code deliberately bypasses it to render raw HTML
explanation: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, |safe. Modern XSS is almost always an explicit opt-out, which makes it something you can search the codebase for.

prompt: What is the most reliable way to stop a user reading another user's records?
optionA: Load the record first, then check its ownership before returning it
optionB: Check the referring page before serving the record
optionC: Use identifiers that are too long to guess by hand
optionD: Include the user id in the query, so a foreign row is never loaded
correctAnswerText: Include the user id in the query, so a foreign row is never loaded
explanation: Scoping the query makes the wrong row unreachable rather than merely rejected. Load-then-check is correct and relies on the check never being forgotten.

prompt: What is the right shape for input validation?
optionA: Define what is dangerous and reject those values
optionB: Define what is acceptable and reject everything else
optionC: Accept everything and then escape it wherever it is used
optionD: Accept everything and check it when it is read back
correctAnswerText: Define what is acceptable and reject everything else
explanation: An allowlist fails closed; a blocklist fails open on whatever you did not think of. The attacker only has to find one thing you missed.

prompt: A site accepts profile picture uploads. What is the most important precaution?
optionA: Rename each file to a randomly generated identifier
optionB: Limit the size of the file that may be uploaded
optionC: Serve them from somewhere they can never be executed
optionD: Check that the file extension is a known image file type
correctAnswerText: Serve them from somewhere they can never be executed
explanation: An extension is a claim the uploader makes. Everything else on that list is worth doing, and none of it matters if the file can be executed.

prompt: What protects a login form against password guessing?
optionA: A password policy requiring symbols and numbers
optionB: A slow hash, which makes each attempt expensive
optionC: A login message that does not reveal which of the fields was wrong
optionD: Rate limiting by account and by source, with increasing delays
correctAnswerText: Rate limiting by account and by source, with increasing delays
explanation: The slow hash helps if the database leaks; it does not stop somebody trying ten thousand passwords against your live login. Limiting attempts does.

prompt: An API key was committed to a public repository last month. What must you do?
optionA: Make the repository private and continue using the key
optionB: Add the file to .gitignore so that it is never committed again
optionC: Rotate the key immediately, then remove it from the history
optionD: Remove the commit from the history and keep the key
correctAnswerText: Rotate the key immediately, then remove it from the history
explanation: Assume it was copied within minutes — scanners watch public repositories continuously. Rotation is the fix; cleaning the history is tidying up afterwards.

prompt: What should never appear in application logs?
optionA: The time each request took to be processed
optionB: The identifier of the user who made each request
optionC: Passwords, tokens, card numbers and full personal records
optionD: The endpoint that was called and the response status it returned
correctAnswerText: Passwords, tokens, card numbers and full personal records
explanation: Logs are copied, shipped to third parties and read by people with no access to the database. Logging a whole request body is the usual way this happens.

prompt: How should a team keep dependencies from becoming a liability?
optionA: Pinning every version so nothing changes unexpectedly
optionB: Automated scanning and small regular updates
optionC: A full review of every dependency once a year
optionD: Using only dependencies from well-known publishers
correctAnswerText: Automated scanning and small regular updates
explanation: Small and regular is what keeps it possible; a year of deferred upgrades becomes a project nobody schedules. Pinning without updating is how systems get stranded.

prompt: Orders are arriving with a total of one penny. The checkout sends the price in the request. What happened?
optionA: A discount code was applied more times than allowed
optionB: The currency conversion was applied incorrectly
optionC: A rounding error reduced the totals to a penny
optionD: Somebody edited the request before it was sent
correctAnswerText: Somebody edited the request before it was sent
explanation: The price belongs to the server, which knows what things cost. Anything the client sends is a suggestion, and the browser is not the only thing that can send one.

prompt: Logs show one account requesting /invoices/1 through /invoices/50000. What is being attempted?
optionA: A denial of service attack against the invoice endpoint
optionB: A crawler indexing the site for a search engine
optionC: A load test that was accidentally run against the production system
optionD: Enumeration, to find records the ownership check does not protect
correctAnswerText: Enumeration, to find records the ownership check does not protect
explanation: Sequential ids make it trivial to try. Random ids slow it down; only the ownership check actually stops it.

prompt: A script runs for every user who views one particular profile. Where did it come from?
optionA: It was saved in a profile field and is rendered unescaped
optionB: It was introduced by a man-in-the-middle on the connection
optionC: It was injected into the page by a browser extension
optionD: It was served from a compromised third-party script
correctAnswerText: It was saved in a profile field and is rendered unescaped
explanation: Stored XSS: the payload is in your database and fires for every visitor. That is what makes it more serious than the reflected kind.

prompt: A normal user reached the admin dashboard by typing its URL. What was the flaw?
optionA: The page checked only that the user was logged in
optionB: The navigation menu was showing the wrong links
optionC: The admin URL was easier to guess than expected
optionD: The user was given an administrator role by mistake
correctAnswerText: The page checked only that the user was logged in
explanation: Authentication without authorisation. Hiding the link from the menu was the only thing keeping ordinary users out, and a link is not a control.

prompt: A site emails you your existing password when you click "forgot password". What does that prove?
optionA: The site keeps a separate copy for support purposes
optionB: The email was generated before the password was hashed
optionC: The password is stored in a form the site can reverse
optionD: The password was cached from the last successful login
correctAnswerText: The password is stored in a form the site can reverse
explanation: A hash cannot be reversed, so anything that can send you the original was never hashed. A reset link is the only correct behaviour.

prompt: "We are on HTTPS, so the application is secure." What is wrong with that?
optionA: HTTPS only protects requests, not the responses
optionB: HTTPS certificates expire and are quite often not renewed in time
optionC: HTTPS protects the channel and nothing about the application
optionD: HTTPS can be downgraded to HTTP by an attacker
correctAnswerText: HTTPS protects the channel and nothing about the application
explanation: Injection, broken access control and weak password storage are all entirely unaffected. A phishing site has a padlock too.

prompt: Passwords have been found in the application logs. How does this usually happen?
optionA: An error handler printed the exception that contained it
optionB: The logging library stores every variable in memory
optionC: The password field was named in a way that bypassed masking
optionD: A whole request body was logged for debugging and left in
correctAnswerText: A whole request body was logged for debugging and left in
explanation: Logs go to places the database never goes — third-party aggregators, support tooling, a laptop. Logging whole payloads is how sensitive data escapes quietly.

prompt: Records have appeared with values the form does not allow. How?
optionA: The form validation was disabled by a browser setting
optionB: The records were all created before the validation was ever added
optionC: The validation rules differ between browsers
optionD: The request was sent without going through the form at all
correctAnswerText: The request was sent without going through the form at all
explanation: curl, Postman, a script, an old mobile build. Client validation is a convenience for honest users and is invisible to everybody else.

prompt: A system was compromised through a library flaw published eighteen months earlier. What failed?
optionA: The library author failed to notify the users of the flaw
optionB: Nothing was watching for published vulnerabilities in dependencies
optionC: The attacker had unusually detailed knowledge of the internal system
optionD: The system was running on an unsupported operating system
correctAnswerText: Nothing was watching for published vulnerabilities in dependencies
explanation: No skill was required — the vulnerability and often the exploit were public. Most breaches use something that was fixed long before.

prompt: Reviewing an application for security, where do you look first?
optionA: The encryption being used for all of the data stored inside the database
optionB: The firewall rules and the network configuration
optionC: The strength of the password policy being enforced
optionD: Everywhere untrusted input enters, and every endpoint's access check
correctAnswerText: Everywhere untrusted input enters, and every endpoint's access check
explanation: Injection and broken access control are where the real incidents come from. Network configuration matters and is rarely what let somebody in.

prompt: What do SQL injection, XSS and command injection have in common?
optionA: All three are prevented by validating user input
optionB: All three require the attacker to be authenticated
optionC: Data was allowed to become instructions
optionD: All three depend on a flaw in a third-party library
correctAnswerText: Data was allowed to become instructions
explanation: One mistake in three languages, so one defence in three shapes: keep structure and data apart rather than trying to recognise dangerous input.

prompt: Why is a structural defence better than a careful one?
optionA: Structural defences are faster to execute at runtime
optionB: Vigilance fails eventually; a structure that forbids it does not
optionC: Structural defences can be verified by automated tooling more easily
optionD: Careful defences require more code to be written
correctAnswerText: Vigilance fails eventually; a structure that forbids it does not
explanation: A query builder that cannot concatenate, a template that always escapes, a query scoped by user id. The safe path becomes the only path.

prompt: What happens when security controls are made too burdensome?
optionA: The application becomes measurably slower to use
optionB: People find ways around them, and the system ends up less safe
optionC: The controls stop being applied to new features
optionD: Users eventually move to a competitor that has fewer restrictions
correctAnswerText: People find ways around them, and the system ends up less safe
explanation: Thirty-day password rotation produced Password1, Password2. A control people route around is worse than a weaker one they follow.
